Install a server DNS customised (as BIND) in an instance EC2 the VPC, configured as conditional forwarder for both directions.
Return to private hosted public area, allowing servers DNS on-premises to consult over the internet.
Configure only one Route 53 Solve inbound endpoint to deal with resolution DNS bidirectional between on-premises and VPC.
questions.explanation: Inbound endpoints of Route 53 Solving allows you to consult DNS originating outside the VPC (as on-premises servers) are solved by solving the VPC, including records of private hosted areas; outbound endpoints with referral rules allow you to VPC forward specific domain queries (such as body.example.internal) to servers DNS on-premises. Together, on the existing hybrid connection, meet bidirectional resolution without exposing DNS Publicly.
questions.hint: Think of the two types of endpoint of Route 53 Solve: one for queries that enter the VPC coming from outside, and another for consultations that come out of VPC towards external servers.
optionRationales: Inbound endpoints of Route 53 Solving allows you to consult DNS originating outside the VPC (as on-premises servers) are solved by solving the VPC, including records of private hosted areas; outbound endpoints with referral rules allow you to VPC forward specific domain queries (such as body.example.internal) to servers DNS on-premises. Together, on the existing hybrid connection, meet bidirectional resolution without exposing DNS Publicly.

Convert area to public display records DNS the Internet, violating the requirement not to expose the DNS Publicly, and still would not solve the reverse direction (resources of the VPC solving on-premises names).

Inbound endpoints deal only with queries that reach the VPC from outside; solving on-premises domains from resources within the VPC requires outbound endpoints with forwarding rules — a single inbound endpoint does not cover both directions.

This customized solution requires operation and maintenance of a server DNS in its own, reimplementing with significant effort a functionality that the Route 53 Solving already offers natively, managed and highly available through your input and output endpoints.

questions.text: A company has standardized the use of a third-party virtual firewall application (available in the AWS Marketplace) for deep packet inspection, and needs to insert this application in a transparent way in the traffic flow of multiple VPCs through a VPC Centralized inspection, with automatic scaling according to the volume of traffic and ensuring that the return traffic of a flow passes through MESMA application instance (symmetric rotation). Which architecture meets this requirement?
options: Use AWS Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) to distribute traffic between a fleet of third-party firewall application instances in VPC Centralized Inspection, with Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints (GWLBe) in Spoke VPCs (or via Transit Gateway) directing traffic transparently to applications.
Use one Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic between the instances of the firewall application.
Install the firewall application in a single instance EC2 large capacity in each VPC, routing all the traffic to it through entries in the route table.
Use AWS Network firewall to execute third-party firewall application AWS Marketplace within the VPC Centralized Inspection.
questions.explanation: The Gateway Load Balancer was designed specifically to insert third-party applications (firewalls), IDS/IPS) transparently in the traffic flow, operating in the layer 3 with encapsulation GENEVE; it guarantees 'flow stickiness' (symmetric rotation, maintaining a flow in the same instance of the application) and automatically scales the fleet of applications according to the volume of traffic, meeting all the requirements.
questions.hint: Think about the type of load balancer specifically designed to insert transparent third-party applications on the road to traffic, ensuring that traffic from the same flow always returns to the same instance.
optionRationales: The Gateway Load Balancer was designed specifically to insert third-party applications (firewalls), IDS/IPS) transparently in the traffic flow, operating in the layer 3 with encapsulation GENEVE; it guarantees 'flow stickiness' (symmetric rotation, maintaining a flow in the same instance of the application) and automatically scales the fleet of applications according to the volume of traffic, meeting all the requirements.

The AWS Network Firewall is the own managed firewall service AWS (based on Suricata) and does not allow execution of virtual applications of third parties of AWS Marketplace within it; it does not meet the requirement to use the specific application already standardized by the company.

The Application Load Balancer operates in the layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and terminates connections, which is inadequate for inspection of network traffic in layer 3/4 by a firewall application, besides not preserving the original headers necessary for inspection and not offering symmetrical flow routing.

A single instance represents a single point of failure and a fixed scalability limit, without automatic scaling, health check and symmetrical flow routing that the Gateway Load Balancer natively provides for fleets of applications.

questions.text: The security team suspects that an instance EC2 committed is exfiltrating large volumes of data to an unknown external IP address over several months. They need to analyze historical network flow data from all VPCs to identify abnormal patterns of output data transfer (e.g. sustained bytes count for a specific destination), economically, without high storage/consult costs for a multiple-month history. What approach meets this requirement?
options: Use data events of AWS CloudTrail for S3 and EC2 to identify the exfiltration, since the CloudTrail records all network traffic.

Ensure that VPC Flow Logs are enabled and delivered to a pocket Amazon S3 (in Parquet format, partitioned by date), and use the Amazon Athena to carry out queries SQL on the historical data of flow logs, filtering and adding by transferred bytes, IPs of origin/destination and time interval.
Enable VPC Flow Logs delivered only to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and use the CloudWatch Logs Insights to consult several months of historical data.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty and rely exclusively on your finding to identify the specific flow of exfiltration and destination IP, without analyzing the flow logs.
questions.explanation: Deliver VPC Flow Logs to S3 in partitioned Parquet format significantly reduces the storage cost and data volume scanned by query; Amazon Athena allows queries SQL ad-hoc about months of historical data, filtering by transferred bytes and specific IPs, in an economical and scalable way — ideal to identify patterns of exfiltration over time.
questions.hint: Think of the combination of a low-cost storage destination for historical network flow data in columnar format and a query service SQL on request.
optionRationales: Deliver VPC Flow Logs to S3 in partitioned Parquet format significantly reduces the storage cost and data volume scanned by query; Amazon Athena allows queries SQL ad-hoc about months of historical data, filtering by transferred bytes and specific IPs, in an economical and scalable way — ideal to identify patterns of exfiltration over time.

Maintain several months of high volume flow logs in CloudWatch Logs has a significantly higher storage cost than in S3, and consultations of the CloudWatch Logs Insights on large volumes of historical data tend to be slower and more expensive than queries Athena on data partitioned in columnal format in S3.

The GuardDuty may generate a relevant finding (e.g. abnormal volume of traffic), but for a detailed forensic analysis of historical flow patterns (bytes over time, IPs/specific ports for months), it is necessary to direct analysis of flow logs, which the GuardDuty does not replace.

The CloudTrail records calls from API (management and service data events supported), non-gross network traffic between IP addresses; it would not capture a compromised instance exfiltrating data via a network socket directly to an arbitrary external IP.

questions.text: A company needs to ensure that TODO object sent to a pocket S3 specific is encrypted with a CMK of the KMS and that uploads that do not specify that encryption are REJEITADOS when uploading — regardless of permissions IAM granted to the user who is uploading (deep defense). Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Enable default encryption of the pocket with SSE-KMS using the CMK designated, without any additional Bucket Policy.
Create a rule of AWS Configure ('s3-Bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled') with automatic repair that re-crypts non-compliant objects after upload.
Attach to each user IAM a policy that requires the cryptography header in calls s3:PutObject.

Create a Bucket Policy with a Deny Instruction for Action s3:PutObject when the condition 's3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id' do not match ARN of CMK (or the cryptography header is not 'aws:kms').
questions.explanation: An explicit Deny Bucket Policy is evaluated independently of permissions IAM the main one that makes the request; condition this denial to the cryptography header (and the ID of the CMK specific) ensures that any upload that does not specify the correct encryption is rejected at the resource level, even if the user has permissions IAM wide s3:PutObject.
questions.hint: Think about the type of policy applied directly to the resource (not to identity) that can deny an action based on conditions on the headings of the request itself, regardless of who does it.
optionRationales: An explicit Deny Bucket Policy is evaluated independently of permissions IAM the main one that makes the request; condition this denial to the cryptography header (and the ID of the CMK specific) ensures that any upload that does not specify the correct encryption is rejected at the resource level, even if the user has permissions IAM wide s3:PutObject.

Standard encryption automatically applies specified encryption to objects that do not explicitly specify an encryption configuration, but do not REJEITA uploads that explicitly specify a different encryption (or none depending on the client's configuration); it does not act as a rejection control.

A restriction only in politics IAM the user would not protect against uploads made by other identities (such as administrative roles) whose policy IAM does not include this restriction, not taking into account the requirement that rejection takes place regardless of the permissions IAM of applicant.
This approach is detective and reactive: the object is first accepted without the correct encryption and only then corrected, which does not meet the REJECTION requirement at the time of upload.

questions.text: Courts EC2 in private sub-networks (without NAT Gateway or Internet Gateway) run an application that makes frequent calls to kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey to describe data on the client's side. The security team requires that TODAS these calls from API to KMS remain within the private network of AWS, without any dependence on internet connectivity. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Provide one NAT Gateway in a public sub-network and route the outbound traffic of private sub-networks to the internet through it.
Use AWS Encryption SDK to make local cache of data keys, eliminating the need for calls to KMS.
Create a Gateway VPC Endpoint for the AWS KMS in private sub-networks.

Create a VPC Interface Endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink) for the AWS KMS in private sub-networks, allowing for the EC2 make calls from API to KMS through private connectivity, without need of internet access.
questions.explanation: The AWS KMS offers support to VPC Interface Endpoints via PrivateLink, allowing calls from API as kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey are made entirely through the private network of AWS, without depending on a NAT Gateway, Internet Gateway or any route to the public internet.
questions.hint: Think about the specific type of VPC Endpoint KMS supports, based on technology that provides private connectivity to services of the AWS through a network interface in the sub-network.
optionRationales: The AWS KMS offers support to VPC Interface Endpoints via PrivateLink, allowing calls from API as kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey are made entirely through the private network of AWS, without depending on a NAT Gateway, Internet Gateway or any route to the public internet.

The AWS KMS does not support Gateway VPC Endpoints — this type of endpoint is only available for Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB; for the KMS, the type of endpoint supported is the Interface Endpoint via PrivateLink.

Although one NAT Gateway allow the bodies to reach the public endpoint of the KMS, this makes calls depend on connectivity with the internet (even within the backbone of the AWS), violating the explicit requirement of no internet dependence, besides incuring data processing costs of the NAT Gateway.

Data key cache reduces call frequency to KMS, but does not completely eliminate the need for periodic calls (when the cache expires) nor does it establish private connectivity for such calls by itself — does not solve the network path requirement.

questions.text: In a security audit, the team needs to check, in a complex architecture with multiple route tables, NACLs, Security Groups, peering connections and attachments to Transit Gateway, if there is any unintentional network path that allows access from the Internet (via Internet Gateway) even a set of sensitive internal databases — even if this path has never been effectively used. TODOS the possible paths that correspond to this unwanted access pattern throughout the network configuration?
options: AWS Network Access Analyzer, defining a Network Access Scope that describes the unwanted access pattern (e.g., a Internet Gateway even resources with the tag 'sensitive'), generating finding for all network paths that correspond to this scope.
Use security checks of the AWS Trusted Advisor to identify Security Groups with open rules.
Analyze the VPC Flow Logs with Amazon Athena to identify traffic originating from the internet towards internal databases.
VPC Reachability Analyzer, testing the connectivity between a specific pair of origin and destination.
questions.explanation: The AWS Network Access Analyzer was designed to analyze the entire network configuration (road tables), NACLs, Security Groups, peering, Transit Gateway, etc.) in search of paths that correspond to a user-defined Network Access Scope, proactively identifying unintentional access paths — even if never used — without requiring point-to-point manual testing.
questions.hint: Think of the service that allows you to formally define an unwanted 'access scope' and sweep all network configuration in search of any possible path that satisfies it, even if it has never been used.
optionRationales: The AWS Network Access Analyzer was designed to analyze the entire network configuration (road tables), NACLs, Security Groups, peering, Transit Gateway, etc.) in search of paths that correspond to a user-defined Network Access Scope, proactively identifying unintentional access paths — even if never used — without requiring point-to-point manual testing.

The Reachability Analyzer tests point-to-point connectivity between a specific source and destination, being useful to diagnose a known connectivity problem; it was not designed to scan the entire network for TODOS the paths that correspond to a general pattern of unwanted access among many resources.

The VPC Flow Logs show the traffic effectively observed, not potential paths that could exist in the configuration but were never used; this analysis would not identify an unintentional path that has not yet been explored.

The Trusted Advisor offers general checks of good practice (such as Security Groups with open doors), but does not perform an analysis of end-to-end network paths through multiple components (wheels), NACLs, peering, Transit Gateway) to identify a specific unwanted access scope.

questions.text: An event-oriented architecture uses rows Amazon SQS and topics Amazon SNS to transmit messages containing sensitive customer data (PII) a compliance requirement determines that the body of these messages is encrypted EM REPOUSO while in line/topic, using a key under company control (rotational and auditable). Which configuration meets this requirement with the least implementation effort?
options: Trust only in transit encryption (TLS) of calls from API to SQS and SNS, since the messages remain in the queue/topic for a short time.
Replace SQS and the SNS by storing messages in pocket S3 with SSE-KMS, since the S3 natively supports cryptography with KMS.
Encrypt the body of messages in the application layer using a key AES fixed embedded in the code, before publishing them in SQS/SNS.

Enable server side encryption (SSE) in rows SQS and on topics SNS using a CMK managed by the customer at AWS KMS, ensuring that producers and consumers are allowed kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt required.
questions.explanation: Both SQS the SNS natively support server side encryption (SSE) using a CMK of the client; this encrypts the body of the messages at rest while they remain in the queue/topic, with the key being fully controlled, rotateable and auditable (via CloudTrail) by the company, requiring only the configuration of the SSE and the permissions of KMS for producers/consumers.
questions.hint: Both the rows and the message topics of this architecture have native support for a specific type of cryptography at rest using customer-managed keys — it is not necessary to reinvent this in the application layer.
optionRationales: Both SQS the SNS natively support server side encryption (SSE) using a CMK of the client; this encrypts the body of the messages at rest while they remain in the queue/topic, with the key being fully controlled, rotateable and auditable (via CloudTrail) by the company, requiring only the configuration of the SSE and the permissions of KMS for producers/consumers.

Encryption in transit (TLS) protects the data during transmission to/from the service, but does not meet the explicit requirement that the body of the message be encrypted EM REPOUSO while stored in the queue or topic, nor does it provide a key under company control/audit for those stored data.

This approach introduces a significant burden of key management (safe storage, rotation, auditing of a custom key) that the KMS it is natively solved; encrypting with a fixed key embedded in the code is also a bad safety practice compared to the SSE native based CMK.

Replace rows and topics by storage in S3 would fundamentally change the event-oriented decoupling architecture (files/pub-sub) to an object storage model, an unnecessary change since both the SQS the SNS support natively SSE with customer CMKs.

questions.text: A SaaS company exposes a service through a AWS PrivateLink VPC Endpoint Service. SOMENTE a specific list of account IDs AWS (your paying customers) can create Interface VPC Endpoints connecting to this service — connection requests from any other account AWS must be automatically rejected — and new customers added to the list without requiring individual manual approval for each connection attempt.?
options: Restrict access using a Security Group no Network Load Balancer behind the service, allowing only the blocks CIDR of customers' VPCs.
Enable 'Acceptance required' no VPC Endpoint Service, and have a team member manually approving each connection request as you arrive.

Configure the VPC Endpoint Service with 'Acceptance required' disabled, and add main account RNAs AWS Allowed (paying customers) to the list of permitted service principals (via ModifyVpcEndpointServicePermissions).
Use a resource-based policy in a IAM roll to control which accounts can create the VPC Endpoint Service.
questions.explanation: The list of 'allowed mains' of a VPC Endpoint Service determines which accounts AWS can create Interface VPC Endpoints for service; with 'Acceptance required' disabled, account connections present in this list are automatically established (without manual approval), while off-list attempts are automatically rejected — meeting both requirements.
questions.hint: Think about the configuration of your own VPC Endpoint Service which defines, in a self-service manner, which accounts AWS are allowed to connect without requiring manual approval for each new request.
optionRationales: The list of 'allowed mains' of a VPC Endpoint Service determines which accounts AWS can create Interface VPC Endpoints for service; with 'Acceptance required' disabled, account connections present in this list are automatically established (without manual approval), while off-list attempts are automatically rejected — meeting both requirements.

This approach directly contradicts the requirement that new customers be added without requiring individual manual approval for each connection attempt, and does not scale operationally as the number of customers grows.

In connections via PrivateLink, the blocks CIDR of the VPCs of customers are not directly visible or relevant to the Security Groups of the provider in the form required for an account AWS, in addition to CIDRs of customers can overlap or be unknown by the provider; access control to the service is done by the list of main allowed, not by Security Groups.

Control of which accounts AWS can connect to a VPC Endpoint Service is done through the list of 'allowed mains' configured directly in the service itself (ModifyVpcEndpointServicePermissions), not through policies based on resource IAM roles.

questions.text: A company is going through an audit SOC 2 and PCI DSS, and the external auditor requests compliance reports from himself AWS (as reports SOC and certifications ISO) and review/acceptance of agreements such as Business Associate Addendum (BAA), as evidence that the underlying infrastructure of AWS meet relevant standards. Where the team can quickly obtain these reports and agreements, under self-service regime, without opening a call for support?
options: Conformity Packages AWS Config, which automatically generates certification reports SOC and PCI DSS of AWS.
AWS Trusted Advisor, providing compliance reports on the infrastructure of the AWS specific to the customer account.
AWS Audit Manager, which automatically collects certifications SOC and PCI DSS of AWS to attach to the client's audit reports.

AWS Artifact, a self-service portal that provides on-demand access to compliance reports from the AWS (SOC, PCI DSS, certifications ISO) and allows to review and accept agreements such as the BAA and NDAs.
questions.explanation: The AWS Artifact it was specifically designed as a self-service portal for downloading audit reports and compliance certifications of its own AWS (SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, among others), in addition to allowing the online review and acceptance of agreements such as the Business Associate Addendum, meeting exactly the need for audit.
questions.hint: Think of the self-service portal created specifically to provide customers with third-party audit reports on the infrastructure itself of the AWS and legal agreements related to compliance.
optionRationales: The AWS Artifact it was specifically designed as a self-service portal for downloading audit reports and compliance certifications of its own AWS (SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, among others), in addition to allowing the online review and acceptance of agreements such as the Business Associate Addendum, meeting exactly the need for audit.

The Trusted Advisor provides specific recommendations on the resources of the customer's own account (cost, security, performance, limits), not third party audit reports on the overall infrastructure of the AWS required by an auditor SOC 2/PCI DSS.

Conformity Packages AWS Config evaluate the CONFIGURATION DOS RECURSOS DO CLIENTE in relation to a compliance framework, but do not generate or provide third-party audit reports on the infrastructure of its own AWS.

The AWS Audit Manager helps the customer to collect evidence about the USO QUE ELE FAZ of AWS to support their own audits; third-party audit reports on the infrastructure of the AWS in itself are obtained through the AWS Artifact.

questions.text: Several instances EC2, distributed in multiple AZs, mount a file system Amazon EFS shared containing sensitive financial records. A compliance requirement determines that the file system is encrypted EM REPOUSO and that all traffic NFS between the instances EC2 and the EFS is encrypted in a cross-section, with the least possible configuration complexity on the client's side. AMBOS requirements?
options: Create File System EFS with cryptography at rest enabled (using a CMK of the KMS, defined at the time of creation) and assemble it in the instances EC2 using the EFS mount helper (amazon-efs-useful) with the option 'tls', which automatically establishes a tunnel TLS for traffic NFS.
Enable rest cryptography in a file system EFS existing and unencrypted via the 'Modify' option on the console.
Trust only in rest cryptography, since the traffic of EFS remains within the network of the AWS and does not need additional cryptography in transit.
Configure a tunnel VPN IPsec between each instance EC2 and mount targets of EFS.
questions.explanation: Cryptography at rest of EFS is defined at the time of creation of the file system using a CMK of the KMS; o EFS mount helper with the option 'tls' automatically establishes (via stunnel) an encrypted tunnel for all traffic NFS between the customer and the EFS, meeting both requirements with minimum configuration on the customer side.
questions.hint: For both requirements (on rest and in transit), think of when each type of encryption should be defined and in which mounting utility already offers native support to one of these protections with a simple option.
optionRationales: Cryptography at rest of EFS is defined at the time of creation of the file system using a CMK of the KMS; o EFS mount helper with the option 'tls' automatically establishes (via stunnel) an encrypted tunnel for all traffic NFS between the customer and the EFS, meeting both requirements with minimum configuration on the customer side.

Just like it happens with the RDS, the cryptography at rest of the EFS can only be defined at the time of creation of the file system; it cannot be later enabled in an existing and unencrypted file system — it would be necessary to create a new encrypted file system and migrate the data (e.g. with AWS DataSync).

Stay within the network of AWS does not meet an explicit requirement for encryption in transit; traffic NFS is not encrypted by default, and the mount helper 'tls' option is required to meet this explicit compliance requirement.

The EFS does not require or is designed to use tunnels VPN IPsec for transit encryption; the supported and simple mechanism for this is the tls option embedded in the EFS mount helper, based on stunnel.

questions.text: An organization wants that relevant security events (such as GuardDuty and policy changes IAM detected via CloudTrail) generated in dozens of member accounts are automatically routed, in almost real time, to a custom event bus in a central security account, where automated response flows (Step Functions, Lambda) are activated — using an event-oriented architecture and weakly coupled, without polling. What configuration meets this requirement?
options: Configure each member account to publish events in a topic SNS in the central account, and have a function Lambda in the security account doing polling the GuardDuty in each account periodically.

In the central security account, create a custom event bus from Amazon EventBridge with a resource-based policy that allows PutEvents of the member accounts (using the condition) aws:MainOrgID); in each member account, create rules of the EventBridge which correspond to relevant events and have the central bus as the destination between accounts.
Use one AWS config aggregator in the security account to receive Findings from GuardDuty and policy changes IAM Member accounts.
Configure scheduled queries no CloudTrail Lake from the security account to periodically recover relevant events from member accounts.
questions.explanation: A custom event bus from EventBridge with resource policy allowing PutEvents of the entire organization (via aws:MainOrgID) allows rules of the EventBridge in each member account they send relevant events (such as GuardDuty, available in the standard event bar) directly to the central bar as a destination between accounts, in almost real time and without polling.
questions.hint: Think of the event routing service that allows rules in member accounts to send events directly to a custom bus on another account, controlled by a resource-based policy.
optionRationales: A custom event bus from EventBridge with resource policy allowing PutEvents of the entire organization (via aws:MainOrgID) allows rules of the EventBridge in each member account they send relevant events (such as GuardDuty, available in the standard event bar) directly to the central bar as a destination between accounts, in almost real time and without polling.

Do regular polling of API of the GuardDuty in dozens of accounts introduces latency, does not scale well and it is exactly the polling-based pattern that event-oriented architecture seeks to avoid, in contrast to routing by rules and busses of the EventBridge.

Aggregaters of the AWS config aggregates configuration data and resource compliance between accounts, not finding the GuardDuty or arbitrary events detected via CloudTrail; is not the appropriate mechanism to route these specific events.

The CloudTrail Lake allows you to consult historical events via SQL, but scheduled consultations represent a periodic polling model, not a router mechanism oriented to events in near real time, comparable to the barrages and rules of the EventBridge between accounts.

questions.text: A company uses AWS Backup to centrally manage instance backups RDS, volumes EBS and tables DynamoDB in multiple accounts via AWS Organizations. A new regulatory requirement determines that such backups are unchangeable for a minimum retention period — NEM MESMO an account administrator with total permissions in AWS Backup must be able to delete recovery points or reduce the retention period before its termination as ransomware protection. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Enable AWS Backup Vault Lock in Compliance mode in backup safe, with a defined minimum retention period.
Enable AWS Backup Vault Lock in Governance mode in the backup safe, with a defined minimum retention period.
Create a policy IAM denying backup action:DeleteRecoveryPoint for all roles except a roll named 'backup-admin''.
Enable S3 Object Lock in storage S3 underlying used by AWS Backup.
questions.explanation: The AWS Backup Vault Lock in Compliance mode prevents any user — including administrators with total permissions in AWS Backup and root user — excludes recovery points or reduces retention periods before the defined term; furthermore, Vault Lock itself cannot be removed during the compliance period, ensuring total immutability.
questions.hint: Think about the specific immutability mechanism of the managed backup service of AWS, equivalent in concept to the Object Lock of S3, but applied to backup safes.
optionRationales: The AWS Backup Vault Lock in Compliance mode prevents any user — including administrators with total permissions in AWS Backup and root user — excludes recovery points or reduces retention periods before the defined term; furthermore, Vault Lock itself cannot be removed during the compliance period, ensuring total immutability.

In Governance mode, users with specific permissions may still exclude recovery points or remove the vault lock before the end of the retention period, not meeting the requirement that NEM MESMO an administrator can do that.

The roll itself 'backup-admin' (or anyone with permission to change policies IAM) could still exclude recovery points or modify this policy, not offering the guarantee of immutability provided by Vault Lock in Compliance mode.

The AWS Backup stores recovery points in your own managed storage, not in a pocket S3 accessible by the customer where Object Lock can be configured directly; the equivalent immutability mechanism for the AWS Backup is Vault Lock.

questions.text: A multi-tenant application encrypts data from different clients using the MESMA CMK of the AWS KMS through calls kms:Encrypt/kms:Decrypt. The security team wants an additional layer of integrity and audit so that: (a) an encrypted ciphertext for the 'tenant A' cannot be successfully described if presented with the context of the 'tenant B', even using the same CMK; and (b) the logs of the CloudTrail clearly show which holder belongs to each cryptography/description call to KMS. What's the use of KMS responds to AMBOS requirements?
options: Embed the holder ID as a prefix in the clear text data before encryption, and validate this prefix in the application layer after description.

Use an encryption context (a set of key-value pairs, e.g.: {"tenant_id": "A"}) in every call kms:Encryption and kms:Decrypt; or KMS it uses as additional authenticated data (AAD) — the description fails if the context does not correspond exactly to the one used in the encryption — and the encryption context is recorded in clear text in the CloudTrail for each call from API of the KMS.
Trust the annual automatic rotation of the CMK to ensure that data from different holders are never described with incorrect key material.
Apply resource tags to CMK identifying each holder who uses it.
questions.explanation: The Encryption context of the KMS works as additional authenticated data (AAD): if the context provided in the call kms:Decrypt does not match exactly the one used during kms:Encrypt, operation fails cryptographically, even using the same CMK — meeting the requirement (a); moreover, the KMS records the context encryption in clear text in the events of CloudTrail, allowing to identify which holder each call refers to — meeting the requirement (b).
questions.hint: Think about the optional parameter that can be passed on encryption/description calls from KMS, which acts as additional authenticated data and also appears in the audit records of each call.
optionRationales: The Encryption context of the KMS works as additional authenticated data (AAD): if the context provided in the call kms:Decrypt does not match exactly the one used during kms:Encrypt, operation fails cryptographically, even using the same CMK — meeting the requirement (a); moreover, the KMS records the context encryption in clear text in the events of CloudTrail, allowing to identify which holder each call refers to — meeting the requirement (b).

This validation occurs only in the application layer, after the description has already been successful by KMS independently of the holder; or KMS would not refuse the operation for an incorrect context, and this approach does not generate any record by holding in the logs of the CloudTrail of calls to KMS.

Resource Tags on CMK are metadata applied to the key as a whole (helpful for organization, allocation of costs or ABAC on the key itself), but do not link a specific ciphertext to a tenant nor appear as context by call in the logs of the CloudTrail of individual cryptography/description operations.

The automatic key rotation periodically generates new cryptographic material, but the previous material is retained to describe old data; this rotation does not link a specific ciphertext to the context of a holder nor prevents cross-description between holders who share the same CMK.

questions.text: A SaaS company stores data from hundreds of customers (tenants) in a shared table of Amazon DynamoDB and in a pocket S3 shared. A new corporate client requires 'tenant cryptographic isolation': the ability to independently revoke access APENAS to the data of this client (disabling or scheduling the deletion of a key), without affecting the other tenants, and the guarantee that the data of this client were encrypted with a dedicated key, not shared with other tenants.?
options: Use SSE-S3 (AES-256 with keys of ownership of the AWS) for the data of each holder, since the AES-256 already offers strong encryption by object.
Partitioning the Tenants into Tables DynamoDB and prefixes S3 separate, depending on policy conditions IAM for isolation, without involving the KMS.

Use Envelope Encryption with a CMK of the AWS KMS dedicated by tenant; the items/objects of each tenant are encrypted using data keys generated from the CMK specific to the holder, allowing to disable or schedule the exclusion of the CMK of an individual holder to cryptographically revoke access only to his data.
Use a single CMK shared for all the tenants, applying policies IAM different by application roll of each holder.
questions.explanation: With a CMK dedicated by holding, disabling or deleting the key of a specific holding makes its cryptographic data inaccessible (even if the item/object still exists in shared storage), without affecting the data keys derived from the CMKs of other holding, precisely meeting the requirement of cryptographic isolation and revocation by holding.
questions.hint: Think of how envelope encryption, combined with a customer-managed key by entity, makes specific cryptographic data inaccessible without affecting other data that share the same physical storage.
optionRationales: With a CMK dedicated by holding, disabling or deleting the key of a specific holding makes its cryptographic data inaccessible (even if the item/object still exists in shared storage), without affecting the data keys derived from the CMKs of other holding, precisely meeting the requirement of cryptographic isolation and revocation by holding.

With a CMK shared, disable this key would affect TODOS the holders simultaneously; there is no way to cryptographically revoke the access to the data of a single holder independently when the underlying key material is shared by all.

The SSE-S3 uses keys property of the AWS without key separation for each holder and without the possibility of the customer disabling a key for a specific holder; offers confidentiality, but not cryptographic revocation at the holder level.

Partitioning based on access control (IAM) offers logical access isolation, but not CRIPTOGRAPHIC isolation; a compromised credentials or a poorly configured policy could still expose the data, and this approach does not offer the key-revocation mechanism required by the customer.

questions.text: A mobile application uses Amazon Cognito Identity Pools to provide temporary credentials to both authenticated users (via User Pool) and unauthenticated users ('guest', who navigate through public content before registering). The security team is concerned that the role IAM attributed to unauthenticated identities may be with excessive permissions, allowing guest users to access resources intended only for authenticated users. What is the recommended practice to mitigate this risk without eliminating the experience of 'navigating as a guest''?
options: Use a single roll IAM shared for authenticated and un authenticated identities, relying on application logic to prevent guests from calling sensitive APIs.
Allow unauthenticated role the managed AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess policy, since 'read only' is considered inherently safe for guest users.

Configure Two Roles IAM SEPARADAS in Identity Pool — one for authenticated identities and one for un authenticated identities — with the un authenticated role strictly restricted to the minimum permissions of reading/public content (last privilege), and periodically review this policy.
Completely disable unauthenticated access to Identity Pool, requiring all users, including visitors browsing public content, to log in via User Pool first.
questions.explanation: The Cognito Identity Pool allows you to associate roles IAM distinct for authenticated and unauthenticated identities; restricting the unauthenticated role to the minimum necessary (only public reading resources) ensures that guest credentials never be able to access actions or resources reserved for authenticated users, preserving the browsing experience as a guest with least privilege.
questions.hint: Remember that Identity Pool allows you to assign roles IAM different for each type of identity — the problem lies in the scope of the specific role policy, not in the unauthenticated access functionality itself.
optionRationales: The Cognito Identity Pool allows you to associate roles IAM distinct for authenticated and unauthenticated identities; restricting the unauthenticated role to the minimum necessary (only public reading resources) ensures that guest credentials never be able to access actions or resources reserved for authenticated users, preserving the browsing experience as a guest with least privilege.

Disableing unauthenticated access would eliminate the legitimate experience of 'navigating as a guest' before the registration the application requires, being an excessive correction rather than simply restricting correctly unauthenticated roller permissions.

Depending on customer-side logic for authorization control is insecure as a malicious user could bypass the application and use guest credentials directly to call any action allowed by the shared role, including actions intended for authenticated users.

AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess policy grants read access to TODOS the pocketes and objects S3 of the account, not only to those intended for public content, which could expose private newsletters to unauthenticated users, violating the principle of lesser privilege.

questions.text: A company wants access logs from Application Load Balancers, snapshots of AWS Config and other logs/exports generated by dozens of your accounts AWS Organizations are delivered to a pocket S3 centralized in a logging account — without individually listing each of the account IDs in the bucket policy, which would be difficult to maintain as accounts are added or removed from the organization. What configuration in the centralized bucket policy meets this requirement in a scalable way?
options: Grant the necessary permissions (ex.: s3:PutObject) to the mains in the policy of the pocket using a condition with aws:MainOrgID corresponding to the organization's ID, so that any current or future account within the organization is automatically authorized to deliver logs.
Create a Bucket S3 separate in each account and use S3 Cross-Region Replication to replicate the logs for the central bucket.
Individually list each account ID of the dozens of accounts as main allowed in the main element of the pocket policy.
Use one SCP to force all accounts to record logs only in the centralized bucket.
questions.explanation: The global condition aws:MainOrgID allows you to restrict access to any principal who belongs to the specified organization, without needing to list individual account IDs; new accounts added to the organization are automatically covered by the condition, and removed accounts automatically lose access, without requiring manual updates in the bucket policy.
questions.hint: Think about the overall political condition of the IAM which refers to the entire organization of the AWS Organizations, instead of individual account IDs.
optionRationales: The global condition aws:MainOrgID allows you to restrict access to any principal who belongs to the specified organization, without needing to list individual account IDs; new accounts added to the organization are automatically covered by the condition, and removed accounts automatically lose access, without requiring manual updates in the bucket policy.

This approach is operationally fragile: to each account added or removed from the organization, the bucket policy would need to be manually updated, and the AWS have a maximum size limit that could be reached with many listed account RNAs.

This approach adds unnecessary infrastructure (one bucket per account) and replication cost/configuration, when a single centralized bucket with an organization level condition is a much simpler solution.

SCPs restrict or allow which actions the main PODEM the centralised Bucket's policy of recourse is not granted by themselves the permission to RECEBER recording of these accounts; the policy of the pocket still needs to explicitly authorize access between accounts.

questions.text: A company maintains a hierarchy of private certification authority (CA root + CA subordinate) in AWS Certificate Manager Private CA, in a central security account, used to issue certificates TLS multiple application accounts need to issue certificates from this MESMA CA hierarchy — for all internal certificates to bind up to the same reliable root distributed to internal customers — without each account creating its own separate CA (which would require multiple reliable roots to be distributed).?
options: Create a hierarchy independent of ACM Private CA on each application account, distributing the separate root certificate from each account to all internal customers.

Share subordinate CA of ACM Private CA from the security account with the application accounts using the AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM); the application accounts can then apply for certificates via ACM issued by this shared CA, all chaining up to the same root.
Export CA's private key to the security account and import it into ACM Private CA of each application account.
Use a delegated administrator of the AWS Organizations for the ACM Private CA, so that application accounts automatically inherit a copy of CA.
questions.explanation: The AWS RAM allows you to share a CA of ACM Private CA between accounts; application accounts that receive the sharing may request certificates from ACM using this shared subordinate CA, ensuring that all certificates issued, in any account, chain up to the same root hierarchy, without doubling CAs.
questions.hint: Think about the service used to share the resources of AWS (including private CAs) between accounts without doubling them.
optionRationales: The AWS RAM allows you to share a CA of ACM Private CA between accounts; application accounts that receive the sharing may request certificates from ACM using this shared subordinate CA, ensuring that all certificates issued, in any account, chain up to the same root hierarchy, without doubling CAs.
The AWS Certificate Manager Private CA does not permit the export of CA's private key for security reasons; this operation is not supported and is not a viable way to replicate CA between accounts.

This approach multiplies the number of reliable root certificates that need to be distributed and managed in all internal clients, increasing operational complexity and contradicting the goal of a single hierarchy of shared trust.

The ACM Private CA does not have a delegated administrator model of the Organizations which automatically replicates an AC to member accounts; the use between accounts of a single CA hierarchy is obtained through sharing via AWS RAM.

questions.text: Security team wants permission set 'AdministratorAccess' from IAM Identity Center, used for emergency access ('break-glass'), generate credentials that expire after maximum 1 time, forcing re-authentication for any continuous privileged work; already the Permission Set 'ReadOnlyAccess', used for routine monitoring, can have longer sessions (8 which configuration meets this differentiation?
options: Use AWS STS GetSessionToken with the parameter DurationSeconds manually defined by each user when taking over the Permission Set AdministratorAccess.
Attach one SCP automatically revoke any session with more than 1 time for mains using Permission Set AdministratorAccess.
Configure a single definition of maximum session duration at the account level of the IAM, also applied to all Permission Sets of IAM Identity Center.
Configure the session duration independently in each Permission Set IAM Identity Center — defining 1 Time for Permission Set AdministratorAccess and 8 hours for Permission Set ReadOnlyAccess.
questions.explanation: No. IAM Identity Center, the duration of the session is a configuration defined individually by Permission Set; each Permission Set controls how long the credentials obtained through it remain valid, allowing exactly the desired differentiation. (1 time for emergency administration, 8 hours for routine reading access).
questions.hint: Think about what level of granularity the IAM Identity Center allows you to configure the lifespan of credentials — on a full account or by individual permission set.
optionRationales: No. IAM Identity Center, the duration of the session is a configuration defined individually by Permission Set; each Permission Set controls how long the credentials obtained through it remain valid, allowing exactly the desired differentiation. (1 time for emergency administration, 8 hours for routine reading access).

The duration of the sitting at IAM Identity Center is configured by Permission Set, not as a single account level configuration; a global configuration could not provide different durations (1h vs. 8(h) for Permission Different sets.

Allowing users themselves to choose the duration of their session does not guarantee the mandatory maximum limit of 1 time; duration should be centrally configured in the Permission Set by an administrator, not left to the user's choice.

SCPs do not have a mechanism to track the age of a session and revoke active sessions based on the time elapsed; the expiry of the session is determined by the configured duration of the credentials, defined in Permission Set itself.

questions.text: A company connects production and non-production VPCs (distributed in multiple accounts) to a single AWS Transit Gateway The safety requirement is that production VPCs can communicate with each other and with a VPC of shared services, but non-production VPCs NUNCA must be able to route traffic from/to production VPCs, while non-production VPCs can communicate freely with each other and with the VPC all VPCs share the same Transit Gateway. Which architecture meets this requirement?
options: Create two separate Transit Gateways — one for production and one for non-production — and a third for VPC of shared services, without peering among them.
Trust Security Groups in each VPC to block traffic between intervals CIDR production and non-production, keeping all the annexes in the standard route table of the Transit Gateway.

Create separate route tables in Transit Gateway (one 'production' and another 'non-production'), associate each Annex to VPC the appropriate table, and spread routes so that the production table has only routes for production VPCs and the VPC of shared services, and the non-production table only has routes for non-production VPCs and the VPC of shared services.
Use Network ACLs in the sub-networks of the Annexes to Transit Gateway to deny traffic between intervals CIDR Production and non-production.
questions.explanation: The Transit Gateway allows to associate each Annex of VPC to a specific route table and control which routes are propagated for each table; creating separate tables for production and non-production, each containing only the appropriate routes (including VPC of services shared in both, but never routes between production and non-production), complete network segmentation is obtained within a single Transit Gateway.
questions.hint: Think about the resource of Transit Gateway which allows for control, by Annex VPC, which destinations are visible/routeable — without multiple Transit Gateways.
optionRationales: The Transit Gateway allows to associate each Annex of VPC to a specific route table and control which routes are propagated for each table; creating separate tables for production and non-production, each containing only the appropriate routes (including VPC of services shared in both, but never routes between production and non-production), complete network segmentation is obtained within a single Transit Gateway.

A VPC of shared services needs to be reachable both by production and by non-production, which would require attaching it to both Transit Gateways (greater complexity and cost) or establishing peering between them; a single Transit Gateway with multiple route tables achieves segmentation in a simpler and more economical way.

The standard route table would propagate routes between all the annexes, making production and non-production VPCs routeable between them in the network layer; depend only on Security Groups (filtering at the instance level/ENI, not at the routing level of the Transit Gateway) leaves the underlying route path open, not being the recommended segmentation approach.

Annexes Transit Gateway do not NACLs directly associated (NACLs apply to sub-networks within a VPC); this approach would not provide the segmentation at route level between annexes of VPC that separate route tables from Transit Gateway provide.

questions.text: A company has a critical database Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. In case of primary node failure (e.g. due to interruption in your Availability Zone), the requirements are: automatic failure without manual intervention, RPO close to zero (synchronous replication) and the application should continue to use the MESMO endpoint/DNS after the failover. Which configuration meets the TODOS these requirements with the least complexity?
options: Amazon ElestiCache as a write-through cache in front of RDS, to mask primary bank interruptions.
Implementation RDS Multi-AZ, with synchronous replication for a standby instance in another Availability Zone.
Automated backups of RDS (snapshots) with restoration from the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone during an interruption.
A Read Replica in another Availability Zone, manually promoted the independent instance during an interruption.
questions.explanation: The RDS Multi-AZ replicates data synchronously to a standby instance in another AZ; in the event of primary failure, the RDS performs automatic failover for the standby, updating the log CNAME the endpoint to point to the new primary instance — the application continues to use the same endpoint, without manual intervention, and the RPO is close to zero thanks to synchronous replication.
questions.hint: Think about the resource of RDS designed specifically for automatic failure with synchronous replication and endpoint preservation, in contrast to replicas used for reading scalability.
optionRationales: The RDS Multi-AZ replicates data synchronously to a standby instance in another AZ; in the event of primary failure, the RDS performs automatic failover for the standby, updating the log CNAME the endpoint to point to the new primary instance — the application continues to use the same endpoint, without manual intervention, and the RPO is close to zero thanks to synchronous replication.

Read Replicas use ASSIGNANCE replication, which may result in data loss (RPO greater than zero) in case of primary failure; moreover, promotion is an action MANUAL which requires operator intervention and usually requires updating of the endpoint used by the application, increasing the RTO.

Restore from a snapshot has RPO equal to the interval between backups (potentially lost data hours) and RTO high (time to provide a new instance from snapshot), much higher than the almost immediate and automatic failure of Multi-AZ.

Cache layers meet requirements of LEITURA with cached data, but they can't attend operations of ESCRITA during an interruption of the primary database, and do not provide automatic failover of the underlying database itself.

questions.text: One Auto Scaling Group is associated with a Application Load Balancer. The cases EC2 are passing on status checks of the EC2 (hardware/hypervisor OK), but the application running on them has stopped and is returning HTTP 500 in the health check of ALB. Even so, the Auto Scaling Group is not replacing these unhealthy instances. Which configuration change solves this problem?
options: Decrease the 'healthy threshold count' ALB so that the instances are marked as healthy more quickly.
Replace Application Load Balancer by a Network Load Balancer, that performs health checks more reliable.
Increase the health check grace period Auto Scaling Group to give the application more time to recover.
Change the type of health check Auto Scaling Group of 'EC2' for 'ELB' (or enable both), so that the ASG consider the results of the health check of ALB.
questions.explanation: When the type of health check ASG It's just 'EC2', o ASG ignores the outcome of health checks of ALB and considers any instance that passes in the status checks of the EC2 (hardware/hypervisor level); change to 'ELB' (or enable both) does the ASG consider application level failures detected by ALB (as HTTP 500) and automatically replace unhealthy instances.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between Auto Scaling Group checks by default (status of instance) and what the load balancer check (health of application) — and how ASG can be configured to consider both.
optionRationales: When the type of health check ASG It's just 'EC2', o ASG ignores the outcome of health checks of ALB and considers any instance that passes in the status checks of the EC2 (hardware/hypervisor level); change to 'ELB' (or enable both) does the ASG consider application level failures detected by ALB (as HTTP 500) and automatically replace unhealthy instances.

The grace period is just late QUANDO the health checks begin to be evaluated after the launch of the instance; it does not solve the problem of ASG no DETECTAR application level failures, since the type of health check configured is only 'EC2'.

Reducing the limit of healthy checks does not solve the root cause, which is the ASG not consulting the results of the health check ALB due to the health check type configuration; ALB would continue to mark the instance as unhealthy (HTTP 500), but the ASG Just don't act on that information..

The NLB operates in the layer 4 and your health checks would not detect better an application returning HTTP 500 (a layer failure 7); the central problem is the configuration of the TIPO of health check ASG, not the type of load balancer used.

questions.text: A company executes its primary application stack in us-east-1 and maintains a standby battery in us-west-2. The requirements are: Amazon Route 53 should automatically route users to us-west-2 SOMENTE when us-east-1 be unavailable (detected via health check at an endpoint of the application), and reroute to us-east-1 automatically when this region recovers — without manual intervention in either case. Route 53 meets this requirement?
options: Weighted Routing Policy with Weight 100% for us-east-1 and 0% for us-west-2, changing the weights manually during an interruption.
Multivalue Answer routing policy with health checks on both records.
Latency-based routing policy with records for both regions.
Failover routing policy, with a record PRIMARY pointing to the endpoint in us-east-1 associated with a health check of Route 53, and a record SECONDARY pointing to the endpoint in us-west-2.
questions.explanation: In the policy of routing Failover, the Route 53 return the record PRIMARY while your health check is intact; if the health check fails, the Route 53 automatically returns the log SECONDARY (us-west-2), and return the PRIMARY automatically when the health check passes again — meeting both requirements without manual intervention.
questions.hint: Think about the policy of routing the Route 53 which explicitly defines 'primary' and 'secondary' roles linked to health checks.
optionRationales: In the policy of routing Failover, the Route 53 return the record PRIMARY while your health check is intact; if the health check fails, the Route 53 automatically returns the log SECONDARY (us-west-2), and return the PRIMARY automatically when the health check passes again — meeting both requirements without manual intervention.
Changing weights manually during a break requires a human operator to detect failure and update records DNS, what does not meet the AUTOMATICAL health check-based router requirement.

Latency routing always directs users to the region with less latency for them, INDEPENDENTEMENTE of the primary region be healthy or not; it does not provide failover behavior linked to a designated primary region that the requirement requires.

Multivalue Answer returns until 8 Randomly healthy records to customers (for basic load/availability distribution); it does not designate a record as primary and another as secondary/standby with the structured behavior of failure-to-fail required.

questions.text: A global game application requires players in North America, Europe and Asia to read E ESCREVAM in a table 'player profile' with low latency from their respective regions, with changes made in one region automatically propagated to the others (multi-active-active region). The application must continue with total reading and writing capacity in any region even if another region is not available.?
options: Use Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables, setting up replica tables in each of the three Regions.
Use Amazon Aurora Global Database, setting up clusters in Asia and Europe as primary writers.
Installing tables DynamoDB in each region and use AWS DMS to continuously replicate the changes bidirectionally between the three tables.
Use a single table DynamoDB in a region (e.g. us-east)-1) with clusters of DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) implemented in Europe and Asia.
questions.explanation: The DynamoDB Global Tables offers multi-region and multi-active replication: writings made in any replica are propagated to all other replicas (possibly consistency), and applications in each region can read and write locally with full availability, even if other regions are not available — meeting exactly the active-active requirement.
questions.hint: Think about the native resource of DynamoDB specifically designed for multi-region replication with local reading and writing in each region, without the need for external replication tools.
optionRationales: The DynamoDB Global Tables offers multi-region and multi-active replication: writings made in any replica are propagated to all other replicas (possibly consistency), and applications in each region can read and write locally with full availability, even if other regions are not available — meeting exactly the active-active requirement.

The DAX is a layer of CACHE in memory that accelerates LEITURAS of a table in a SINGLE Region; it does not replicate the underlying table to other Regions, does not offer the ability to ESCRITA location in Europe/Asia, and a break in us-east-1 would make the table unavailable everywhere.

The Aurora Global Database has A primary cluster (read-write) and even 5 secondary regions read only; it does not support simultaneous active-active writings from multiple regions, which the requirement requires.

The AWS DMS is designed for migration/replication (typically one-way or with limited bi-way support) between databases, and is not the native mechanism recommended by AWS for multi-region replication active-active of DynamoDB; o DynamoDB Global Tables is the native resource specifically designed for this purpose.

questions.text: A company uses AWS Backup to create daily volume backups EBS and databases RDS in us-east-1. By regulatory requirement of disaster recovery, copies of these backups should also be stored in us-west-2, so that resources can be restored in us-west-2 even if we-east-1 (including your backups) is completely unavailable. Which configuration meets this requirement in an automated way?
options: Configure the backup box in us-east-1 with replication between regions enabled, similar to the Cross-Region Replication of the S3.
Enable Multi-Region mode of AWS Backup at account level, which automatically mirrors all backup vaults to a secondary region.
Create manual snapshots of volumes EBS and instances RDS and use the console of EC2/RDS to manually copy each snapshot to us-west-2 after each backup.

Configure the backup plan of the AWS Backup with a copy to destination rule (copy rule) that automatically copies each recovery point created in us-east-1 for a backup vault (backup vault) in us-west-2.
questions.explanation: The copy rules of AWS Backup, defined within the backup plan, automatically copy each recovery point to a safe in another Region as soon as backup is completed, ensuring that there are independent copies in the DR region without the need for recurring manual actions.
questions.hint: Think of what element of a configuration PLANO backup (not from the vault) allows you to automatically copy recovery points to another region.
optionRationales: The copy rules of AWS Backup, defined within the backup plan, automatically copy each recovery point to a safe in another Region as soon as backup is completed, ensuring that there are independent copies in the DR region without the need for recurring manual actions.

The safes of the AWS Backup do not have an automatic replication feature in style S3 CRR at the vault level; copies between regions are configured by copy rules/copy actions within the backup plan itself, not by replicating the vault.

The manual copy of snapshots, resource by resource, is operationally unfeasible and prone to errors for a recurring DR requirement; the copy rules of AWS Backup automates this process as part of the regular backup plan.

The AWS Backup does not have a single alternator ('Multi-Region mode') at the account level that mirrors all the vaults automatically; the copy between regions must be explicitly configured by copy rules in each backup plane.

questions.text: An order processing flow uses the AWS Step Functions to orchestrate multiple functions Lambda. One of the functions occasionally fails due to the throttling of a downstream service (transitional error). The architecture team wants the state machine to try this step again automatically with exponential backoff a few times before giving up, and that if all attempts fail, the execution is directed to a separate branch of 'manual revision' instead of failing the entire flow. Step Functions meets this requirement?
options: Configure the function's own asynchronous invocation retry settings Lambda (2 auto-tests), since Step Functions invokes the Lambda asynchronous by pattern.
Use a row SQS with a redirection policy (redrive policy) between each state of Step Functions to deal with the attempts.

Configure a 'Retry' field in the relevant state with ErrorEquals corresponding to the exception of throttling, IntervalSeconds, BackoffRate and MaxAttempts appropriate for exponential backoff; and additionally a 'Catch' field in the same state that directs to the 'manual revision' state if attempts are exhausted.
Envelope function code Lambda in a try/catch block with a custom retry loop using thread() delays, and do the Step Functions Invoke her only once.
questions.explanation: Retry and Catch are native resources of Amazon States Language: 'Retry' allows you to set automatic attempts with configurable exponential backoff for specific errors, and 'Catch' allows you to capture the remaining error (after attempts run out) and direct the execution to an alternative state (manual revision), all of this visible in the running history of the Step Functions.
questions.hint: Think of the two fields of Amazon States Language designed specifically for the treatment of declaratory errors within a state machine state, without additional code.
optionRationales: Retry and Catch are native resources of Amazon States Language: 'Retry' allows you to set automatic attempts with configurable exponential backoff for specific errors, and 'Catch' allows you to capture the remaining error (after attempts run out) and direct the execution to an alternative state (manual revision), all of this visible in the running history of the Step Functions.

Implement the retry logic within the code of Lambda consumes execution time (and cost) of the function during the waits, does not offer native visibility of the Step Functions on attempts in the execution history, and does not support in a clean way the requirement to 'direct for manual revision after exhausting attempts' in the orchestration layer.

The Step Functions invokes the Lambda by default (waiting for response), does not asynchronize; therefore, the asynchronous invocation retry configurations of the Lambda do not apply — attempts must be configured in the state machine definition itself.

Enter rows SQS between states adds unnecessary complexity and latency; the Step Functions already natively supports the Retry and Catch fields directly in the definition of Amazon States Language, no need for external line infrastructure.

questions.text: A media company stores end-to-end and unchangeable video assets in a pocket S3 in us-east-1. For disaster recovery, it is necessary to keep an automatic copy of each new object in a pocket on eu-west-1, preserving the same storage class transitions and encryption configurations, so that if we use-east-1 be unavailable, copy in eu-west-1 can serve as a source for recovery. Which configuration meets this requirement?
