Use AWS DataSync to make a single copy (one-time) of the bulk content for eu-west-1.
Configure a Lifecycle Rule from S3 to transition objects to the storage class S3 Glacier in me-west-1 after 30 days.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration in us-east pocket-1 to accelerate access from eu-west-1.
questions.explanation: The Cross-Region Replication of S3 automatically keeps a copy of new and updated objects in a pocket from another Region, preserving settings such as storage class and encryption (with the appropriate key setting KMS in destination); versioning is a prerequisite both in origin and in destination.
questions.hint: Think about the native resource of S3 designed to keep continuous and automatic copies of objects in a pocket from another region, preserving storage and encryption settings.
optionRationales: The Cross-Region Replication of S3 automatically keeps a copy of new and updated objects in a pocket from another Region, preserving settings such as storage class and encryption (with the appropriate key setting KMS in destination); versioning is a prerequisite both in origin and in destination.

The Acceleration Transfer accelerates UPLOADS for the S3 from geographically distant customers using edge locations of the CloudFront; it does not create or maintain a replicated copy of the objects in another pocket/region.
Lifecycle Rules of the S3 transition objects between storage classes DENTRO of the same bucket/region; they cannot move or copy objects to a bucket in another region.
A single copy of the DataSync would not automatically replicate NOVOS objects added after the initial copy; a CRR provides continuous and automatic replication of new and updated objects as required.

questions.text: An order processing system uses a row SQS consumed by a function Lambda. Occasionally, a malformed message ('poison message') does the function Lambda fail repeatedly, and the SQS continues to redirect this same message to the function, consuming invocations of the Lambda and delaying the processing of other valid messages behind her in the queue. The team wants poisonous messages to be automatically isolated after some failed attempts, without blocking the processing of subsequent valid messages. What configuration meets this requirement?
options: Reduce line visibility timeout SQS for 0 seconds, so that failed messages are immediately reprocessed.
Increase reserved competition in the function Lambda for more instances to process messages in parallel, reducing the impact of the message.
Configure queue message retention period SQS for 1 minute, so that problematic messages quickly expire.
Configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for the row SQS of origin, with a redive policy specifying maxReceiveCount (ex.: 3).
questions.explanation: With a DLQ and maxReceiveCount configured, after a message is received (and fails in processing) the number of times specified, the SQS automatically moves to the DLQ, removing it from the source row; this unlocks the processing of subsequent valid messages and allows monitoring/inspecting the DLQ separately.
questions.hint: Think of the mechanism of SQS which automatically isolates messages that fail repeatedly after a configurable number of attempts, separating them from the main row.
optionRationales: With a DLQ and maxReceiveCount configured, after a message is received (and fails in processing) the number of times specified, the SQS automatically moves to the DLQ, removing it from the source row; this unlocks the processing of subsequent valid messages and allows monitoring/inspecting the DLQ separately.

A visibility timeout of 0 it would make the message immediately visible to other consumers after each attempt fails, potentially causing an even faster retentative loop in the poisonous message, consuming invocations of the Lambda more quickly, without isolating it.

Increasing competition allows processing more valid messages in parallel, but does not prevent the poison message itself from continuing to be redirected and reprocessed indefinitely, continuing to consume invocations.

Reduce retention to 1 minute would make TODAS messages (including valid still unprocessed) are deleted after only one minute, which may cause loss of valid messages before they are processed — an excessively aggressive measure and not specifically directed to poisonous messages.

questions.text: An application uses the Amazon ElasiCache for Redis as session storage. The architecture team requires that if the primary node of the Redis replication group fails (for example, due to an AZ interruption), a replica is automatically promoted to the primary with minimal disruption, without the application needing to be reconfigured with a new endpoint.?
options: Create two independent ElastiCache for Redis clusters in different AZs and set up the application to write on both simultaneously.
Perform manual snapshots of the Redis cluster every few minutes and restore from the latest snapshot in a new cluster if the primary fails.
Enable Multi-AZ with Automatic Failover in the ElastiCache for Redis replication group, with at least one read replica in another Availability Zone.
Use ElastiCache for Memcached instead of Redis, since Memcached natively supports multi-no replication with automatic failover.
questions.explanation: With Multi-AZ and Automatic Failover enabled, ElastiCache automatically detects the failure of the primary node and promotes a replica to the primary, updating the record DNS from the primary endpoint of the replication group to point to the new primary — the application continues to use the same configured endpoint, without manual reconfiguration.
questions.hint: Think about the specific feature of ElastiCache for Redis that allows automatic replication promotion to primary in case of failure, preserving the endpoint used by the application.
optionRationales: With Multi-AZ and Automatic Failover enabled, ElastiCache automatically detects the failure of the primary node and promotes a replica to the primary, updating the record DNS from the primary endpoint of the replication group to point to the new primary — the application continues to use the same configured endpoint, without manual reconfiguration.

Memcached is a cache distributed in memory SEM replication or embedded persistence; it does not have the concept of primary node/replicator or automatic failure, making it inadequate for this requirement — it is the Redis (with replication groups) that supports Multi-AZ and automatic failure.

Writing in two independent clusters from the application introduces complexity and potential data inconsistency between the caches, and is not how ElastiCache's native multi-AZ failover was designed to work; this approach shifts the logic of failover to application unnecessarily.

Manual snapshot followed by restoration would result in significant data loss (since the last snapshot) and a RTO high (time to provide a new cluster and restore), in addition to requiring manual intervention — unlike the automatic Multi-AZ failover, which is almost immediate and automated.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon EFS for shared file storage of an executed application in instances EC2 in us-east-1. To disaster recovery, you need to keep a replica of the file system in us-west-2, continuously updated with low RPO, which can be quickly promoted read-write case us-east-1 What approach meets this requirement?
options: Use Amazon EFS Replication to configure replication between regions from the source file system in us-east-1 for a new replica file system read only in us-west-2; in a DR event, promote the replica of reading-writing.
Mount the same file system EFS directly in fora EC2 located in us-west-2.
Use AWS DataSync to make a single copy (one-time) of the file system EFS for a new file system EFS in us-west-2.
Using Lifecycle Management (Lifecycle Management) EFS to move files to the storage class EFS Infrequent Access in us-west-2.
questions.explanation: The EFS Replication maintains continuous and managed replication between regions, with low RPO, automatically creating a read-only replica in the destination; in case of disaster recovery, this replica can be promoted to an independent read-write file system, meeting exactly the requirement.
questions.hint: Think about the native resource of EFS, released specifically to keep continuously synchronized copies of one file system in another region.
optionRationales: The EFS Replication maintains continuous and managed replication between regions, with low RPO, automatically creating a read-only replica in the destination; in case of disaster recovery, this replica can be promoted to an independent read-write file system, meeting exactly the requirement.

A single copy does not keep the replica up to date with the continuous changes made to the source file system after the initial copy; the lower requirement RPO requires continuous replication, not a one-time copy.

File systems EFS and its mount targets are regional resources; it is not possible to mount directly, between regions, the same file system from instances in another region without using a replication feature like the EFS Replication.
Lifecycle Management EFS move files between storage classes DENTRO of the same file system/Region; it does not copy or replicate files to a different file system in another Region.

questions.text: An application maintains a large number of persistent connections to a bank Amazon RDS for MySQL in Multi-AZ mode. During a Multi-AZ failure, the application faces connection errors and takes a long time to reconnect and recover, causing unavailability perceived by users. Which approach reduces the unavailability time perceived by the application during the failure, without rewriting the logic of reconnection of the application?
options: Enable connection drainage (deregistration delay) in a Application Load Balancer positioned in front of the database.
Place the Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the instance RDS, maintaining a managed connection pool.
Configure the application to use a Read Replica as the primary connection endpoint.
Increase the database instance class to a larger type, with more vCPUs and memory.
questions.explanation: The RDS Proxy maintains a pool of connections to the database and, during a Multi-AZ failover, automatically redirects connections to the new primary instance, significantly reducing the failure time perceived by the application without requiring changes in the application retry logic.
questions.hint: Think about the managed service of AWS acting as a pool of connections between the application and RDS, designed specifically to reduce the impact of failureovers on the connection time.
optionRationales: The RDS Proxy maintains a pool of connections to the database and, during a Multi-AZ failover, automatically redirects connections to the new primary instance, significantly reducing the failure time perceived by the application without requiring changes in the application retry logic.

A larger instance does not improve the treatment of connections during failover; failover time is related to the spread of DNS and the re-establishment of connections, not the processing capacity of the instance.

Read Replicas are intended to download traffic from LEITURA; writing operations need to go to the primary instance, so using a read replica as the primary connection endpoint would not support writing and would not resolve the treatment of failure.

ALBs do not stand in front of database connections (databanks use connections TCP direct, no HTTP); connection drainage is a resource of ELB for listeners HTTP/TCP directed to web application targets, does not apply to direct connections with the bank.

questions.text: A company is choosing a disaster recovery strategy for a critical workload.: RTO of a few minutes, RPO of a few minutes, and the company is willing to pay for a pre-provided infrastructure, but reduced (scaled-down), in the DR region, avoiding the cost of keeping a copy on a full scale of the production running continuously.?
options: Backup and restore — perform regular backups and restore infrastructure from them during a disaster.
Multi-site active/active — keep both regions running full production traffic simultaneously.
Warm standby — maintain a functional, but reduced (scaled-down) copy of the continuously running production environment in the DR region, scaling it to full capacity during a disaster.
Pilot light — keep only the essential infrastructure (e.g. a replica database) running in the DR region, providing the other components only during a disaster.
questions.explanation: Warm standby keeps all the components of architecture running, but on a small scale, in the DR region; during a disaster, it is enough to scale this infrastructure to total capacity, achieving RTO/RPO from the order of minutes to a moderate cost — exactly the equilibrium sought.
questions.hint: Think of the DR strategy that keeps all the components of the architecture running, but in reduced capacity, balancing cost and recovery speed.
optionRationales: Warm standby keeps all the components of architecture running, but on a small scale, in the DR region; during a disaster, it is enough to scale this infrastructure to total capacity, achieving RTO/RPO from the order of minutes to a moderate cost — exactly the equilibrium sought.

In the pilot light, computational/application components need to be provided and configured from zero during the disaster, which usually results in RTO more than a few minutes; does not meet the requirement of RTO of minutes as the warm standby, which already keeps these components in reduced execution.

Backup and restore is the lowest cost strategy, but typically presents the largest RTO/RPO, measured in hours, as the entire infrastructure needs to be built from backups during the disaster — does not meet the requirement of RTO minutes.

Multi-site active/active offers the best RTO/RPO (close to zero), but at the highest cost, demanding infrastructure in total production capacity running continuously in both regions; the company explicitly seeks a pre-provided 'reduced' infrastructure, indicating that it is not willing to pay for the total cost of the asset/asset.

questions.text: A company has VMware on-premises servers running critical applications. It wants a DR solution that continuously replicates these servers (at block level) to AWS, allowing fast failover — launching recovery instances in AWS in a few minutes — in the event of an on-premises disaster, with minimal continuous changes in the source servers. AWS meets this requirement?
options: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS).
AWS Storage Gateway (Volume Gateway) to replicate VM disks on-premises for the S3, manually creating instances EC2 from these volumes during a disaster.
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS).
AWS Server Migration Service (SMS).
questions.explanation: The AWS DRS performs continuous replication at block level of on-premises servers (or other clouds) to a low cost staging area at AWS; in case of disaster, DRS Automatically launches recovery instances from replicated data in a few minutes, providing low RTO/RPO for DR type lift-and-shift.
questions.hint: Think of the service of AWS developed from continuous block-level replication technology, specifically designed for lift-and-shift DR of on-premises or other cloud servers.
optionRationales: The AWS DRS performs continuous replication at block level of on-premises servers (or other clouds) to a low cost staging area at AWS; in case of disaster, DRS Automatically launches recovery instances from replicated data in a few minutes, providing low RTO/RPO for DR type lift-and-shift.

The DMS specifically replicates data from BANCO OF DADOS, no full server images (including operating system, applications and settings); is a database migration/replication tool, not a full server DR solution.

The SMS performs periodic and incremental replication of VM snapshots (less frequent than continuous replication at block level), was designed mainly for single migration, is discontinued and does not offer the RPO low with continuous replication nor automated failure in minutes than the AWS DRS offers.

The Gateway Volume replicates VOLUMES for the S3 as snapshots, but reconstructing complete servers (operational system, applications, configurations) from raw volume snapshots during a disaster is a manual process, slow and prone to errors, not a ready-made DR orchestration solution like the AWS DRS.

questions.text: A company is migrating to the AWS an on-premises application that uses Apache ActiveMQ for messaging (via protocol) JMS), and wants to minimize code changes in the application while getting high availability between Availability Zones with automatic failover of the message broker. What approach meets this requirement?
options: Run two brokers Amazon independent MQ in different AZs and configure the application to post messages on both.
Migrate the application to use the Amazon SQS, which is inherently highly available.
Implant Amazon MQ in cluster mode with multiple active brokers sharing the load.
Use Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ in active/standby deployment mode between two Availability Zones.
questions.explanation: In active/standby mode, or Amazon MQ replicates broker message storage data to a standby broker in another AZ and performs automatic failover to the standby (keeping the same endpoint) if the active broker is unavailable — without requiring changes to the application protocol, which continues to use APIs JMS/ActiveMQ.
questions.hint: Think of the model of high availability that Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ offers natively between Availability Zones, preserving the same endpoint and protocol.
optionRationales: In active/standby mode, or Amazon MQ replicates broker message storage data to a standby broker in another AZ and performs automatic failover to the standby (keeping the same endpoint) if the active broker is unavailable — without requiring changes to the application protocol, which continues to use APIs JMS/ActiveMQ.

Although the SQS is highly available, this approach would require REESCREVER the application to use the API of the SQS instead of protocol JMS/ActiveMQ, contrary to the requirement to minimize code changes.

The Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ does not offer a cluster mode with multiple active brokers simultaneously sharing the same rows; its high availability model for ActiveMQ is active/standby (an active broker + a standby) — the cluster mode with multiple active node is available for Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ.

Independent brokers without shared storage/replication would result in messages divided between brokers (without shared queue state), requiring consumers to consume both — this does not provide adequate failover and completely alters the semantics of messages.

questions.text: One Auto Scaling Group of a critical application is distributed in only 2 Availability Zones, with desired capacity of 10 cases (5 If an AZ fails, only one remains. 50% the total capacity, potentially overloading the surviving AZ. The architecture team wants to redesign to increase the resilience to failures of a single AZ, maintaining the same total capacity and with minimal cost increase.?
options: Increase the desired capacity of Auto Scaling Group for 200% of the normally necessary, while maintaining the distribution in the 2 Existing AZs.
Redesign VPC and the Auto Scaling Group to cover 3 Availability zones, distributing the same total capacity between the 3 AZs instead of 2.
Configure the Auto Scaling Group with a 'Single AZ' positioning strategy to simplify network configuration.
Use the 'Capacity Rebalancing' feature of Auto Scaling configured for On-Demand instances in 2 Existing AZs.
questions.explanation: Distributing the same total capacity (10 (a) between 3 AZs (approximately 3-4 by AZ), if an AZ fails, the 2 Remaining AZs retain approximately 2/3 total capacity (instead of 50% with 2 AZs) — reducing the impact of a single AZ failure, with minimal additional cost (even the total number of instances, only distributed among more AZs, requiring the creation of additional sub-networks).
questions.hint: Think of how the number of Availability Zones used affects the fraction of total capacity that remains available after the loss of a single AZ.
optionRationales: Distributing the same total capacity (10 (a) between 3 AZs (approximately 3-4 by AZ), if an AZ fails, the 2 Remaining AZs retain approximately 2/3 total capacity (instead of 50% with 2 AZs) — reducing the impact of a single AZ failure, with minimal additional cost (even the total number of instances, only distributed among more AZs, requiring the creation of additional sub-networks).

Folding the ability to oversupply against AZ failures significantly increases the cost (executing twice as many instances required all the time), compared to simply distributing the same capacity between 3 Azs.
Deliberately running in a single AZ would make the availability of all the application dependent on that AZ, the opposite of improving resilience.

Capacity Rebalancing is specific to proactively replace Spot Instances with high risk of interruption; it does not apply significantly to On-Demand instances nor solves the problem of capacity distribution between AZs described.

questions.text: A Network Load Balancer has 2 Registered availability zones, but with different numbers of healthy targets in each (AZ-A has 8 targets, AZ-B has 2 targets after a recent scale-in). NLB distributes traffic in approximately the same way ENTRE The Azs (50/50), not between individual targets — making the 2 targets AZ-B receive, each, much more traffic than 8 targets AZ-A, overloading them. Which configuration corrects this unbalanced?
options: Manually record additional 'placeholder' targets at AZ-B to balance the target count.
Enable 'Slow Start' mode in target group of NLB.
Replace Network Load Balancer by a Classic Load Balancer, which always balances equally between all targets regardless of AZ.
Enable Cross-Zone Load Balancing on Network Load Balancer.
questions.explanation: With Cross-Zone Load Balancing enabled, or NLB distributes traffic equally between TODOS the registered healthy targets, regardless of AZ; thus, each of the 10 targets (sounding the two AZs) receive approximately the same fraction of traffic, instead of the traffic being divided first equally by AZ.
questions.hint: Think about the configuration of NLB determining whether traffic is distributed by AZ first or directly among all healthy targets, regardless of their AZ.
optionRationales: With Cross-Zone Load Balancing enabled, or NLB distributes traffic equally between TODOS the registered healthy targets, regardless of AZ; thus, each of the 10 targets (sounding the two AZs) receive approximately the same fraction of traffic, instead of the traffic being divided first equally by AZ.

Slow Start gradually increases the proportion of requests sent to newly registered targets during a configurable heating period; it does not resolve the imbalance in traffic distribution between AZs caused by uneven target counts by AZs.

Fictitious targets would receive real production traffic and could not meet it properly (returning errors) or waste resources — an inadequate solution instead of correcting the distribution mechanism.

Although the Classic Load Balancer have cross-zone load balancing enabled by default, replace the TIPO of load balancer is an unnecessarily disruptive change (losing specific resources of the NLB, as static IPs and very high transfer rate) when simply enable the existing cross-zone configuration in NLB solve the problem directly.

questions.text: A development team accidentally executed, 2 hours, a failed migration script against the bank Amazon RDS for MySQL production, corrupting several tables. It is necessary to recover the database for the exact state IMEDIATAMENTE ANTES the execution of the faulty script (a point in the specific time, not necessarily aligned to a daily snapshot), with minimal loss of data from transactions occurring between the last snapshot and that point in time. RDS meets this requirement?
options: Enable binary logging in instance RDS and manually reproduce the binary logs to the desired point in the same instance.
Restore the latest automated daily snapshot, which contains data from the backup window of the previous night.
Use the 'Reboot with failover' option RDS in the Multi-AZ implementation to reverse for standby data.
Use automated backups from RDS with Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR), restoring one NOVA instance for the exact timestamp immediately prior to running the faulty script.
questions.explanation: The PITR of the RDS reproduces transaction logs from the latest automated backup to the specified second exact, creating a new instance with the data as they were at that time; this new instance can then be used to redirect the application or migrate the required data, taking into account the recovery requirement for an exact point in time with minimal data loss.
questions.hint: Think about the resource of RDS which allows restoring a new instance to an exact timestamp, instead of relying only on the nearest daily snapshot.
optionRationales: The PITR of the RDS reproduces transaction logs from the latest automated backup to the specified second exact, creating a new instance with the data as they were at that time; this new instance can then be used to redirect the application or migrate the required data, taking into account the recovery requirement for an exact point in time with minimal data loss.

The most recent daily snapshot may have been done before the script is executed in some cases, but it may also be many hours before the required (losing additional valid transactions) or, if done after the script, already contain corruption; the requirement asks for recovery for the PONTO EXATO in the time immediately prior to the script, not for the nearest daily snapshot.

The reboot with failover alternates to the standby instance, but the standby is replicated in a SYNCRON way and would also contain the corrupted data by the faulty script (already replicated to it); this option does not offer any recovery capacity for a specific point in time.

The RDS does not expose direct manual binary logs management/playing in the production instance in this way for point-in-time recovery of MySQL; the PITR via automated backups + transaction logs (restoring for one NOVA instance) is the mechanism supported by RDS.

questions.text: A company executes an application with intermittent traffic in Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 (compatible with PostgreSQL), with significant traffic variation throughout the day. It needs this database to maintain high availability with automatic failover between Availability Zones, similar to Aurora the provisioning, continuing to benefit from automatic capacity scaling of the Aurora Serverless v2. This is possible, and how?
options: No — Aurora Serverless v2 supports only one instance write in a single AZ, without replica options; for HA Multi-AZ, the cluster needs to be converted entirely to instances Aurora Provisioned.
No — achieving HA Multi-AZ would require manually routing snapshots between AZs and restoring a new Serverless v2 instance from the snapshot if the primary AZ fails.
Yeah, but just using the Aurora Global Database, with a secondary region configured as the 'standby' Multi-AZ.

Yes — Aurora Serverless v2 supports Multi-AZ deployments by adding one or more Aurora Replicas (which can also be Serverless v2) in different AZs within the same cluster Aurora; the automatic failover mechanism of the Aurora promotes a replica to write if the primary instance is unavailable, while each Serverless v2 instance of the cluster scales its capacity (ACUs) independently, according to its own load.
questions.explanation: The Aurora Serverless v2 can coexist with Aurora Replicas (Serverless v2 or provided) within the same cluster, in different AZs; the native automatic failover Aurora promotes one of these replicas to write in case of failure of the primary instance, and each instance continues to scale its capacity independently — providing Multi-AZ HA without losing automatic scaling.
questions.hint: Think of how the Aurora separates the concept of 'instance within a cluster' from the concept of 'capacity mode (provided vs. serverless)' — and if replicas in other AZs can use any of these modes.
optionRationales: The Aurora Serverless v2 can coexist with Aurora Replicas (Serverless v2 or provided) within the same cluster, in different AZs; the native automatic failover Aurora promotes one of these replicas to write in case of failure of the primary instance, and each instance continues to scale its capacity independently — providing Multi-AZ HA without losing automatic scaling.

This statement is incorrect: instances Aurora Serverless v2 can be combined with other Serverless v2 instances or provided as Aurora Replicas within the same cluster, supporting Multi-AZ HA without need of total conversion to provided.

The Aurora Global Database is intended for disaster recovery between REGIONS (secondary regions are read-only, and failure involves a promotion that takes longer than Multi-AZ within the same region); it is a different resource from the high availability Multi-AZ within a single region via Aurora Replicas, and is not required only to get Multi-AZ HA within a region.
This approach describes a manual, slow and RTO/RPO the native mechanism of Aurora Replica + Multi-AZ automatic failover Aurora already provides this without the need for manual snapshot scripts.

questions.text: Three independent consumer applications (analytics, fraud detection and archiving) read about it Amazon Kinesis Data Stream. As the number of consumers grows, they start to compete for the fixed reading rate of each shard (2 MB/s, shared among all consumers who use GetRecords), causing increasing reading latency and occasional throttling for all — impacting the consumer's near-real-time requirement for fraud detection. How to resolve this without excessively increasing the number of shards (and cost), ensuring that each consumer reliably receives their own dedicated transfer rate by shard?
options: Increase the number of shards in Kinesis Data Stream proportional to the number of consumers.
Configure each consumer with a different consumer group name, similar to Apache Kafka, to receive independent reading rate.
Make every consumer application read from a row SQS separate, populated by a function Lambda activated by the Kinesis stream.
Enable Enhanced Fan-Out and make every consumer register as an enhanced fan-out consumer using the API SubscribeToShard.
questions.explanation: With Enhanced Fan-Out, every registered consumer receives their own dedicated pipe from 2 MB/s by shard (deliver via HTTP/2, by push), eliminating the consumer transfer fee dispute without requiring additional shards.
questions.hint: Think about the resource of Kinesis Data Streams delivering records via push (HTTP/2) and provides each registered consumer with their own dedicated shard transfer fee.
optionRationales: With Enhanced Fan-Out, every registered consumer receives their own dedicated pipe from 2 MB/s by shard (deliver via HTTP/2, by push), eliminating the consumer transfer fee dispute without requiring additional shards.

Increase shards raises the total transfer rate and the cost, but in the standard fan-out model (non-enhanced), the read rate per shard (2 MB/s) remains COMPARTILHADA among all consumers who use GetRecords in that shard, regardless of the total number of shards — the dispute between consumers in a given shard remains.

Add a layer of fan-out via SQS+Lambda introduces latency, complexity and additional cost, compared to the use of the native Enhanced Fan-Out resource Kinesis, designed exactly for this multi-consumer throughput problem.

The Amazon Kinesis Data Streams does not have a native partitioning model by 'Consumer Group' such as Kafka, in which readings are automatically isolated; the reading rate isolation feature in the Kinesis is the Enhanced Fan-Out via SubscribeToShard.

questions.text: An order processing system publishes OrderPlaced events in a topic SNS, that makes fanout for 3 rows SQS consumed by independent microservices (Storage, Invoicing and Shipping). SQS the sending service is occasionally incorrectly configured by the responsible team, causing the deliveries of the SNS for this row fail; after attempts to forward, these notifications are PERDIDAS (the Send team has no way of knowing which OrderPlaced events have stopped arriving. The architecture team wants faulty deliveries for a specific subscriber to be captured for later reprocessing., SEM require changes in how Stock and Invoicing signatures operate. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Configure a reddrive policy with a dead-letter queue (DLQ) specifically in ASSINATURA SNS corresponding to the row SQS Sending.
Change Topic SNS for a topic FIFO, so that the delivery order guarantees avoid delivery failures.
Add a retry loop in the Send microservice code to repeatedly consult the SNS in search of lost notifications.
Configure a single dead-letter queue at the TOPIC level SNS, shared by all signatures.
questions.explanation: The DLQs of SNS are configured by ASSINATURA (subscription), not at the topic level; after the SNS to exhaust its policy of retentatives for deliveries to this specific signature, the failed notification is sent to the DLQ configured in this signature, for subsequent inspection/reprocessing — independently of other signatures (Storage and Invoice), which continue to operate normally.
questions.hint: Think about what level of configuration of the SNS — topic or individual signature — allows to isolate the treatment of delivery failures for a single subscriber.
optionRationales: The DLQs of SNS are configured by ASSINATURA (subscription), not at the topic level; after the SNS to exhaust its policy of retentatives for deliveries to this specific signature, the failed notification is sent to the DLQ configured in this signature, for subsequent inspection/reprocessing — independently of other signatures (Storage and Invoice), which continue to operate normally.

The dead-letter tails of SNS are configured by ASSINATURA, not at the topic level; a DLQ shared at the topic level is not like the redrive policies of the SNS work, and mix failed messages from different subscribers without clear attribution.

The SNS does not offer one API for consumers to 'consult lost notifications'; SNS performs push delivery for subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, etc.) and is not a log pull-based and replayable as the Kinesis.

Topics FIFO ensure ordination and delivery characteristics accurately-once, but do not prevent or resolve delivery failures caused by a poorly configured subscriber queue policy; ordination guarantees are not related to the treatment of delivery failures to a specific subscriber.

questions.text: An application in containers is executed as a service ECS no Fargate, with all the tasks of the service being launched currently in sub-networks of a ONLY Availability Zone (because the configuration of the service specifies only one sub-network). If this AZ suffers an interruption, all the tasks are unavailable. ECS must be configured to ensure resilience to a single AZ failure?
options: Increase the 'desired count' of service tasks ECS to perform more replicas within the same single AZ.
Configure a health check Route 53 automatically restart the tasks ECS in another AZ if the current AZ becomes unhealthy.
Configure the network configuration (awsvpcConfiguration) of the service ECS to specify subnets in MULTIPLES Availability Zones.
Use a Placement Group from EC2 with spread strategy for the underlying clusters ECS.
questions.explanation: The ECS automatically distributes the service tasks between the specified sub-networks/AZs; thus, an AZ failure affects only the tasks running in that AZ, and the ECS can restart lost tasks in remaining healthy AZs to maintain desired count.
questions.hint: Think about what part of the service network configuration ECS determines in which Availability Zones your tasks can be launched.
optionRationales: The ECS automatically distributes the service tasks between the specified sub-networks/AZs; thus, an AZ failure affects only the tasks running in that AZ, and the ECS can restart lost tasks in remaining healthy AZs to maintain desired count.
More replicas in a ONE AZ does not provide resilience to the failure of that AZ; all replicas would be unavailable simultaneously if that AZ fails.

The Fargate does not use instances EC2 managed by the client or placement groups (is serverless); even in ECS based on EC2, the distribution between AZs of tasks is controlled by the sub-networks specified in the service network configuration and by task positioning strategies, not by placement groups of the EC2.

Health checks Route 53 are used to fail DNS between ENDPOINTS, not to trigger task scheduling/positioning actions of the ECS; the distribution of tasks between AZs is determined by the configuration of sub-networks of the service, not by Route 53.

questions.text: One Auto Scaling Group executes application servers that, when finished (for example during a scale-in), need to complete an ordered shutdown procedure — unregister a service registry, save buffers to memory in S3 and notify a monitoring system — leading up to 3 minutes, ANTES that the instance is effectively terminated. Currently, the instances are terminated immediately in the scale-in, causing data loss in buffers. ASG must be configured to allow this graceful closing process to be completed?
options: Configure a lifecycle hook Auto Scaling for the transition 'Terminating'' (autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING).
Set the 'shutdown behavior' of the instances EC2 like stop instead of finish.'.
Use Amazon EventBridge to schedule a function Lambda performing cleaning tasks 3 minutes ANTES of each scheduled scale-in event.
Increase health check grace period Auto Scaling Group for 3 minutes.
questions.explanation: The lifecycle hook places the instance in the state 'Terminating:Wait' by a configurable heartbeat timeout (which can cover the 3 necessary minutes, or more with heartbeat records); during this period, the instance closing script can complete its cleaning tasks before signaling completion (CompleteLifecycleAction) or before the timeout expires and the termination continues.
questions.hint: Think of the mechanism of Auto Scaling which places an instance in a waiting state during a transition (as termination), allowing a script to complete tasks before the action continues.
optionRationales: The lifecycle hook places the instance in the state 'Terminating:Wait' by a configurable heartbeat timeout (which can cover the 3 necessary minutes, or more with heartbeat records); during this period, the instance closing script can complete its cleaning tasks before signaling completion (CompleteLifecycleAction) or before the timeout expires and the termination continues.

The health check grace period applies to newly-launched instances (giving time to pass the health checks before being considered for replacement), not to instances being TERMINADAS during the stairway; it does not delay or control the termination process.

The Shutdown behavior attribute of EC2 controls what happens when the SISTEMA OPERACIONAL starts a shutdown (stop vs. finish the instance), but does not provide a hook for the ASG wait for a graceful closure procedure at the application level before proceeding with the end of the scale-in.

This approach would require precise provision of QUANDO the scale-in events will occur (which are driven by dynamic scaling policies based on metrics, not by a fixed schedule), making this approach unreliable; the same ASG needs to pause the termination via lifecycle hook, not depend on external scheduling.

questions.text: A company executes an active-passive multi-region application (us-east)-1 primary, eu-west-1 secondary), currently using simple failover routing of Route 53 with health checks. She wants a more robust and auditable mechanism for INICIAR a regional failure that: (a) can be safely activated even if the plane/API control of the failed region is degraded (the failure decision should not depend on the unhealthy region being accessible); (b) includes built-in security mechanisms to avoid accidental failure simultaneously for multiple regions ('split-brain'); and (c) provides promptness checks (readiness checks) to confirm that the secondary region can actually withstand total traffic before failure. AWS meets these three requirements?
options: AWS Global Accelerator with custom bearing weights manually adjusted by the console during a failover event.
Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC).
Simple failover routing policy of Route 53 with a manually updated health check.
Runbooks automation of AWS Systems Manager combined with CloudWatch to update records of the Route 53 way API during an interruption.
questions.explanation: The ARC provides Routing Controls (simple turn-on/off switches that can be safely activated even during a regional break, as the flat control and the flat date of the ARC are highly distributed between regions and do not depend on the health of the affected region), Routing Control Safety Rules (e.g. 'at least one of these two controls should be ON', avoiding split-brain or all off controls) and Readiness Checks (continually check if the recovery region has sufficient resources/configuration to take over traffic).
questions.hint: Think of the service of Route 53 designed specifically to orchestrate regional failures in a safe, auditable and independent manner of health of the affected region.
optionRationales: The ARC provides Routing Controls (simple turn-on/off switches that can be safely activated even during a regional break, as the flat control and the flat date of the ARC are highly distributed between regions and do not depend on the health of the affected region), Routing Control Safety Rules (e.g. 'at least one of these two controls should be ON', avoiding split-brain or all off controls) and Readiness Checks (continually check if the recovery region has sufficient resources/configuration to take over traffic).

That's the mechanism ATUAL, less robust, that the company wants to replace; the failure based only on standard health check does not provide explicit and auditable routing control switches, the rules of safety against split-brain, nor the readiness checks that the ARC add.

Although technically possible to build custom automation, this is an 'make yourself' approach that does not have the specific safety rules of ARC (prevention of split-brain), readiness checks, nor a highly available and independent regional health control plan — ARC is the service of the AWS designed specifically for this use case.

The Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and can redistribute traffic by weight between endpoints, but manually adjust weights during an interruption does not provide structured routing control safety mechanisms, readiness checks, or the guarantee of accessibility of the flat control during a regional interruption that the ARC Provides specifically.

questions.text: An architecture team wants to proactively validate that the mechanisms of resilience of the application (substitution of unhealthy instances by Auto Scaling, cause RDS Multi-AZ, etc.) actually work as expected, deliberately injecting controlled failures (e.g. finishing a percentage of instances EC2 of a ASG, or trigger a failover of the RDS) in a secure, monitored and reversible staging environment — following the principles of chaos engineering. AWS is designed specifically for this?
options: AWS Configure with custom remediation actions configured to 'fail' resources for test purposes.
Verifications of tolerance to faults of the AWS Trusted Advisor, periodically executed against the staging environment.
Canary Islands Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics configured to simulate traffic peaks against application.
AWS Fault Injection Simulator (AWS FIS).
questions.explanation: The AWS FIS is a fully managed service to perform controlled failure injection experiments (e.g.: 'stop X% of instances EC2', 'trigger throttling from API', 'cause a cluster to fail RDS Multi-AZ'), with stop conditions based on alarms of CloudWatch which automatically interrupt the experiment if they cause unexpected impact — supporting chaos engineering to validate resilience.
questions.hint: Think about the managed service of AWS specifically designed to perform chaos engineering experiments with automatic safety shutdown mechanisms.
optionRationales: The AWS FIS is a fully managed service to perform controlled failure injection experiments (e.g.: 'stop X% of instances EC2', 'trigger throttling from API', 'cause a cluster to fail RDS Multi-AZ'), with stop conditions based on alarms of CloudWatch which automatically interrupt the experiment if they cause unexpected impact — supporting chaos engineering to validate resilience.

The AWS Config evaluates resource settings against rules and can trigger remediation for resources NO CONFORMES; it was not designed to deliberately inject failures into healthy resources as part of chaos engineering experiments..

Synthetics canaries are roteirized tests that monitor the availability/performance of out-of-the-box endpoints (synthetic monitoring); they do not inject infrastructure-level failures (such as finishing instances or trigger database failures) into the environment.

The Trusted Advisor provides recommendations/verifications PASSIVAS on good configuration practices (e.g.: 'east ASG covers only 1 AZ'); it does not inject faults actively or perform controlled experiments.

questions.text: An instance EC2 standalone (out of a Auto Scaling Group, for example, a legacy application that requires a stable ID Forum and volumes EBS/Private IP attached) occasionally becomes inaccessible due to an underlying hardware failure detected by the status checks of EC2 (The team wants this instance to be automatic. RECUPERADA (restarted in new underlying hardware, preserving the same ID, private IP, Elastic IP and volume attachments EBS) when this hardware failure is detected — without manual intervention and without using a ASG. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Create an alarm from CloudWatch in the metric 'StatusCheckFailed_Instruction', with the alarm action defined as 'Reboot this instance'.
Create an alarm from CloudWatch in the instance 'StatusCheckFailed_System' metric, with the alarm action defined as 'Recover this instance'' (EC2 Auto Recovery).
Place the instance in a Auto Scaling Group with minimum, maximum and desired capacity defined as 1.
Configure the AWS Systems Manager Automation to execute a document SSM that stops and starts the instance every hour as a preventive measure.
questions.explanation: The StatusCheckFailed_System metric reflects underlying hardware/hypervisor problems (non-OS level checks); by triggering the 'Recover this instance' action, the AWS migrates and automatically restarts the instance into new underlying hardware, preserving your ID Forum, private IPs, Elastic IPs and Volume Attachments EBS.
questions.hint: Think about which specific status check metric EC2 reflects underlying hardware failures (instead of operating system problems), and in which alarm action migrates the instance preserving its identity.
optionRationales: The StatusCheckFailed_System metric reflects underlying hardware/hypervisor problems (non-OS level checks); by triggering the 'Recover this instance' action, the AWS migrates and automatically restarts the instance into new underlying hardware, preserving your ID Forum, private IPs, Elastic IPs and Volume Attachments EBS.

StatusCheckFailed_Instruction reflects SO/software level problems in MESMO underlying host; a simple reboot would not help with a failure of HARDWARE underlying (the instance would probably fail again on the same defective hardware), and the reboot does not migrate the instance to new hardware as Auto Recovery does.

This would change the identity of the instance in the substitution: substitution instances launched by the ASG receive one NOVO Mechanism ID (and usually a new private IP, unless you use a ENI the Auto Recovery preserves the identity of the original instance, while the replacement by ASG creates a new instance.

A fixed-time stop/start is not triggered by a truly detected hardware failure (it is a 'dark' preventive action), causing unnecessary unavailability during normal operation and not specifically treating detected hardware failures via status checks.

questions.text: A company executes a API multi-region active-using API Gateway (regional endpoints)) + Lambda + DynamoDB Global Tables, implemented in us-east-1 and me-west-1, with latency routing Route 53 targeting users to the nearest healthy region. DynamoDB Global Tables uses conflict resolution 'last writer wins' with eventual consistency between replicas. What architectural consideration is most important for this active-active architecture avoid silent loss of data/overwritten DURANTE OPERATION NORMAL (not only during failover)?
options: Configure the DynamoDB Global Tables in 'strong consistency' mode for replication between regions, preventing any conflict.
Trust in latency routing Route 53 to ensure that each user is always directed to the same region, eliminating the possibility of competing writings between regions in the same item.
Use transactions from DynamoDB (TransactWriteItems) in any writing to ensure atomicity between replicas of both regions simultaneously.

Design the application so that, for items that can be modified by users in MULTIPLE regions, written in MESMO item from different regions are minimized or use a conflict-resilient pattern (e.g. partitioning items so that each is usually written only from a 'dona' region, use conditional expressions, or design idempotent/additive updates).
questions.explanation: The 'last writer wins' resolution of DynamoDB Global Tables can silently overwrite concurrent updates to the same item made in different regions, even outside a failure scenario; therefore, active-active design needs to consider this from the beginning — through partitioning by 'domestic region', writing conditions or updating patterns that tolerate conflicts — not only during failure.
questions.hint: Think of the conflict resolution model of the DynamoDB Global Tables and how it behaves when the MESMO item is written from different regions in a short time interval, regardless of whether or not there is a failover in progress.
optionRationales: The 'last writer wins' resolution of DynamoDB Global Tables can silently overwrite concurrent updates to the same item made in different regions, even outside a failure scenario; therefore, active-active design needs to consider this from the beginning — through partitioning by 'domestic region', writing conditions or updating patterns that tolerate conflicts — not only during failure.

The DynamoDB Global Tables provides, by design, consistency EVENTUAL for replication between regions; there is no 'strong consistency' configuration option for replications between regions that would prevent competing competing writings from different regions.

Latency routing optimizes for the nearest region based on network conditions, which may change over time (or vary for users close to a border between regions), and not GARANTE that a particular user/item is always routed to a specific region — is a heuristic, not a partitioning/consistency mechanism.

The transactions of the DynamoDB ensure atomicity for multiple operations DENTRO of a single replica/table at the time of transaction; they do not provide atomic/synchronous coordination between regions for replicas of the Global Tables in different regions, which eventually remain consistent.

questions.text: A company's DR plan involves replicating workloads from a VPC in the primary region (us-east-1) for one VPC in the region of DR (us-west)-2). Both VPCs are attached to their respective AWS Transit Regional Gateways. The company needs that resources in VPC Of us-east-1 can communicate with resources in VPC of us-west-2 (for continuous replication of data and DR tests/validation) through the private backbone network of the AWS, without going through the public internet and without setting up VPN. What should be configured?
options: Enable the 'Multi-Region mode' in one of the Transit Gateways so it automatically covers both regions.
Use AWS Direct Connect with a VIF private in both regions to connect the two Transit Gateways.
Configure VPC Peering directly between the VPC Of us-east-1 and the VPC of us-west-2, in addition to the existing annexes to the Transit Gateway.

Configure Transit Gateway Peering (interregional peering annex) between the Transit Gateways of us-east-1 and us-west-2, and add appropriate routes to each route tables Transit Gateway (and the route tables of the attached VPCs) pointing to the peering annex towards the CIDRs of the other region.
questions.explanation: The Transit Gateway Peering provides private connectivity through the global backbone network of AWS between Transit Gateways from different regions; with the appropriate routes configured on both sides, the VPCs attached to each Transit Gateway can communicate between regions without the internet or VPN.
questions.hint: Think about the attachment type of the Transit Gateway specifically designed to connect two Transit Gateways located in different regions by the backbone of AWS.
optionRationales: The Transit Gateway Peering provides private connectivity through the global backbone network of AWS between Transit Gateways from different regions; with the appropriate routes configured on both sides, the VPCs attached to each Transit Gateway can communicate between regions without the internet or VPN.

Although the VPC Peering between regions is technically possible and use the backbone of AWS, it would be redundant/conflicting with existing annexes to Transit Gateway (VPC Peering and annexes TGW for the same VPCs can create router complexity; Transit Gateway Peering is the most consistent approach when both VPCs are already managed via Transit Gateway, especially if more VPCs/accounts need similar connectivity in the future.

The Direct Connect provides connectivity between networks ON-PREMISES and the AWS, not a mechanism to connect two Transit Gateways from AWS in regions different from each other; it is unnecessary and does not directly solve the connectivity TGW-for-TGW between regions.

An appeal Transit Gateway It's REGIONAL; there is no 'Multi-Region mode' that extends a single resource Transit Gateway between regions — connecting Transit Gateways from different regions requires an explicit peering annex.

questions.text: A company executes the Amazon RDS for MySQL in a traditional Multi-AZ deployment (one standby). During failure events, the observed unavailability is 60-120 The company wants to reduce the time to fail to less than one second, and the standby instance cannot be used for reading traffic. ~35 second And manage to download part of the reading traffic for standby instances, keeping the architecture fully managed by RDS (without migrating Aurora). What configuration they should migrate to?
options: Implementation RDS Multi-AZ DB Cluster, with a writer and DUAS readable standby instances distributed in 3 Availability Zones, using a reading endpoint dedicated to booths.
Migrate to Read Replica RDS in the same region, configured as the Multi-AZ standby.
Migratory to Aurora MySQL with a single Aurora Replica.
Increase the instance class of the traditional Multi-AZ deployment to reduce the time to fail.
questions.explanation: The Multi-AZ DB Cluster of RDS provides a writeer and two readable stands in different AZs, with semi-synchronous replication based on quorum that reduces the time to failover to typically less than 35 second; moreover, a dedicated reader (reader endpoint) allows to distribute reading traffic to booths, unlike the traditional Multi-AZ, in which the booth is not accessible.
questions.hint: Think about the latest Multi-AZ implementation variant of RDS which adds a second readable standby and drastically reduces the time to fail compared to the traditional single instance Multi-AZ.
optionRationales: The Multi-AZ DB Cluster of RDS provides a writeer and two readable stands in different AZs, with semi-synchronous replication based on quorum that reduces the time to failover to typically less than 35 second; moreover, a dedicated reader (reader endpoint) allows to distribute reading traffic to booths, unlike the traditional Multi-AZ, in which the booth is not accessible.
Read Replicas use ASSINCRONA replication and are not automatically used to fail the Multi-AZ; manual promotion would be required, which increases the time to fail, contrary to the requirement.

The Aurora is a database engine different from RDS traditional; the requirement explicitly asks for a solution that remains fully managed by RDS (without migrating Aurora), therefore, this option is contrary to the declared restriction.

The failover time of the traditional Multi-AZ (based on update of DNS, ~60-120(s) is largely independent of the size of the instance; increasing the class would not reduce the time to ~35s would not enable reading traffic on standby.

questions.text: A company executes Apache Kafka in Amazon MSK for a critical event streaming pipeline. The cluster MSK is currently provided with brokers in only UMA Availability Zone. To improve the resilience against failure of an AZ (unavailability of brokers causing partition leader elections and potential loss of messages in topics with replication factor 1), what changes should be made?
options: Enable a Multi-Region replication feature from MSK to mirror the cluster synchronously for one cluster in another AZ.
Configure the MSK Connect with a sink connector that backups all the data from the topics to the S3 every few minutes.

Reconfiguring the cluster MSK to implement brokers in (at least) 3 Availability Zones, and set up topics with replication factor of at least 3 (with min.insync.replicas appropriately defined, ex.: 2), so that the replicas of each partition are distributed among multiple AZs/brokers.
Increase the number of partitions of each topic within the single AZ cluster.
questions.explanation: With brokers distributed in multiple AZs and replication factor ≥3, a failure of AZ takes down only one subset of the replicas of each partition; the Kafka leader election mechanism promotes a replica in synchrony (in-sync replica) in a healthy AZ, without loss of data for properly confirmed writing (acks)).
questions.hint: Think of what two aspects of the configuration of the MSK (positioning of brokers and replication factor of topics) determine whether the replicas of a partition survive the failure of a single Availability Zone.
optionRationales: With brokers distributed in multiple AZs and replication factor ≥3, a failure of AZ takes down only one subset of the replicas of each partition; the Kafka leader election mechanism promotes a replica in synchrony (in-sync replica) in a healthy AZ, without loss of data for properly confirmed writing (acks)).

Increasing the number of partitions improves the PARALELISMO/throughput, but does not resolve the resilience at AZ level if all brokers (and therefore all replicas of partitions) reside in the same AZ; a failure of AZ would still knock down all replicas.

The MSK does not have a 'multi-region synchronous mirroring' feature for intracluster resilience between AZs; the AZ level resilience comes from the positioning of brokers between AZs and the configuration of the replication factor within a single regional cluster — replication between regions (for DR) is obtained via MSK Replicator/MirrorMaker, a different concern of AZ resilience in a single region.

Back up for the S3 provides a DR/recovery mechanism for historical data, but does not resolve resilience/availability IMEDIATA of the streaming pipeline in production against a failure of AZ (producers/consumers in progress would still be interrupted); the correction must be in the positioning of brokers/cluster replicas.

questions.text: A developer accidentally executed, there 4 hours, a script that deleted thousands of items from a table DynamoDB The team needs to recover these items, restoring the table to the state at a specific point in the time immediately prior to the script execution, with minimal impact on the table in production (which continued to receive new writings since the incident and should remain operational).?
options: Use AWS Backup to complete table restoration, which automatically mixes restored items with the table in production without creating a new table.
Enable DynamoDB Streams retroactively and reproduce the stream of 4 hours ago to recreate deleted items.
Restore the table from the latest on-demand backup made before the incident, overwriting the current production table.

Use Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) of the DynamoDB to restore the table in a NOVA table reflecting the status in the chosen timestamp (right before exclusion); then identify and selectively copy the excluded items from the restored table back to the production table in use.

questions.hint: Think about the resource of DynamoDB which allows to restore the table status in a specific timestamp for a new table, without affecting the original table in production.
optionRationales: The PITR of the DynamoDB always restores for one NOVA table, reflecting the status in a specific timestamp, without affecting the production table in operation; from this new table, excluded items can be identified and copied selectively back to the table in production (via script or job of the AWS Glue, for example), without interrupting ongoing operations.

Restore a backup SOBRE the table in production (in-place) would discard all the legitimate writings made in the table since the incident, and the restorations of the DynamoDB always create one NOVA table instead of overwriting on site; this approach would cause additional unnecessary data loss.

The DynamoDB Streams retains data by only 24 hours And need to be enabled ANTES of events occur to capture them; enabling it now would not provide retroactively a stream of events of 4 hours ago (before being enabled), therefore exclusion events (and previous states of items) are not available for reproduction.

The AWS Backup (and native restoration of DynamoDB) always restores for one NOVA table, never 'mix' automatically with the table in production; a manual reconciliation step is required regardless of the restoration mechanism used.

questions.text: A function Lambda is invoked in an ASSINCRONA way (for example, from notifications of events of the S3) to process sent files. Occasionally, the function fails after exhausting its automatic retaliatory (2 default retentes for asynchronous invocations). The team wants faulty invocations to be automatically directed to a row SQS for analysis and subsequent reprocessing, SEM modify function code Lambda to add explicit logic of error/filing treatment.
options: Involve the treatment code of the event of the S3 in a try/catch block and use the AWS SDK to manually call SQS SendMessage when capturing an exception.
Configure a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) in the function and add code in the function to publish a custom message in that DLQ by capturing an error.
Configure an on-failure Destination Lambda pointing to a row SQS (or topical SNS/bus EventBridge/other function Lambda).
Increase the reserved competition of the function so that faulty invocations are reprocessed more often before giving up.
questions.explanation: After the asynchronous invocation retentatives are exhausted and the function still fails, the Lambda automatically send a record of the invocation (including the original event payload and error details) to the configured failure destination — no need for any change in function code.
questions.hint: Think about the resource of Lambda, configured outside the function code, which automatically forwards the event and error details to a destination after exhausting the asynchronous invocation retentatives.
optionRationales: After the asynchronous invocation retentatives are exhausted and the function still fails, the Lambda automatically send a record of the invocation (including the original event payload and error details) to the configured failure destination — no need for any change in function code.

Although DLQs are a valid (legacy) mechanism to capture asynchronous invocations with failure, this option describes the need for ADICIONAR code in the function to be published in DLQ — or contrary to the requirement to 'without changing the code'; or Lambda it is already automatically forwarding to the DLQ configured after exhausting the retentatives, but Destinations is the most recent and recommended mechanism, without requiring any code change.

The reserved competition controls the MAXIMUM number of simultaneous executions, not the number of retry attempts for failed asynchronous invocations; it does not direct failed invocations to any place for analysis.

This approach requires changing the function code (against the declared requirement) and would not capture failures that occur FORA of try/catch (e.g. function timeout, memory failure, or crash before reaching the catch) — Lambda Destinations capture faults regardless of failure mode.

questions.text: A function Lambda processes messages from a row SQS, where each message can lead from 30 seconds to 10 minutes to be processed, depending on the size of the payload (the function timeout) Lambda is configured for 15 The visibility timeout of the row SQS is configured for 30 seconds. The team notes that long processing messages (which take several minutes) are being captured and processed by MULTIPLE invocations Lambda competitors simultaneously, causing duplicate processing and waste of resources, even without errors. What is causing this and how to correct?
options: The visibility timeout (30s) is less than the actual processing time of many messages; when it expires (while the original invocation is still processing), the SQS makes the message visible again and another invocation capture, processing it competitively. fix: increase the visibility timeout of the row to be MAIOR that the maximum expected processing time (e.g. at least equal to the timeout of the function, 15 minutes, ideally with margin).
The problem is caused by the queue SQS do not have a dead-letter tail configured, making the messages enter loop indefinitely.
The problem is caused by the batch size of the event source mapping of Lambda be configured with a very high value, making the same message appear in multiple batches.
The problem is caused by the reserved competition of the function Lambda be configured with a very high value, allowing parallel invocations in excess.
questions.explanation: When the visibility timeout expires before the original processing ends, or SQS considers the message available again to other consumers, resulting in duplicate concurrent processing of the same message without any error; aligning the visibility timeout to exceed the maximum processing time ensures that the message remains invisible throughout the processing attempt.
questions.hint: Think of the relationship between the visibility timeout of the row SQS and the real time needed to process a message — what happens if the timeout expires before processing ends?
optionRationales: When the visibility timeout expires before the original processing ends, or SQS considers the message available again to other consumers, resulting in duplicate concurrent processing of the same message without any error; aligning the visibility timeout to exceed the maximum processing time ensures that the message remains invisible throughout the processing attempt.

The reserved competition limits parallelism, but does not explain why the MESMA message is processed multiple times; this specific symptom (the same concurrently reprocessed message) is a problem of visibility timeout, not competition limit.

DLQs handle messages that fail repeatedly after maxReceiveCount attempts; they do not resolve messages that become visible again ENQUANTO they are still being successfully processed due to a very short visibility timeout, which is the symptom described (no errors occurring).).

The SQS ensures that a given message is delivered in just one batch, to one consumer at a time (as invisible); the batch size affects how many messages are grouped by invocation, but does not cause duplication of the message. MESMA message between competing invocations — this is specifically a problem of expiration of visibility timeout.

questions.text: An event-oriented architecture uses the Amazon EventBridge to route events from various producers to multiple consumers (functions) Lambda/Targets). 6 hours, the function Lambda of one of the consumers had a bug that caused her to fail silently by processing certain events correctly (without launching errors that would trigger retaliatory/DLQ). After correcting the bug, the team needs REPROCESSAR all events sent to EventBridge during this window of 6 hours, reproducing them for function Lambda corrected, without affecting other consumers who processed these events correctly the first time. What approach meets this requirement?
options: Use EventBridge Archive (if an archive has been configured on the event bus to retain corresponding events) and the EventBridge Replay to play archived events from the 6 hours for one NOVA rule/target pointing only to function Lambda corrected.
Re-activate original event producers to forward all events from this window 6 hours.
Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to extract the payloads from the events of the log EventBridge and manually invoke the function Lambda for each route AWS CLI.
Increase the retention period of the DLQ function Lambda so that events with this window failure can be reprocessed from the DLQ.

optionRationales: The Replay of EventBridge send the events archived as new events (with a replay metadata marker), directed to the chosen rule(s); when creating a new rule pointing only to the function Lambda corrected, the replay reprocesses only for this consumer, without affecting the original consumers who are not part of the replay.

This would require that producers have retained or could regenerate exactly these historic events, and would forward them to TODOS the original targets/consumers (not just the corrected one), potentially causing unwanted reprocessing in consumers who have already worked correctly the first time.

This is a totally manual process, prone to errors and unscalable on scale for potentially thousands of events; the EventBridge Archive/Replay is the native mechanism specifically designed for this scenario.

The scenario specifies that the function failed SILENCIOSAMENTE (without making mistakes), so the events never entered a DLQ; there's nothing on DLQ for reprocessing, since the EventBridge/Lambda Never recorded these executions as failures.

questions.text: An organization has dozens of applications, each with a defined architecture via CloudFormation/Terraform, but without a formal way of assessing whether the actual configuration of each application in AWS meets the goals of RTO and RPO as defined by the NEGOTIATION, or to identify specific resilience gaps (e.g.: 'the database of this application is not Multi-AZ, but its target of RTO They want a service that analyzes the actual configuration of the resources. AWS of an application in relation to RTO/RPO which service meets this requirement.?
options: AWS Well-Architected Tool with the selected Reliability pillar.
Checks in the 'Fault Tolerance' category of the AWS Trusted Advisor.
AWS Resilience Hub.
AWS Optimizer Computers.
questions.explanation: The AWS Resilience Hub allows you to define an application (importing stack features from CloudFormation, status of Terraform or tag-marked resources), define goals of RTO/RPO based on a chosen resilience policy, and perform an evaluation; the Resilience Hub analyzes the actual configuration (e.g. Multi-AZ configurations, backup configurations) in relation to the goals, producing a resilience score and specific and actionable recommendations to close identified gaps..
questions.hint: Think of the service of AWS specifically designed to define quantitative targets of RTO/RPO for an application and automatically evaluate your real configuration against these goals.
optionRationales: The AWS Resilience Hub allows you to define an application (importing stack features from CloudFormation, status of Terraform or tag-marked resources), define goals of RTO/RPO based on a chosen resilience policy, and perform an evaluation; the Resilience Hub analyzes the actual configuration (e.g. Multi-AZ configurations, backup configurations) in relation to the goals, producing a resilience score and specific and actionable recommendations to close identified gaps..

The Trusted Advisor provides general verifications of good practice (e.g.: ELB has less than 2 health care institutions') in the whole account, but does not allow defining goals of RTO/RPO specific by application or evaluate the architecture of a specific application in relation to these custom goals with a resilience score.
Computer Optimizer provides rightsizing recommendations for computing resources (EC2, Lambda, EBS, etc.) based on use, focused on cost/performance optimization, not on resilience assessment/RTO/RPO.

The Well-Architected Tool is a majority self-assessment process MANUAL, based on questionnaires answered by humans about architecture; it does not automatically analyze the real configurations of the implemented resources in relation to quantitative goals of the RTO/RPO to produce a resilience score as the Resilience Hub does.

questions.text: A company needs to update its database Amazon RDS for MySQL production for a new version MAJOR They are concerned about the risk of a major in-place upgrade (which requires unavailability and brings about a risk of compatibility problems discovered only after the upgrade, with complex rollback). They want to: create a complete copy of the production environment with the new version of the engine, validate it thoroughly with tests equivalent to those of production, and then make the turn (switchover) with minimal unavailability (seconds) — with the ability to quickly revoke if problems are found shortly after the turn.?
options: Perform major in-place update during a maintenance window, relying on the automatic snapshot taken before update to rollback if necessary.
Use AWS DMS to perform a single homogeneous (one-time) migration of the bank in the old version to a new bank running the new version of the engine, and then redirect traffic.

Use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments — o RDS creates a fully managed staging environment ('green'), synchronized with production ('blue') via logical replication, but running the new engine version/configuration; after validation, the RDS performs a switchhover (typically with less than a minute of writing unavailability) that promotes the 'green' the new production, keeping the 'blue' available briefly for fast rollback if necessary.
Create a Read Replica with the new version of the engine, validate it, then promote it to the independent instance and update the connection string of the application.
questions.explanation: The Blue/Green Deployments RDS keeps the green environment synchronized with the continuous changes of the blue via logical replication, allowing complete tests against the green without impacting the production; when ready, the managed switchhover promotes the green with writing unavailability typically less than a minute, and the blue can be temporarily maintained for fast rollback.
questions.hint: Think about the resource of RDS which creates a fully synchronized staging environment with production via logical replication, allowing a managed twistchover with minimal unavailability.
optionRationales: The Blue/Green Deployments RDS keeps the green environment synchronized with the continuous changes of the blue via logical replication, allowing complete tests against the green without impacting the production; when ready, the managed switchhover promotes the green with writing unavailability typically less than a minute, and the blue can be temporarily maintained for fast rollback.

Promote a Read Replica independent instance is a manual and unidirectional operation; changing the connection string of the application introduces more unavailability/coordination than the managed Blue/Green switchhover (which preserves the same endpoint), and there is no integrated fast rollback path back to the original blue environment after promotion.

This is the most risky and unavailable approach that the company explicitly wants EVITAR; reverse from a pre-update snapshot means restoring a new instance from it (losing written after snapshot) and updating endpoints, which is slower and with more data loss than the Blue/Green switchhover/rollback.

A single migration DMS captures the data at a point in time, requiring a cutover plan to deal with continuous writings during migration (the CDC of the DMS may help, but the DMS is not the native and fully managed mechanism of RDS for in-place engine version updates with synchronized staging and quick switchover/rollback, such as Blue/Green Deployments).

questions.text: A global application has its primary writing workload in us-east-1 using Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, and wants to provide access to LEITURA low latency to the same cached data for an application implanted in ap-souteast-1, with cached data kept in almost real-time synchrony of us-east-1 for ap-souteast-1, and the ability to promote the ap-souteast cluster-1 to accept writings (becoming the new primary) if us-east-1 Which ElastiCache resource meets this requirement?
options: Amazon ElestiCache Global Datastore for Redis.
Use ElastiCache for Memcached with Auto Discovery enabled in both regions.
Employ independent ElastiCache for Redis clusters in both regions and use functions Lambda powered by Redis Keyspace Notifications to replicate writings between them.
Configure ElastiCache for Redis with Multi-AZ enabled, which automatically extends the replication group between regions.
questions.explanation: The Global Datastore provides a fully managed replication mechanism between regions, replicating data from a primary cluster (us-east)-1) for one or more secondary clusters in other regions (ap-souteast)-1), allowing low latency local readings in ap-souteast-1; in case of regional interruption, the secondary cluster region can be promoted the new primary, starting to accept written.
questions.hint: Think about the ElastiCache for Redis feature designed specifically for asynchronous replication ENTRE REGIONS with primary secondary cluster promotion capacity.
