optionRationales: The Global Datastore provides a fully managed replication mechanism between regions, replicating data from a primary cluster (us-east)-1) for one or more secondary clusters in other regions (ap-souteast)-1), allowing low latency local readings in ap-souteast-1; in case of regional interruption, the secondary cluster region can be promoted the new primary, starting to accept written.

Build replica between custom regions via Lambda and keyspace notifications is complex, introduces additional latency/cost and brings data inconsistency risks, when ElastiCache Global Datastore already provides this as a fully managed native resource.

Multi-AZ in ElastiCache for Redis provides automatic replication and failure ENTRE ZONAS OF DISPONIBILIDADE DENTRO OF UMA SINGLE REGION; it does not extend between REGIONS — replication between regions specifically requires Global Datastore.

Memcached has no built-in replication mechanism (it's a simple distributed cache without persistence or replication relationships), and Auto Discovery only helps customers to discover cache nodes DENTRO of a single cluster, not to replicate data between regions.

questions.text: A company has two workflows in AWS Step Functions: (1) IoT telemetry processing, with millions of short executions (a few seconds) per day, where the cost per execution is priority and semantic 'at-last-once' (at least once) is acceptable, since the processing is identical; (2) processing of payments, with much smaller volume, longer executions, demanding semantics of execution 'exactly-once' (exactly once) and complete history of execution (visible in the console by up 90 days) for audit/compliance. What type of workflow of Step Functions should be used for (1) and to (2), respectively?
options: Express Workflows for both (1) and (2), since Express Workflows are cheaper and support all the same features as Standard.
Express Workflows for (1) and Standard Workflows for (2).
Express Workflows for (1) and AWS Step Functions Activities (with workers EC2 making polling of tasks) to (2), avoiding Standard Workflows completely.
Standard Workflows for both (1) and (2), since Standard Workflows provide semantics exactly-once for all use cases.
questions.explanation: Express Workflows are precised by duration/number of executions and optimized for high volume and short duration loads at lower cost, but provide semantics 'at-last-once' (with history sent to CloudWatch Logs, not to the history of 90 Console days). Standard Workflows provide semantics 'exactly-once' and maintain running history by up to 90 days in the console of Step Functions, suitable for smaller, longer and more audit-sensitive workflows, such as payment processing.
questions.hint: Think of what two types of workflow Step Functions differ in precision, semantics of execution (at-last-once vs. exactly-once) and retention of the execution history in the console.
optionRationales: Express Workflows are precised by duration/number of executions and optimized for high volume and short duration loads at lower cost, but provide semantics 'at-last-once' (with history sent to CloudWatch Logs, not to the history of 90 Console days). Standard Workflows provide semantics 'exactly-once' and maintain running history by up to 90 days in the console of Step Functions, suitable for smaller, longer and more audit-sensitive workflows, such as payment processing.

Using Standard Workflows for the high volume case of IoT would be considerably more expensive (Standard is precised by state transition, which becomes costly in millions of executions/day) compared to Express, which is optimized exactly for this pattern..

Express Workflows provide only semantic 'at-last-once' and do not retain the execution history of 90 days in the console of Step Functions (the logs go to the CloudWatch Logs); this does not meet the requirements of workflow (2) of semantics exactly-once and history of friendly execution for audit.

Activities are a task integration standard (for integration with external workers)/EC2/on-premises), usable within standard or express workflows; are not a TIPO alternative workflow and do not by themselves provide semantics exactly-once or the execution history of 90 days — these properties come specifically from the Standard Workflow type choice.

questions.text: A company executes an Oracle on-premises production database and wants to keep a warm-standby copy of that database continuously updated in a RDS for Oracle in us-west-2 (the DR region), with the on-premises bank changes replicated with low latency (minutes), without requiring changes in the application used by the on-premises bank. In case of on-premises disaster, the instance RDS in us-west-2 would be promoted/used as a new primary. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Make backups RMAN Oracle on-premises bank journals and restore them in the instance RDS for Oracle every few hours.
Use AWS Conversion Tool Scheme (SCT) to perform a single conversion and migration (one-time) of the schema and data to the RDS for Oracle.
Configure Oracle Data Guard in 'Maximum Performance' mode to replicate directly to instance RDS for Oracle.
Use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) with a replication task configured for 'full load + Change Data Capture (CDC)'.
questions.explanation: The DMS performs an initial full load (full load) of Oracle on-premises for the RDS for Oracle in us-west-2, and then capture and continuously apply the changes (CDC) from the log transaction/network of the home bank, keeping the destination in synchrony almost in real time, without requiring changes in the source application.
questions.hint: Think of the service of AWS designed specifically for continuous replication of databases via change capture for a managed destination bank, without changing the source application.
optionRationales: The DMS performs an initial full load (full load) of Oracle on-premises for the RDS for Oracle in us-west-2, and then capture and continuously apply the changes (CDC) from the log transaction/network of the home bank, keeping the destination in synchrony almost in real time, without requiring changes in the source application.

The SCT is intended primarily for the conversion of SCHEMAS database (especially in heterogeneous migrations) and initial migration; it does not provide continuous replication/CDC to keep the destination synchronized over time.

The RDS for Oracle is a managed service that DOES NOT provide the direct host level access necessary to configure Oracle Data Guard between an on-premises primary and a standby in RDS; Data Guard is not a supported configuration to replicate to RDS for Oracle from external Oracle banks.

Regular backup/restoration provides RPO measured in HORAS (the interval between backups), not the replication 'minutes' CDC almost in real time required, in addition to being a manual/roteirized process operationally heavy compared to the CDC managed DMS.

questions.text: A company owns newsletters S3 with the same replicated data (via S3 Cross-Region Replication) between us-east-1 and me-west-1, for an active-active application. Currently, the application needs to know which bucket/region to use, and implements its own logic to fail to the bucket of the other region if the primary becomes inaccessible. The company wants a ONLY global endpoint that the application can use for requests to S3, with the AWS automatically routing each request for the bucket replica in the lower latency (or healthy) region, eliminating the need for the application to manage endpoints by region and failover logic.?
options: Create a S3 Multi-Region Access Point covering the us-east-1 and me-west-1.
Configure the S3 Transfer Acceleration on both bucks so that requests are automatically routed to the nearest bucket.
Create a distribution of Amazon CloudFront with both bucks S3 configured as an origin group to fail.
Use latency routing Route 53 with two records pointing to the endpoint S3 regional of each bucket.
questions.explanation: The application uses the endpoint/ARN Multi-Region Access Point unique global for all requests to S3; a AWS automatically route each request (using the network of AWS Global Accelerator) for the lower latency healthy bucket replica, with automatic failover for the other region's bucket if one of them is unavailable — the application no longer needs endpoint logic by region.
questions.hint: Think about the resource of S3 designed specifically to provide a single global access point that automatically rotates between replicas of buckets in multiple regions.
optionRationales: The application uses the endpoint/ARN Multi-Region Access Point unique global for all requests to S3; a AWS automatically route each request (using the network of AWS Global Accelerator) for the lower latency healthy bucket replica, with automatic failover for the other region's bucket if one of them is unavailable — the application no longer needs endpoint logic by region.

The CloudFront with origin groups provides failover for delivery of CONTENT to end users (read access style HTTP GET way CDN), but was not designed to be a transparent endpoint for general operations of the API of the S3 of an APPLICATION (e.g.: PutObject from application servers), as the Multi-Region Access Points are.

Bucket Points S3 (especially with virtual address-hosted-style and certificates SSL linked to specific Bucket/Regions names) are usually not designed to be accessed interchangeably via a name DNS customized with automatic router the way the Multi-Region Access Points were purposefully built; this would require meaningful custom engineering and would not provide the same automatic failover semantics for calls from API of the S3.

Transfer Acceleration accelerates transfers PARA A SPECIFIC Bucket Via edge locations of the CloudFront; it does not provide a single endpoint that routes between MULTIPLES buckets in different regions, nor does it provide failover between them.

questions.text: A web application statess runs on a Auto Scaling Group using a single type of instance (m5.large) in 2 AZs, totally with On-Demand instances. The company wants to reduce computing costs by incorporating Spot Instances, but is concerned that: (a) capacity Spot for m5.large may not always be available in sufficient quantity in any of the AZs (stopping the ASG (b) an interruption of the Spot affecting many instances of the same type simultaneously could cause a significant decrease in capacity. ASG must be configured to incorporate the economy of Spot Mitigating AMBAS concerns?
options: Use Scheduled Scaling to pre-provide On-Demand capacity during business hours and scale to zero out of time, avoiding Spot completely.
Migrate fully to Spot Instances with one type of instance, but set up a 'Spot max price' very high, equal to the price On-demand.

Configure the ASG with a 'mixed instance policy' specifying MULTIPLES compatible types of instance (e.g. m5.large, m5a.large, m4.large, m5.xlarge with weighted capacity) in MULTIPLES capacity pools Spot (combination of type of instance + AZ), together with a base number of instances On-Demand (or percentage On-Demand) for minimum guaranteed capacity.
Use a single instance Spot, but request capacity Spot in 4 Different AZs simultaneously to increase the chance of availability.
questions.explanation: Diversifying between types of instance and pools reduces the chance of simultaneous unavailability/interruption in all pools at the same time, while the On-Demand base ensures a minimum capacity always available — taking into account both company concerns.
questions.hint: Think of the recommendation of the AWS to mitigate both the unavailability of capacity and simultaneous interruptions of the Spot: multi-dimensional diversification (type of instance and AZ), combined with a guaranteed capacity base.
optionRationales: Diversifying between types of instance and pools reduces the chance of simultaneous unavailability/interruption in all pools at the same time, while the On-Demand base ensures a minimum capacity always available — taking into account both company concerns.

The ASG current operates on only 2 AZs (presumably where there are sub-networks of VPC); adding arbitrarily more AZs may not be feasible, and diversifying only by AZ (not by type of instance) still leaves a risk if that ONLY type of instance suffers from capacity shortage/wide interruption in all AZs simultaneously — diversification by type of instance is the most effective mitigation according to the recommendations of the AWS.

A higher max price affects only if the request Spot is served at the price Spot current (up to this limit) and the probability of interruption by PRICE, but does not resolve the availability of CAPACIDADE for that single pool type of instance/AZ, no interruptions due to capacity demand by AWS (which may occur irrespective of the price offered).

This approach avoids the Spot completely (not taking into account the cost reduction objective via Spot) and does not address the underlying issues about capacity diversification Spot; is an orthogonal cost optimization, not related to declared concerns.

questions.text: The multi-layer application of a company seems to be healthy according to health checks of infrastructure (status checks of the EC2 and target health of ALB, all green), but users occasionally report that the site's 'checkout' flow (a multi-stage journey involving login, add to cart and finish the purchase) is unavailable by 10-15 minutes before anyone realizes, because none of the existing health checks actually exercise this flow from end to end. The team wants detection PROATIVA and automated this type of problem — regularly simulating the actual journey of the user from outside the infrastructure and alerting in case of failure — to reduce the time to detection.?
options: Create a canary from Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics using a blueprint of the type 'heartbeat'/day that programmably executes the multi-step checkout flow (login, add to cart, finish shopping) on a schedule (e.g. to each 5 minutes) from outside the infrastructure; set up an alarm of the CloudWatch about the canary success rate/duration metrics to alert the team automatically in case of failure or degradation.
Enable AWS X-Ray in all services involved in the checkout flow to identify root cause after a user reports a problem.
Increase frequency of status check alarms EC2 no CloudWatch of 5 minutes to 1 minute.
Configure additional health checks from target group ALB with a more complex verification path that exercises the checkout flow.
questions.explanation: The Canary Islands CloudWatch Synthetics run scripts that simulate real user journeys and multi-stages from outside the infrastructure, on a regular schedule; combined with a CloudWatch on their metrics, provide proactive and automated detection of checkout flow failures before many real users are affected.
questions.hint: Think of the service of CloudWatch designed specifically to execute scripts that simulate real user journeys from outside the infrastructure, on a regular schedule.
optionRationales: The Canary Islands CloudWatch Synthetics run scripts that simulate real user journeys and multi-stages from outside the infrastructure, on a regular schedule; combined with a CloudWatch on their metrics, provide proactive and automated detection of checkout flow failures before many real users are affected.

Health checks ALB are simple periodic requests (HTTP/HTTPS/TCP) for a single path, with limited validation of the expected response; they were not designed to perform multi-stage and stateful user journeys (login → add to cart → purchase) involving multiple requests and session status.

X-Ray helps in root cause analysis AFTER a problem is detected/reported (reactive), but does not provide proactive and scheduled simulation of the user's journey to detect problems before users report them.

Status checks of EC2 reflect the health of the instance/hardware, not the functionality of a multi-stage user journey at application level; increasing its frequency would not detect a bug in the checkout flow when the underlying infrastructure is healthy.

questions.text: A company executes the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in us-east-1 with Multi-AZ enabled (protecting against AZ failures). REGIONAL complete with us-east-1, they create a Cross-Region Read Replica of RDS in us-west-2, knowing that this replica uses asynchronous replication (with some replication lag), RPO In the case of a regional break in us-east-1, what is the correct DR procedure using this replica between regions, and what the team should have in mind?
options: During interruption, PROMOVER manually to Cross-Region Read Replica of us-west-2 to become an instance RDS independent (one-way operation — the replica becomes primary and stops replicating); reconfigure the application (e.g. via updating of DNS/connection string) to point to this newly promoted instance; be aware that, because it is asynchronous replication, some recent transactions still not replicated at the time of interruption may be lost (RPO different from zero); and set up Multi-AZ separately in the instance now promoted in us-west-2 for continuous AZ-level resilience.
Since the replica is in another region, it is already automatically protected by Multi-AZ and does not require additional configuration after promotion.
The Cross-Region Read Replica automatically becomes the new primary and starts accepting written as soon as the health checks from Route 53 detect interruption in us-east-1, with zero data loss.
The application can continue writing on the original endpoint of us-east-1, and the RDS automatically redirect these writings to the instance promoted in us-west-2.
questions.explanation: The promotion of a Cross-Region Read Replica RDS It's an action. MANUAL and unidirectional; since replication is asynchronous, there is no guarantee of zero data loss (RPO > 0); and the promoted instance is a single instance that does not automatically inherit Multi-AZ protection — all this should be explicitly treated by the team as part of the DR procedure..
questions.hint: Think of what aspects of a Cross-Region Read Replica RDS are automatic and which require manual action of the operator — promotion, RPO and subsequent multi-AZ protection.
optionRationales: The promotion of a Cross-Region Read Replica RDS It's an action. MANUAL and unidirectional; since replication is asynchronous, there is no guarantee of zero data loss (RPO > 0); and the promoted instance is a single instance that does not automatically inherit Multi-AZ protection — all this should be explicitly treated by the team as part of the DR procedure..

Cross-Region Read Replica RDS DO NOT automatically promote themselves; promotion is an action MANUAL started by the operator/automation, and since the replication is asynchronous, zero data loss cannot be guaranteed (there is some RPO).

A Cross-Region Read Replica is a unique instance in the destination region; it does not inherit or automatically gain Multi-AZ protection — Multi-AZ should be explicitly configured in it (before or after promotion) if the continuous resilience at AZ level is desired.

During a regional interruption, the endpoint/instance of us-east-1 is not available; there is no automatic mechanism for redirecting writings between regions in RDS — the application should be explicitly reconfigured to point to the newly promoted instance endpoint..

questions.text: A service ECS running no launch type EC2 (no Fargate) has its tasks positioned using the positioning strategy FATHER, which the team discovers tends to concentrate ('binpack') the tasks in few container instances within the same AZ, to optimize the use of resources, leaving other AZs underutilized. This concentration means that a failure of AZ could drop a disproportionate number of service tasks. As the team must configure the positioning of tasks to ensure uniform distribution between AZs (and between instances within each AZ), prioritizing availability on bin-packing efficiency.?
options: Configure one CONSTRAINT 'distinctInstitution' type positioning for the service.
Change the launch type of the service EC2 for Fargate, which automatically distributes the tasks between AZs by default, without configuration.

Configure Service Positioning Strategy ECS as 'spread', using the 'attribute' field:ecs.availability-zone' as the primary distribution field (optionally combined with a secondary spread in instanceId to also distribute between hosts within each AZ).
Reduce the desired service count so that bin-packing naturally results in uniform distribution.
questions.explanation: The 'spread' strategy using 'attribute':ecs.availability-zone explicitly distributes the tasks uniformly between AZs (and, with a secondary spread in instanceId, also between instances within each AZ), exchanging some bin-packing efficiency for greater availability.
questions.hint: Think about the task positioning strategy of ECS which explicitly prioritizes uniform distribution between an attribute (as Availability Zone), rather than maximizing the use of resources.
optionRationales: The 'spread' strategy using 'attribute':ecs.availability-zone explicitly distributes the tasks uniformly between AZs (and, with a secondary spread in instanceId, also between instances within each AZ), exchanging some bin-packing efficiency for greater availability.

The constraint 'distinctInstitution' ensures that two tasks of the service do not rotate in the MESMA container instance, but does not specifically balance the distribution of tasks ENTRE ZONAS OF DISPONIBILIDADE; the tasks could still be concentrated in instances of the same AZ if most instances are there..

Although the standard positioning of the Fargate distributes among the AZs specified in the sub-networks of the service, the scenario specifies that the team uses the launch type EC2 and presumably have reasons (e.g. existing infrastructure, specific types of instance) to remain in EC2; completely changing the launch type is a much larger architectural change than simply changing the Service Positioning STRATEGY EC2 existing.

Reduce the desired count does not change the ALGORITMO of underlying positioning (binpack); with fewer tasks, the binpack would still tend to concentrate them in the least number of instances/AZs possible, not to distribute them evenly.

questions.text: A company runs a multiplayer game backend using protocols UDP customized (no HTTP/HTTPS), with game servers in instances EC2 in 2 Regions (us-east-1 and ap-northeast-1) behind Network Load Balancers in each region. The requirements are: (a) static IP addresses that the game's customers can fix/put on whitelist (no resolution dependent) DNS which could be cached); (b) automatic router of players' traffic to the optimal healthy region (minor latency); and (c) automatic failure for the NLB of the other region if the endpoints of a region become unhealthy. CloudFront does not support traffic UDP arbitrary, which service of AWS meets these requirements?
options: AWS Global Accelerator.
Amazon Route 53 with latency routing and health checks pointing to the name DNS of each NLB regional.
AWS Transit Gateway with multicast support configured between the two Regions.
Amazon CloudFront with two NLBs configured as origin group to fail.
questions.explanation: The Global Accelerator provides 2 static anycast IP addresses that act as a fixed entry point for the application (suitable for fixing/whitelist by the game's customers, supporting both TCP how much UDP), automatically route traffic through the global network of AWS for the group of endpoints (NLB) healthy lower latency based on geographic proximity and health checks, and makes automatic failover to other region's endpoints if NLB primary become unhealthy.
questions.hint: Think of the service of AWS that provides static fixed anycast IPs and supports both TCP how much UDP, with automatic routing and failure between regions — other than CloudFront, which is limited to HTTP/HTTPS.
optionRationales: The Global Accelerator provides 2 static anycast IP addresses that act as a fixed entry point for the application (suitable for fixing/whitelist by the game's customers, supporting both TCP how much UDP), automatically route traffic through the global network of AWS for the group of endpoints (NLB) healthy lower latency based on geographic proximity and health checks, and makes automatic failover to other region's endpoints if NLB primary become unhealthy.

The scenario specifies that the application uses protocols UDP personalized; or CloudFront is designed for content delivery HTTP/HTTPS (and RTMP in some cases legacy) and NOT supports traffic UDP Arbitrary, making it inappropriate here.

Rotation based on DNS provides IP addresses that can change and are subject to cache/TTL of DNS by customers (play clients who fix/place IPs in whitelist would break if the IPs underlying the name DNS change); does not provide IP addresses anycast FIXOS and statics required for fixing/whitelist on the client's side.

The multicast of Transit Gateway is to distribute multicast traffic DENTRO/ENTRE Network VPCs for specific multicast applications; is not a global traffic routing/failover solution to direct external player traffic to the optimal regional endpoint with static IPs.

questions.text: One VPC has an Interface VPC Endpoint (PrivateLink) for the Amazon S3 (or other supported service) configured with an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) in just UMA AZ (AZ-A), although the sub-networks of application of the VPC Cover 3 Azs (AZ-A, AZ-B and AZ-C). Fora in AZ-B and AZ-C currently route their traffic to this service through the ENI in AZ-A, incurring data transfer charges between AZs and creating a single failure point for PrivateLink connectivity if AZ-A How the Endpoint Interface needs to be reconfigured to solve both problems?
options: Configure a Gateway Load Balancer to distribute traffic to the ENI only from 3 Azs.
Edit Interface VPC Endpoint to add additional sub-network associations in AZ-B and AZ-C (one ENI by AZ).
Enable 'Cross-Zone Load Balancing' on Interface VPC Endpoint.
Create 3 Interface VPC Separate endpoints (one per AZ) for the same service, each in a different sub-network.
questions.explanation: With a ENI present in each AZ, instances in each AZ solve the name DNS from the endpoint to the ENI of SUA AZ (avoiding data transfer charges between AZs for PrivateLink traffic), and endpoint connectivity no longer depends on a single AZ.
questions.hint: Think of it as an Interface VPC Endpoint may be present in multiple Availability Zones — which configuration element is added by AZ?
optionRationales: With a ENI present in each AZ, instances in each AZ solve the name DNS from the endpoint to the ENI of SUA AZ (avoiding data transfer charges between AZs for PrivateLink traffic), and endpoint connectivity no longer depends on a single AZ.

Interface VPC Endpoints support adding multiple sub-network associations (AZ) to a single endpoint (creating a ENI by sub-network/associated AZ); create 3 fully separate endpoint resources is unnecessary, each would have names DNS/separate configurations to manage, and it's not how the Multi-AZ Interface Endpoints were designed to be implemented.

The Gateway Load Balancer is used to route traffic through third-party virtual applications (e.g. firewalls); is not a mechanism to provide multi-AZ redundancy of the ENIs of an Interface VPC Endpoint, and add one GWLB introduce unnecessary complexity and its own single point of failure.

Interface VPC Endpoints (PrivateLink) do not have a Cross-Zone Load Balancing configuration; this is a concept of load balancer (ELB) and does not apply to the ENI configuration of a VPC Endpoint. Multi-AZ endpoint resilience is obtained by associating multiple sub-networks, not by a cross-zone alternator.

questions.text: One VPC has private sub-networks in 3 Availability Zones (AZs), but all outbound traffic to the internet (e.g. calls to external APIs, patches downloads) is routed through a single NAT Gateway, implanted in the public sub-network of the AZ-A. During a degradation event affecting the AZ-A, for the private sub-networks of the AZ-B and AZ-C — which remain healthy — they completely lose output connectivity, even without any fault in their own resources. What architecture change solves this unique point of failure, keeping the isolation of failures by AZ?
options: Delete private subnets and move all instances to public subnets, assigning an Elastic IP to each instance
Implant one NAT Gateway in CADA AZ (a public sub-network by AZ) and configure the route table of the private sub-network of each AZ to point 0.0.0.0/0 for the NAT Gateway of SUA AZ PROPERLY
Keep it NAT Gateway only, but to associate with it an Elastic IP — thus, the AWS automatically replicates the feature to other AZs in case of original AZ failure
Replace NAT Gateway by an instance NAT (based on EC2) within a Auto Scaling Group covering the 3 Azs
questions.explanation: Right. NAT Gateway by AZ and routes '0.0.0.0/0' directed to the NAT Gateway local, a failure in AZ-A affects only the output connectivity of the resources QUE I'M ON AZ-A; AZ-B and AZ-C This design also avoids data transfer costs between AZs for the traffic of NAT Gateway, since traffic never crosses the AZ border before arriving at the NAT.
questions.hint: Think about how the output routing of each AZ can remain totally independent of the others, without depending on a shared feature located in a single AZ.
optionRationales: Right. NAT Gateway by AZ and routes '0.0.0.0/0' directed to the NAT Gateway local, a failure in AZ-A affects only the output connectivity of the resources QUE I'M ON AZ-A; AZ-B and AZ-C This design also avoids data transfer costs between AZs for the traffic of NAT Gateway, since traffic never crosses the AZ border before arriving at the NAT.

Incorrect. NAT Gateway is a resource linked to a single sub-network/AZ; AWS does not perform automatic replication or failure of a NAT Gateway if the AZ where he resides fails, the NAT Gateway is unavailable, regardless of the associated Elastic IP, and all private sub-networks that depend on it lose their way to the internet.

Incorrect. NAT In a single ASG, when replaced, it can be restarted in a different sub-network/AZ, requiring manual or automated updating of the route tables, in addition to having throughput and availability less than a NAT Gateway managed. It is a more complex and operationally heavy alternative than simply implementing a NAT Gateway managed by AZ, which is the standard recommended by AWS.

Incorrect. Exposing all instances directly to the internet with public IPs is a serious backlash of security (increases drastically the attack surface) and does not solve the architectural problem reported, which is the lack of redundancy of the NAT Gateway by AZ — not the need for direct access to the Internet by the authorities.

questions.text: A company establishes a connection AWS Site-to-Site VPN between your data center on-premises and a VPC, as part of a hybrid architecture. AWS automatically provide 2 tunnels VPN, each ending in a distinct endpoint (with different public IPs) for redundancy. However, the customer gateway on-premises device is configured to use only UM of the two tunnels, keeping the second completely idle. What is the risk of this configuration and what action corrects the problem?
options: Replace Site-to-Site VPN by AWS Direct Connect, requiring no redundant tunnels

This configuration is expected and requires no action — the AWS activates the second tunnel automatically only when the endpoint of the first tunnel enters maintenance, without the need for configuration on the client side

Configure the custom gateway on-premises to establish AMBOS tunnels (ideally in active-active mode via BGP/ECMP, or at least with automatic failure for the second tunnel); otherwise, maintenance or unavailability at the end point of the tunnel currently in use will cause total loss of connectivity, since the second tunnel — provided precisely for this scenario — is not being used
Increase rekey intervals IKE/Active tunnel IPsec to reduce connection drop chance
questions.explanation: Correct. AWS provision 2 tunnels with distinct endpoints specifically for the client to configure redundancy on the on-premises side. If the customer gateway only recognizes/uses a tunnel, the endpoint's unavailability (planned or not) AWS from that tunnel results in complete loss of connectivity VPN, even if the second tunnel is perfectly operational on the side of the AWS.
questions.hint: A AWS always delivers two tunnel endpoints for a Site-to-Site connection VPN — think about who is responsible for ensuring that both are effectively used.
optionRationales: Correct. AWS provision 2 tunnels with distinct endpoints specifically for the client to configure redundancy on the on-premises side. If the customer gateway only recognizes/uses a tunnel, the endpoint's unavailability (planned or not) AWS from that tunnel results in complete loss of connectivity VPN, even if the second tunnel is perfectly operational on the side of the AWS.

Incorrect. AWS manage the failure of SEU side in a transparent way, or CUSTOMER GATEWAY needs to be configured to recognize and use AMBOS tunnel endpoints (each with a distinct public IP on the side) AWS). If the on-premises device only has the configuration of an active tunnel, connectivity will be lost if precisely ESSE endpoint is affected, regardless of the AWS Do your side..

Incorrect. AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated connectivity option, with longer supply process and generally higher cost, and POSSUI its own resilience model (which typically requires multiple connections/places for redundancy) — it is not correct to say that it 'does not require redundancy'. Moreover, this replacement does not directly solve the immediate problem of underutilization of tunnels VPN already provided.

Incorrect. Adjusting the rekey intervals is a lower tuning parameter for the stability of AN individual tunnel, but does not solve the fundamental redundancy gap — which is the fact that only one of the two tunnels provided for is in use.

questions.text: A team often overwrites or accidentally deletes important objects in a pocket from Amazon S3 (scenario within a single region, without DR cross-region requirement) due to bugs in the application or human error. They want to get back the previous version of an overwritten object, or 'undo' the accidental deletion of an object, SEM depend on a separate backup system, while at the same time need to control the additional storage cost generated by the retention of older versions.
options: Configure Replication Between Regions (CRR) for a bucket in another region
Enable S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode in the pocket

Enable Versioning in the Bucket S3: each PUT (overwritten) creates a new version preserving the previous one (recoverable by the ID version), and a DELETE without version ID only adds an 'Exclusion Marker' (the object appears to be excluded, but the previous versions remain and can be restored by removing the marker); combine with a Lifecycle rule to expire versions NO ATUAIS after a period, controlling the cost of storage
Configure daily jobs from AWS Backup for the Bucket S3 and restore from previous day's backup when accidental deletion occurs
questions.explanation: Correct. The Version of the S3 maintain a complete history of each object, allowing you to recover any previous version or undo an deletion by removing the deletion marker (delete marker) — exactly the desired 'undo' behavior, without the need for a separate backup system. Lifecycle rules for non-current versions (NoncurrentVersionExpiration) control the growth of storage cost.
questions.hint: Think of how each write or delete operation on an object can be treated as a new entry in a history, instead of a definitive replacement.
optionRationales: Correct. The Version of the S3 maintain a complete history of each object, allowing you to recover any previous version or undo an deletion by removing the deletion marker (delete marker) — exactly the desired 'undo' behavior, without the need for a separate backup system. Lifecycle rules for non-current versions (NoncurrentVersionExpiration) control the growth of storage cost.

Incorrect. Object Lock in Compliance mode prevents QUALQUER exclusion or overwriting of objects (even by root user) until the end of the retention period. Although technically avoids loss, it would also prevent the team from intentionally excluding/overwriting objects when necessary (e.g. legitimate updates), being excessively restrictive for this constantly changing application scenario.

Incorrect. CRR replica operations of PUT and DELETE for the destination pocket; an overwritten or accidental exclusion at the origin would also be replicated to the destination (by default), therefore the CRR In isolation does not protect against accidental overwriting/exclusions — it is a DR/availability resource between regions, not a ‘undo' mechanism at object level.

Incorrect. Daily backups allow recovery only to the state of the last backup (up to 24h of granularity/loss), and restoring an entire backup is a much heavier operation and 'everything or nothing' compared to recovery by object and by specific version offered by Version.

questions.text: An operating team wants to automatically fix a recurring problem: when using a drive from an instance EC2 specific (customised metric-way monitoring of CloudWatch Agent) exceeds 90%, must be executed automatically and without session SSH or human intervention, a cleaning script (removal of old logs) in the instance itself, triggered automatically by the alarm of the CloudWatch.
options: Configure the alarm CloudWatch to directly invoke an action of 'Reboot' in the instance EC2 when disk usage exceeds 90%
Configure the alarm CloudWatch to send a notification via SNS for the e-mail of the operations team, instructing them to access the instance via the SSH and execute the cleaning script manually

Create an Alarm CloudWatch on the disc usage metric, with an alarm action (or the rule of EventBridge) that shoots a runbook from AWS Systems Manager Automation (or a document SSM Run Command) directed to the affected instance; runbook/document executes the cleaning script in the instance via SSM Agent, no need for SSH
Use AWS Configure to detect when disk usage exceeds 90% and trigger a remedial action that finishes and replaces the instance automatically
questions.explanation: Correct. Integration CloudWatch Alarm → SSM Automation (or Run Command) allows automated runbooks/scripts execution directly in the instance via SSM Agent, no SSH and without human intervention — exactly the self-healing pattern described.
questions.hint: Think of what service the AWS allows to execute commands or runbooks directly within an instance EC2 without need of access SSH, and how it can be triggered by an alarm.
optionRationales: Correct. Integration CloudWatch Alarm → SSM Automation (or Run Command) allows automated runbooks/scripts execution directly in the instance via SSM Agent, no SSH and without human intervention — exactly the self-healing pattern described.

Incorrect. Restarting the instance does not release the disk space occupied by the old log files (they remain after reboot); this action does not address the root cause (accumulation of logs) and still causes unnecessary unavailability.

Incorrect. AWS Config assesses CONFIGURATION of resources compliance, is not the appropriate tool for arbitrary custom metrics of disk use of CloudWatch Agent; in addition, complete/replace an autonomous instance (outside a ASG) would destroy your status/identity — a disproportionate remedy for a simple disk cleaning.
Incorrect. This approach requires intervention HUMANA (access SSH manual and script execution), contrary to the explicit requirement of an automated process without human intervention.

questions.text: An application has a slow and complex bootstrap process: after the launch of an instance EC2, are necessary 8 a 10 minutes to install and configure the software before the instance passes the health checks and starts to meet traffic. During sudden peaks of demand, the Auto Scaling Group (ASG) scale horizontally, but the new instances take 8-10 minutes to get ready, causing degradation/errors during this window. The team wants to reduce this scale-out latency to close to zero, without keeping a large number of instances fully running (and charged at the normal computer rate) as a standby for a capacity used only occasionally.
options: Increase the minimum capacity of ASG to permanently maintain fully active instances sufficient to meet peak traffic at any time
Use a Launch Template with a larger instance type to speed up the bootstrap process
Create a AMI customized with the application already installed, eliminating the need for any bootstrap process

Configure a Warm Pool Auto Scaling: o ASG maintains a set of pre-initialized instances (which have already completed the bootstrap process) in state PARADO (stopped) or other low-cost state; when the scale-out is required, these instances are moved to the service much faster than launch and initialize from zero, and instances stopped in the warm pool do not generate computer charge (storage only)
questions.explanation: Warm Pools keep pre-initiated instances ready to go into service quickly when the ASG scale, eliminating bootstrap time from the critical scale-out path, while instances in the 'stopped' state in the warm pool are not charged by the computer — simultaneously meeting the near-zero latency requirement and the cost requirement.
questions.hint: Think of an intermediate state for instances EC2 which have already gone through the initialisation process, but are not being charged as if they were fully implemented.
optionRationales: Warm Pools keep pre-initiated instances ready to go into service quickly when the ASG scale, eliminating bootstrap time from the critical scale-out path, while instances in the 'stopped' state in the warm pool are not charged by the computer — simultaneously meeting the near-zero latency requirement and the cost requirement.

Incorrect. Keeping peak capacity permanently fully active and charged at the normal rate, even during periods of low demand, directly contradicts the requirement to avoid 'a large number of instances fully running... charged at the normal rate' as standby.

Incorrect. Bootstrap time is dominated by install/configuration steps of software, which are usually not significantly faster with a larger instance type (especially if the gargalo is package download, execution of configuration tools, etc.); this does not reliably resolve a booting process of 8-10 minutes.

Incorrect. Although pre-constructing a AMI with the installed application is a good practice that can REDUZIR the bootstrap time, the scenario describes a 'slow and complex' process, suggesting additional steps of dynamic configuration/service record that can still occur in the boot; even with a faster boot, only the Warm Pools ensure near-zero scale-out latency while maintaining already fully initialized and ready instances, without the fully active standby capacity cost.

questions.text: A company is migrating a critical containerized application to the Amazon EKS. The requirements are: (a) the Kubernetes flat control must be resilient to the failure of a single Availability Zone, without the team having to manage the flat control infrastructure; and (b) the workers nodes (where pods run) must also be distributed among multiple AZs, with automatic replacement of unhealthy nodes.?
options: ((a) O Amazon EKS automatically executes Kubernetes managed plan control (API server, etcd, etc.) distributed in MULTIPLES AZs within the chosen region, by default and without any additional client configuration; (b) create a EKS Managed Node Group specifying multiple sub-networks in multiple AZs — managed node groups automatically distribute workers nodes between specified AZs and integrate into EC2 Auto Scaling to replace unhealthy us automatically
((a) Configure 3 clusters EKS separate (one per AZ) and use a Kubernetes federation tool to unify them into a single logical plane control
((a) Implement 3 cases EC2 running self-managed components of Kubernetes flat control (kube-apiserver, etcd) in 3 AZs, registered for a NLB Internal
((b) Use profiles of the EKS Fargate only for all workloads, since pods of Fargate are automatically distributed among multiple AZs without any node group configuration
questions.explanation: Right. The multi-AZ resilience of the plane control is a characteristic inherent in the EKS managed, without configuration; for workers nodes, a Managed Node Group with multiple AZs sub-networks ensures distribution between AZs and automatic replacement of us via integration with Auto Scaling — meeting both requirements without additional operational overhead.
questions.hint: Separate what the AWS it guarantees automatically for the flat control of the EKS of what needs to be explicitly configured for worker nodes based on EC2.
optionRationales: Right. The multi-AZ resilience of the plane control is a characteristic inherent in the EKS managed, without configuration; for workers nodes, a Managed Node Group with multiple AZs sub-networks ensures distribution between AZs and automatic replacement of us via integration with Auto Scaling — meeting both requirements without additional operational overhead.

Incorrect. This approach greatly complicates the architecture; the management plan control of the EKS It is already Multi-AZ within a single cluster/region by default — there is no need to federate multiple clusters to achieve AZ resilience in the plane control.

Incorrect. This describes a Kubernetes SELF-MANAGED (not the managed plan control of EKS), which is exactly the operational effort that the EKS was designed to eliminate; the EKS already provides multi-AZ resilience of plane control as managed service, without this complexity.

Incorrect. Although the EKS Fargate abstracts the management of us, the scenario specifies that the 'workers nodes' should be distributed between AZs (i.e., by applying us based on EC2, for example for specific instance types or DaemonSets not supported in Fargate); for worker knots EC2, the distribution between AZs is configured by the selection of sub-networks of the Managed Node Group, not automatically as in pod abstraction of the Fargate.

questions.text: Within a single region of the AWS, a company owns a pocket S3 of 'production' in Account A and needs an automatic copy, in real time, of all new objects in a pocket S3 separate from 'compliance/audit' in Account B (one account AWS dedicated and separate, for unchangeable storage of compliance), by regulatory requirement of segregation of data by account/property — without incurring in latency or costs of data transfer between regions, since the resources of both accounts are in the same Region.
options: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR), but define the region of destination equal to the region of origin
Use AWS DataSync to perform continuous and real-time synchronization between the two bucks in the same Region

Configure the Amazon S3 Same-Region Replication (SRR) from the production pocket in Account A to the compliance pocket in Account B (replication between accounts in the same Region); SRR Supports replication to another account property pocket AWS, with version enabled on both the bucks, and can optionally change the object property to the destination account and/or use S3 Replica Time Control (RTC) for predictable replication times — no latency or transfer cost between regions
Grant to Bucket S3 from Account B cross-account reading permissions on the A-Bucket Bucket via Bucket Policy, and have the applications in Account B read the objects directly from Account A's Bucket
questions.explanation: Correct. SRR is specifically designed for replication within the same Region, including cross-account scenarios, taking into account the requirement of data segregation by account without the costs/latence of a replication between regions.
questions.hint: Consider which recourse to replication of the S3 is designed to operate within the limits of a single region, including between accounts AWS different.
optionRationales: Correct. SRR is specifically designed for replication within the same Region, including cross-account scenarios, taking into account the requirement of data segregation by account without the costs/latence of a replication between regions.

Incorrect. CRR is designed specifically for replication ENTRE Regions DIFERENTES; this is not how replication is configured within the same Region — the correct resource for this (including cross-account scenarios) is Same-Region Replication (SRR).

Incorrect. AWS DataSync is usually used for scheduled/disparate data transfer tasks (often for migration or periodic synchronization between storage systems, including on-premises), not for native replication of the S3, continuous and by object, with the same level of integration of the Replication of S3 — introducing more operational overhead than native resource SRR.

That doesn't create a COPY. SEPARADA of the objects in the B Account pocket (declared requirement); only grants read access to objects that continue to reside in the A Account pocket, which does not meet the requirement for data segregation by account/property with an independent copy for compliance.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon CloudFront with origin in a Application Load Balancer in front of web servers EC2. During traffic peaks, even with the cache of CloudFront enabled, the origin (ALB/EC2) suffers high load, because each edge location of the CloudFront worldwide makes its own request for 'cache miss' to origin by searching for the same popular object (when its regional cache does not yet have it), multiplying the load on the origin. How to reduce this charge without changing the cache behavior by object?
options: Replace Application Load Balancer by a Network Load Balancer to support greater throughput at source
Configure multiple distributions of CloudFront, one by geographical region, each pointing to a separate origin
Enable a Origin Shield of the CloudFront, choosing a region close to origin
Increase TTL (Time to Live) cache CloudFront for the maximum value on all objects
questions.explanation: Right. Shield acts as an additional centralized cache layer between border/regional caches of the CloudFront and origin, consolidating requests so that only one request per object reaches the origin even if multiple edge locations have 'cache miss' simultaneously, significantly reducing the load on the origin.
questions.hint: Think of an additional cache layer, positioned between border locations and origin, which consolidates duplicate requests.
optionRationales: Right. Shield acts as an additional centralized cache layer between border/regional caches of the CloudFront and origin, consolidating requests so that only one request per object reaches the origin even if multiple edge locations have 'cache miss' simultaneously, significantly reducing the load on the origin.

Incorrect. Increase or TTL reduces the frequency of mass caches over time, but does not solve the problem of 'thundering herd' when multiple edge locations error the cache simultaneously (e.g. right after expiration of the TTL or for new-popular content); the Origin Shield solves this concentration of requests regardless of the configuration of TTL.

Incorrect. Changing the type of load balancer increases the capacity of throughput, but does not reduce the number of redundant requests that arrive at the origin from multiple edge locations of the CloudFront for the same object — treats a symptom, not the multiplication of requests itself.

Incorrect. Creating multiple distributions/origins adds operational complexity (managing multiple origins, caching invalidation between them) and does not inherently solve the problem of multiple searches at origin from different border locations; the Origin Shield solves this within a unique distribution.

questions.text: A high-traffic application uses Amazon ElastiCache for Redis (cluster mode disabled, with primary and replicas) to store session data and frequently consulted results. With traffic growth, a single Redis node has become a gargalo both for the total size of the dataset (exceeding the memory of a single node) and for the writing throughput (all writings go to the same primary). How to scale horizontally to solve both problems?
options: Increase the number of existing unique shard cluster read replicas
Migrate from ElastiCache for Redis to ElastiCache for Memcached, which natively supports multi-no writing distribution
Switch to a larger ElastiCache knot type (vertical scaling) within the same unique shard cluster
Enable Cluster Mode (Cluster Mode Enabled) with multiple shards
questions.explanation: Correct. ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode enabled partitions data between multiple shards (each with its own primary and optional replicas), distributing both the dataset (via hash slots) and the throughput of writing between multiple primary nos, allowing horizontal scalability beyond the memory and writing capacity of a single node.
questions.hint: Think of a Redis configuration that partitions data between multiple primary nos instead of relying on a single primary with replicas.
optionRationales: Correct. ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode enabled partitions data between multiple shards (each with its own primary and optional replicas), distributing both the dataset (via hash slots) and the throughput of writing between multiple primary nos, allowing horizontal scalability beyond the memory and writing capacity of a single node.

Incorrect. Adding more reading replicas increases the ability to LEITURA and provides additional copies of the data, but does not solve the limit of TAMANHO of the dataset (still limited by the memory of the primary) nor the THROUGHPUT OF ESCRITA (all writings continue to go to the only primary).

Incorrect. Vertical scaling (no greater) may temporarily increase capacity, but has a higher limit (the largest type of knot available) and still represents a single point for all writings; it does not provide the same horizontal scalability of sharding.

Incorrect. Although sharding on the client's side of Memcached distributes data between us, switching engine is a major architectural change that loses Redis specific features (data structures, persistence, replication) on which the application may depend; Redis Cluster Mode provides equivalent horizontal writing scalability natively within Redis.

questions.text: A latency-sensitive transactional database, executed in EC2, requires IOPS extremely high and consistent (well above 64.000) and sub-millisecond latency, with very low IO error rates. IOPS SSD) currently, in a type of instance without support to Block Express, it cannot reach the ceiling of IOPS What should be done??
options: Migrate the database to use Forum Store volumes (NVMe SSD) for maximum IOPS
Use a volume EBS io2 Block Express attached to a type of Nitro-based instance supported by Block Express (e.g. eligible instance families as R5b))
Increase the configuration of IOPS provided from current volume io2 to above 64.000 in the existing instance
Combine (strip) multiple volumes gp3 using RAID 0 at the level of the operating system to add IOPS
questions.explanation: Right. I2 Block Express offers even 256.000 IOPS, until 4.000 MB/s of throughput, sub-millisecond latency and durability of 99,999%, being designed specifically for the most demanding workloads in I/O, exceeding the limits of standard io2 volumes.
questions.hint: Consider which variant of the volume EBS Provisioned IOPS it was specifically designed to overcome the roof of 64.000 IOPS, and which bodies support it.
optionRationales: Right. I2 Block Express offers even 256.000 IOPS, until 4.000 MB/s of throughput, sub-millisecond latency and durability of 99,999%, being designed specifically for the most demanding workloads in I/O, exceeding the limits of standard io2 volumes.

Incorrect. RAID 0 between volumes gp3 can increase the IOPS/throughput aggregates to a certain point, but manage RAID in software adds operational complexity, does not provide the same roof of IOPS by volume nor the characteristics of sub-millisecond latency and durability of 99,999% of the Io2 Block Express, and the failure of a single volume in the array RAID 0 causes total loss of array data.

Incorrect. Volumes Forum Store offer IOPS/throughput very high, but are EFFEMERS (data lost when stopping/finalizing the instance or in case of failure), making them inadequate for a transactional database that requires durability, despite meeting the requirement of IOPS.

Incorrect. Volumes io2 (not Block Express) have a roof of 64.000 IOPS regardless of the required provision value; exceeding this ceiling requires io2 Block Express in a compatible Nitro instance type, not simply increasing the provision value in an incompatible configuration.

questions.text: A media company has users all over the world uploading large video files directly to a single bucket S3 in us-east-1. Users in Asia and Australia face slow upload speeds and frequent timeouts due to long network distance and variable internet route to us-east-1, as users close to us-east-1 The company wants to improve upload speed/reliability for remote users, without creating regional newsletters or requiring users to manually choose a 'closer' endpoint'.
options: Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration in the pocket and get customers to upload via the different endpoint 's3-accelerated'
Create Buckets S3 separate in multiple regions (e.g. ap-souteast)-2, ap-northeast-1) and make the client application choose the nearest bucket based on the user location
Use AWS Direct Connect from the location of each user to establish a dedicated network connection to the Bucket Region S3
Increase the size of the parts (parts) in the multipart upload to reduce the number of requests HTTP large files
questions.explanation: Correct. S3 Transfer Acceleration route uploads through the edge location of CloudFront nearest (using the global network of edge locations of the AWS) through an optimized path to the Bucket Region, significantly improving throughput/reliability for geographically distant uploaders, without requiring region selection logic on the client's side.
questions.hint: Think of a resource of the S3 taking advantage of the global network of edge locations of the AWS to accelerate uploads to the destination region without requiring additional newsletters.
optionRationales: Correct. S3 Transfer Acceleration route uploads through the edge location of CloudFront nearest (using the global network of edge locations of the AWS) through an optimized path to the Bucket Region, significantly improving throughput/reliability for geographically distant uploaders, without requiring region selection logic on the client's side.

Incorrect. Although multi-region buckets can reduce latency, this requires significant logic in the application to detect the user's location, route to the correct bucket and additional complexity to consolidate/replicate data back to a primary bucket — a much more complex solution than enabling a single feature in the existing bucket.

Incorrect. Direct Connect requires dedicated physical connections from specific locations (typically data centers of companies, not devices/locations of individual end users around the world), making it completely impractical for arbitrary end users by uploading from their own devices.

Incorrect. Although multipart upload (and size/competition adjustment of parts) helps with large file uploads in general and improves resilience to failures in individual parts, this does not solve the fundamental problem of latency/network routing for geographically distant customers — requests still travel the same long-distance path to us-east-1.

questions.text: The reading traffic of an application grew significantly, and the team added several Aurora Replicas to a cluster Aurora MySQL to scale the readability. However, the application connects using a fixed (hardcoded) list of individual replica endpoints, requiring manual updating whenever replicas are added/removed, and the load is not evenly distributed (some replicas receive more connections than others, depending on which endpoint developers used). As the application must connect to automatically distribute the read load among all current replicas?
options: Configure the application to use the cluster 'reader endpoint' Aurora for all consultations read only
Use weighted routing records of the Amazon Route 53 pointing to the individual endpoint of each replica, manually updating the weights as the replicas change
Implementing a Network Load Balancer in front of all instances Aurora Replica and make the application connect via the NLB
Configure the application to connect to the 'cluster endpoint' (write endpoint) for all reading queries, as it always points to the current primary instance
questions.explanation: Correct. The endpoint reader automatically balances the connections between all the Aurora Replicas available (and the writer, if there are no replicas), and automatically reflects the current set of replicas as they are added or removed, without requiring endpoint list management by the application.
questions.hint: The Aurora provides a specific endpoint, separated from the endpoint of the writer, which already performs load balancing between replicas automatically.
optionRationales: Correct. The endpoint reader automatically balances the connections between all the Aurora Replicas available (and the writer, if there are no replicas), and automatically reflects the current set of replicas as they are added or removed, without requiring endpoint list management by the application.

Incorrect. Cluster/writer endpoint always points to the only instance WRITER ATUAL; routing all reading traffic for it would NOT distribute cargo between the Aurora Replicas — would focus all readings (and written) on the write instance, nullifying the purpose of having replicas reading.

Incorrect. Build and maintain manually one load balancer in front of the fora Aurora Replica duplicate functionality that the native endpoint reader of Aurora already provides, adding unnecessary infrastructure and operating overhead, and would not automatically follow changes in the composition of replicas as the endpoint reader does.

Incorrect. This requires manual record management DNS whenever replicas are added/removed (exactly the problem described) and does not provide the automatic and real-time load balancing, nor the connection drainage, of the native endpoint reader of the Aurora.

questions.text: An application realizes millions of reading requests per second to a table of the DynamoDB, most repeated readings of the same 'hot' items (e.g., popular product details), and the application tolerates readings eventually consistent with up to a few seconds lag for these items. auto scaling of the DynamoDB, reading costs are high and reading latency (a few milliseconds) is too slow for the latency requirement in microseconds of the application for these specific readings of hot items..
options: Add a Global Secondary Index (GSI) in the attribute frequently accessed to accelerate these readings
Enable DynamoDB Streams and use a function Lambda to pre-compute and cache the results of hot items in a table DynamoDB separate
Substantially increase the Read Capacity Units (RCUs) provided in the table, or change to On-Demand Capacity Mode
Implement o Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as a cache layer in memory in front of the table DynamoDB
questions.explanation: Correct. DAX is a cache service compatible with the API of the DynamoDB, write-through, which reduces reading response times from a few milliseconds to microseconds in 'hot' items (cache), transparently treating cache invalidation/population, and application tolerance eventual consistency in these readings aligns with possibly consistent cache readings (standard) of the DAX.
questions.hint: Think of a cache service in memory, compatible with the API of the DynamoDB, designed specifically to reduce reading latency from milliseconds to microseconds.
optionRationales: Correct. DAX is a cache service compatible with the API of the DynamoDB, write-through, which reduces reading response times from a few milliseconds to microseconds in 'hot' items (cache), transparently treating cache invalidation/population, and application tolerance eventual consistency in these readings aligns with possibly consistent cache readings (standard) of the DAX.

Incorrect. Increasing RCUs (or moving to On-Demand) can deal with greater THROUGHPUT OF LEITURA and avoid throttling, but does not alter the fundamental feature of latency of few milliseconds of direct readings of the DynamoDB — does not meet the microsecond latency requirement.

Incorrect. GSI changes the FATHER OF CONSULTA/access path (e.g. consult for a different attribute), but does not reduce the fundamental latency of a reading operation of the DynamoDB for microseconds — readings via GSI have latency characteristics similar to the basic table readings.

Incorrect. This is a complex custom cache solution (using the own DynamoDB as cache) which would still display reading latency at millisecond level of the DynamoDB for the 'cache' table — does not provide the latency characteristics in memory, in microseconds, of a dedicated cache layer such as the DAX.

questions.text: A real-time multiplayer gaming company runs gaming servers in instances EC2 behind Network Load Balancers in multiple regions of AWS. Players all over the world face inconsistent latency and occasional routing problems because their traffic runs through the public internet (with unforeseeable peering/routing) to the NLB The company wants to improve and stabilize latency for players globally, routing traffic to the global high performance network of AWS As soon as possible, using static IP addresses that do not change even if the Backend Regions/endpoints change.
options: Use latency-based routing of Route 53 to direct players to NLB regional with the lowest latency from their location
Implement o Amazon CloudFront in front of the NLBs to cache and speed up the game traffic
Implement o AWS Global Accelerator with regional NLBs as endpoints
Set up connections AWS Direct Connect from the location of each player to the Region AWS nearest
questions.explanation: Correct. Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses which, once traffic enters the edge location of the AWS closer, are routed by the private global network of AWS (instead of the public internet) to the ideal healthy endpoint, improving the consistency/performance of latency and providing static IPs independent of changes in the underlying endpoints — meeting both latency and static IP requirements.
questions.hint: Think of a service that provides static anycast IPs and takes traffic to the private backbone network of AWS as close as possible to the origin, operating at the level of TCP/UDP.
optionRationales: Correct. Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses which, once traffic enters the edge location of the AWS closer, are routed by the private global network of AWS (instead of the public internet) to the ideal healthy endpoint, improving the consistency/performance of latency and providing static IPs independent of changes in the underlying endpoints — meeting both latency and static IP requirements.

Incorrect. CloudFront is a CDN focusing on HTTP/HTTPS, designed to cache content; real-time multiplayer game traffic usually uses connections TCP/UDP persistent (non-requisitions HTTP (see section 4.4), making the CloudFront inadequate as the main acceleration mechanism for this type of traffic, unlike Global Accelerator, operating at the level TCP/UDP.

Incorrect. Latency-based routing helps direct players to the nearest geographic/network region, but routing based on DNS has limitations (cache)/TTL of the DNS causing outdated routing, no protection against sub-optimal paths on the public internet after traffic leaves the ISP of the player) and does not provide static IPs or route traffic through the private network of the AWS — o Global Accelerator solve both gaps.

Incorrect. Direct Connect requires dedicated physical connections from specific locations, being completely impractical for individual arbitrary players connecting from their homes/offices around the world.

questions.text: A company executes a fleet of containerized and computer intensive microservices in the EC2 (types of instance based on x86, e.g. m5.xlarge) behind a ALB. The application is built in a runtime/language with native support to ARM64, and the team wants to improve the price-performance (performance per dollar) of this workload without altering the architecture of the application or the amount of instances, only changing the architecture of CPU the underlying, since the workload is suitable for processors based on ARM.
options: Exchange from On-Demand to Reserved Instances of the same type of instance x86 to reduce cost
Migrate instances EC2 for instance types based on AWS Graviton (e.g. m7g.xlarge))
Enable Enhanced Networking (ENA) in the existing x86 instances to improve the price-performance
Move workload to the AWS Lambda to eliminate the costs of EC2 completely
questions.explanation: Right. Processors AWS Graviton (CPUs Customized Arms designed by AWS) offer significantly better price-performance (commonly cited in ~40% better) compared to x86 equivalent instances for compatible workloads, requiring that the application be recompiled/available for architecture ARM64, but without change in general architecture, amount of instances or orchestration.
questions.hint: Think of a family of custom processors from AWS, based on an architecture CPU different, known for offering better performance per dollar for compatible workloads.
optionRationales: Right. Processors AWS Graviton (CPUs Customized Arms designed by AWS) offer significantly better price-performance (commonly cited in ~40% better) compared to x86 equivalent instances for compatible workloads, requiring that the application be recompiled/available for architecture ARM64, but without change in general architecture, amount of instances or orchestration.

Incorrect. Reserved Instances reduce the price POR HORA by an undertaking, but do not change the performance characteristics per dollar of the same type of instance x86 — it is an optimization of price/commitment, not an improvement of price-PERFORMANCE (computational efficiency) as requested.

Incorrect. Enhanced Networking improves throughput/latence/PPS of network, but does not fundamentally change the price-performance relationship of CPU for intensive workloads in computing — addresses a different performance dimension (network) from which is being optimized (general price-performance of computing via architecture of the CPU).

Incorrect. Move to the Lambda is a larger architectural change (the specific scenario 'without changing the architecture of the application') and may not be suitable for long-term containerized microservices with sustained computing needs; it does not simply represent 'change the architecture of CPU underlying' as requested.

questions.text: A company executes clusters Amazon EMR for processing big data (Jobs Spark) that read input data and record output data on Amazon S3. They want the cluster to scale dynamically according to the workload and use a flexible combination of instance types/purchase options to optimize availability and performance, ensuring that the data persists regardless of the cluster life cycle (so that the cluster can be completed after each job without loss of data).).
options: Replace Amazon EMR completely by Apache Spark self-managed clusters in instances EC2, using local instance store for HDFS
Configure the cluster EMR with a fixed instance groups set using only one type of instance, and store the data in HDFS in volumes EBS cluster locations for maximum performance

Use EMRFS (EMR File System) to read/record directly at S3 as persistent storage (instead of HDFS in local cluster storage), and configure the EMR with Fleets Forum (allowing multiple types of instance and a combination of On-Demand/Spot in the fleet)
Use a single cluster EMR large and dedicated, in execution 24/7 with HDFS based on EBS for all storage, to avoid dynamic overhead scaling
questions.explanation: Correct. Unplug the storage (S3 way EMRFS) (cluster) EMR transient) allows to finish the cluster after each job without loss of data, while Forum Fleets provide flexibility in the selection of instance type/purchase option to optimize availability and cost/performance.
questions.hint: Think about how to uncouple the persistent storage of the processing cluster life cycle, and what resource the EMR allows you to combine instance types and purchase options.

questions.text: A workload of HPC (High Performance Computing) strongly coupled (e.g., scientific simulation based on MPI) is executed in many instances EC2 that communicate frequently with each other, requiring the lowest possible network latency and the highest possible network throughput between the instances. The team wants to ensure that these instances are physically close to each other within a single AZ to minimize network latency between instances.
options: Launch instances in a Partition Placement Group with multiple partitions
Distribute instances among multiple Availability Zones using one Auto Scaling Resilience Group
Launch instances in a Spread Placement Group distributed by multiple AZs to maximize availability
Launch instances in a Cluster Placement Group, within a single AZ
questions.explanation: Correct. A Cluster Placement Group groups nearby instances within a Availability Zone, providing low latency and high throughput network performance between instances, ideal for working loads of HPC strongly coupled that require frequent communication between us.
questions.hint: Think of what type of placement group groups as physically close as possible within a single Availability Zone, to minimize network latency between them.
optionRationales: Correct. A Cluster Placement Group groups nearby instances within a Availability Zone, providing low latency and high throughput network performance between instances, ideal for working loads of HPC strongly coupled that require frequent communication between us.

Incorrect. A Spread Placement Group positions instances in distinct underlying hardware to MINIMIZAR correlated failures (maximizing availability), which is the OPOSTO of the objective here — that AUMENTARIA the network latency between instances when distributing them between racks/AZs, instead of minimizing it.

Incorrect. Partition Placement Groups are designed for large scale distributed/replicated workloads (ex.: HDFS, Cassandra, Kafka), where you want to limit the impact of a hardware failure to a partition, but do not provide the same lower latency network performance and physical grouping as a Cluster Placement Group for communication HPC strongly coupled.

Incorrect. Distributing instances between AZs increases network latency between them (latency between AZs is greater than within an AZ), which is contrary to the requirement of the workload of HPC of less latency possible between instances.

questions.text: A machine learning team performs training jobs distributed in a cluster of instances EC2 based on GPU (ex.: P4d), using collective communication based on MPI (ex.: NCCL) between instances. The network performance between instances is currently limited by the overhead of the network stack. TCP/standard IP, and the team wants to achieve the lowest possible latency between us and the largest throughput for this strongly coupled and compatible communication pattern OS-bypass.
options: Replace instances with GPU by Compute Optimized (family C) instances, which have higher base network performance
Enable Only Enhanced Networking (ENA) standard, without the EFA
Enable Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) in the forums (in addition to placing them in a Cluster Placement Group))
Use Jumbo Frames (MTU 9001) the VPC cluster to reduce overhead per package
questions.explanation: Correct. EFA is a network device that provides communication with OS-bypass, allowing applications that use libraries like libfabric (and frameworks like NCCL/MPI) communicate directly with the network hardware, bypassing the stack TCP/Traditional IP, drastically reducing latency and improving throughput for working loads of HPC/Highly coupled training ML — exactly the scenario described.
questions.hint: Think of a network device that allows applications to bypass the network stack of the operating system for direct communication with hardware, complementing the Enhanced Networking default.
optionRationales: Correct. EFA is a network device that provides communication with OS-bypass, allowing applications that use libraries like libfabric (and frameworks like NCCL/MPI) communicate directly with the network hardware, bypassing the stack TCP/Traditional IP, drastically reducing latency and improving throughput for working loads of HPC/Highly coupled training ML — exactly the scenario described.

Incorrect. ENA Improve Throughput/PPS/general network latency in relation to the standard virtualized network stack, but still passes through the network stack of the operating system (TCP/IP); does not provide the ability to OS-bypass required for the lowest possible latency in collective communication based on MPI/NCCL — o EFA specifically extends the ENA with OS-bypass for use of HPC/ML.

Incorrect. Jumbo frames can modestly reduce overhead per package in large transfers, but this is a lower optimization compared to the way of communication with OS-bypass at hardware level provided by EFA, and does not fundamentally change the latency characteristics of collective communication patterns used in distributed training.

Incorrect. Family C instances are not designed for ML training based on GPU (do not have GPUs); replace the instances with GPU would eliminate acceleration by GPU on which the training job depends — this does not address the network requirement and still breaks the main computing requirement of the workload.

questions.text: One API latency-sensitive synchrony (via API Gateway → Lambda) has occasional peaks in latency p99. The investigation shows that these peaks correlate with 'cold startups' — when the Lambda it needs to initialize a new execution environment (loading code, executing initialization code) before meeting a request, adding hundreds of milliseconds to seconds of latency, especially after periods of low traffic or during sudden increases in traffic. The team wants to ensure that a base number of execution environments is always pre-initialized and ready to respond immediately, even during periods of low traffic.
options: Change function runtime Lambda from an interpreted language (e.g. Python) to a compiled language (e.g. Go) to reduce cold start time
Increase function memory allocation Lambda for maximum (10.240 MB)
