Configure Provided Competition in function Lambda (and consider the Application Auto Scaling to adjust the level of competition provided on the basis of a target schedule or use)
Configure Reserved Competition equal to the expected peak of competing requests
questions.explanation: Correct. Provided Competition maintains a specified number of run environments initialized and ready to respond in milliseconds of a single digit, eliminating cold start latency for this basic capacity, directly solving p99 latency peaks caused by cold start.
questions.hint: Think of a resource of the Lambda which keeps running environments already 'heated' and ready to respond immediately, eliminating the need for on-demand initialization.
optionRationales: Correct. Provided Competition maintains a specified number of run environments initialized and ready to respond in milliseconds of a single digit, eliminating cold start latency for this basic capacity, directly solving p99 latency peaks caused by cold start.

Incorrect. Increasing memory increases proportionally the allocation of CPU and can accelerate the execution of function code itself (and even the initialization code to some extent), but does not eliminate the fundamental phenomenon of cold start (the need to create a new running environment) — a cold start with maximum memory is still a cold start, possibly just faster.

Incorrect. Reserved Competition sets a maximum (and minimum guaranteed available) limit of competition for the function, avoiding high-competitive throttling and ensuring that the capacity is not consumed by other functions, but does NOT pre-initialize running environments — does not solve cold startups; moreover, setting it very low could cause throttling.

Incorrect. Although different runs have different basic cold start characteristics (languages compiled with smaller runs usually have faster cold start), this requires rewriting the function in another language (a considerable effort) and AINDA does not eliminate cold starters completely — the Provided Competition eliminates them for the provided capacity, regardless of runtime.

questions.text: A company uses CloudFront to serve a site and needs to perform a very light and high volume operation in CADA the viewer's request on the edge: inspect a header of the request and, based on the value, modify the URI of the request ANTES of it to be evaluated by the cache behaviors (e.g. for A/B tests or normalization of URL). The operation must run with sub-millimeter overhead and minimum cost in extremely high volumes of requests (potentially millions of requests per second in all edge locations), and does not need access to the body of the request or the network/file system.
options: Implement this logic using CloudFront Functions (executed in the 'viewer request' event')
Implement this logic using Lambda@Edge no event 'origin request'
Implement this logic using Lambda@Edge in event 'viewer request''
Implement this logic in the application code on the source server, after the CloudFront re-apply
questions.explanation: Correct.. CloudFront Functions are designed for lightweight JavaScript operations, of very high scale and latency reviews, natively executed at each edge location of the CloudFront with sub-millisecond initialization times and an optimized cost model for high volume invocations — ideal for simple head/rewrite inspection of URL no stage of viewer request.
questions.hint: Think of what computational mechanism on the edge of the CloudFront it was designed specifically for extremely light operations, of very high volume and very low latency in the event of request of the viewer.
optionRationales: Correct.. CloudFront Functions are designed for lightweight JavaScript operations, of very high scale and latency reviews, natively executed at each edge location of the CloudFront with sub-millisecond initialization times and an optimized cost model for high volume invocations — ideal for simple head/rewrite inspection of URL no stage of viewer request.

Incorrect. Lambda@Edge supports the viewer request event and PODE execute this kind of logic, but it rotates in an execution environment Lambda Node.js/Python with overhead and invocation cost greater than the CloudFront Functions, usually recommended for more complex operations requiring network access, more computing/memory or longer execution times — for this simple and very high volume case, the CloudFront Functions is the most economical, native choice and less latency.

Incorrect. The origin request event is only triggered in cache MISSES (after the behavior cache has already been evaluated), therefore it would be too late to modify the URI of the request ANTES of it to be evaluated by cache behaviors, as required by the scenario.

Incorrect. Executing this logic at source means that TODA requisition (even those that could be served identically by the cache after normalization of the URI) would need to arrive at the origin, nullifying the purpose of normalizing the URI before evaluating the behavior cache, and adds latency when demanding a go back and forth to the origin for a logic that could run on the edge.

questions.text: A team is choosing an ElastiCache engine for a simple cache layer and statess in front of a relational database, storing mainly results from read-heavy queries as simple key-value pairs (strings)/JSON). The application was built to scale horizontally with many small cache nodes, requires multi-thread access to maximize the use of CPU by node, and explicitly NOT need data persistence, replication, complex data structures (lists, sets, sorted sets) or pub/sub — only the simplest and most horizontally scalable key-value cache possible.
options: Choose the Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode disabled
Choose the Amazon ElestiCache for Memcached
Choose the Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode enabled and Multi-AZ with automatic failover
Choose the Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as a cache layer
questions.explanation: Correct. Memcached is a memory key-value storage, simple, multi-thread, without persistence, replication or complex data structures, designed to be easily scaled horizontally by adding us (with partitioning on the client side/auto discovery), making it suitable for this case of simple and horizontally scalable use, just for cache, which explicitly does not need the advanced resources of Redis.
questions.hint: Think of which ElastiCache engine is, by design, simpler, multi-threaded and optimized for pure horizontal scaling as key-value cache, without advanced persistence/replication features.
optionRationales: Correct. Memcached is a memory key-value storage, simple, multi-thread, without persistence, replication or complex data structures, designed to be easily scaled horizontally by adding us (with partitioning on the client side/auto discovery), making it suitable for this case of simple and horizontally scalable use, just for cache, which explicitly does not need the advanced resources of Redis.

Incorrect. Redis (even with cluster mode disabled) is single-threaded by shard (limiting the use of CPU by node for this workload that wants multi-thread access), and provides persistence, replication and complex data structures that this use case explicitly does not need — choosing the Redis here adds capacity/complexity beyond what is needed.

Incorrect. This adds the replication/failover capabilities of Redis (and associated cost/complexity), none of which is necessary for a workload that explicitly does not require persistence or replication — and the single-threaded model by Redis shard does not align with the declared need for multi-thread access by node.

Incorrect. DAX is designed specifically as a cache in memory NA FRENTE Tables DynamoDB (using the API of the DynamoDB), not as a general use cache for query results from a relational database — is the wrong tool to cache results from a relational database.

questions.text: A team is implementing a cluster application (e.g. a cluster recognition file system or a cluster database that manages its own consistency/lock between us) in EC2, where multiple instances EC2 within the same AZ need concurrent read/write access to MESMO underlying block storage volume, and the application itself treats the sorting of writings and the consistency between knots (the storage layer does not need to provide this).
options: Use a volume EBS (i1 or i2) with Multi-Attach enabled, attached to multiple instances EC2 within the same Availability Zone
Use Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) mounted in all instances
Use a volume EBS gp3 with Multi-Attach enabled
Create a single volume EBS and attach it to an instance EC2, and then use this instance as a server NFS for the other instances
questions.explanation: Correct. EBS Multi-Attach allows a single volume provided IOPS SSD (Io1/io2) is simultaneously attached to multiple instances in the same AZ, each with complete read/write permissions; the APPLICATION should coordinate the writings (e.g. via cluster recognition file system or localization at application level), since the same EBS does not provide orderly consistency of writing between the annexes — aligned with the premise of the scenario that the application deals with this.
questions.hint: Think about what kind of volume EBS supports being simultaneously attached to multiple instances in the same AZ, with reading/writing, leaving consistency coordination for application.
optionRationales: Correct. EBS Multi-Attach allows a single volume provided IOPS SSD (Io1/io2) is simultaneously attached to multiple instances in the same AZ, each with complete read/write permissions; the APPLICATION should coordinate the writings (e.g. via cluster recognition file system or localization at application level), since the same EBS does not provide orderly consistency of writing between the annexes — aligned with the premise of the scenario that the application deals with this.

Incorrect. Although the EFS support concurrent access of many instances (including between AZs) and technically allow shared access, the scenario specifically describes storage requirements in BLOCO for an application with cluster recognition managing its own block level consistency (common in certain database architectures/cluster file system) — the EFS is a shared storage system at file level (NFS), a different storage paradigm from the one described.

Incorrect. This introduces a single point of failure/gargalo (the instance that serves NFS) and an additional I/O network/latence jump from all other instances, instead of providing direct concurrent block-level access to the underlying volume from multiple instances, as Multi-Attach provides.
Incorrect. Multi-Attach is supported only in Volumes Provided IOPS SSD (i1 and i2), not in gp3 volumes (General Purpose SSD) — gp3 does not support Multi-Attach feature.

questions.text: An application uploads large files (from several GB to TB) to the Amazon S3. Using uploads from PUT unique standard, the team observes that any network interruption during upload requires rebooting TODO the upload from the beginning, wasting significant bandwidth and time for large files, and the general upload throughput is limited by the bandwidth of a single connection TCP. They want to improve the resilience of upload (avoid sending the entire file after a transient failure) and increase the overall throughput by parallelizing the transfer of a single large object.
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to these uploads
Use Multipart Upload from Amazon S3
Compress files before upload to reduce your size and upload time
Use AWS Snowball to physically transfer the large files to AWS
questions.explanation: Right. The large object is divided into multiple parts (each sent independently, potentially in parallel by multiple connections), and if a part fails in upload, only ESSA part needs to be sent (not the whole object); once all parts are sent, the S3 the mounts in the final object — directly improving both the resilience (partial retry) and the throughput (parallel sending of parts) for large objects.
questions.hint: Think of a resource of the S3 which divides a large object into smaller parts, sent independently and possibly in parallel, allowing retry only by the party that fails.
optionRationales: Right. The large object is divided into multiple parts (each sent independently, potentially in parallel by multiple connections), and if a part fails in upload, only ESSA part needs to be sent (not the whole object); once all parts are sent, the S3 the mounts in the final object — directly improving both the resilience (partial retry) and the throughput (parallel sending of parts) for large objects.

Incorrect. Transfer Acceleration optimizes the CAMINHO OF REDE (routing through edge locations of the CloudFront) even the Bucket Region, which can help with latency for geographically distant uploaders, but does not, by itself, divide a large object into independently re-enviable and parallelizable parts — can be used together with the multipart upload for additional benefit, but does not replace it for declared requirements (partial retry in case of failure, parallelization of the transfer of a single object).

Incorrect. Compression may reduce the amount of data transferred (useful for upload time), but does not solve the fundamental problem of uploading data to the PUT only need to restart entirely in case of failure, nor does it provide parallelization of the upload of a single object in multiple connections.

Incorrect. Snowball is designed for mass data transfer, offline (often for initial migrations involving very large datasets, e.g.: many TB to PB, over weeks), not for the continuous and online upload flow of an application that needs resilience and improved throughput for individual uploads of large files.

questions.text: An e-commerce application has a table DynamoDB 'Orders' with OrderId partition key and a 'Status' attribute (ex.: 'PENDING', 'SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED'). To find all the requests 'PENDING' for processing, the application currently performs a Scan operation in the entire table, filtering by Status='PENDING' — this is slow and consumes RCUs proportionally to the size of TODA the table, even if requested PENDING are a small fraction of the total. How to make this consultation efficient (avoiding full scans) as the table grows for millions of items?
options: Create a Global Secondary Index (GSI) scattered, where the partition key of the GSI is a dedicated attribute (ex.: 'GSI_PK') Population APENAS for requests with Status=PENDING (omitted/removed for other statuses)
Increase the Read Capacity Units provided in the table to deal with the cost of Scan operation more efficiently
Add a Secondary Index Location (LSI) about the attribute 'Status''
Use DynamoDB Streams to keep a separate list of 'orders' PENDING' in an external system such as the Amazon S3, and consult this list instead of the table
questions.explanation: Correct. DynamoDB index in one GSI only items containing the key attributes of the GSI; a scattered index containing only requests PENDING allows a Query (not Scan) operation that reads only the relevant items, with reading cost proportional to the number of corresponding items, not the whole table.
questions.hint: Think of how a secondary index can contain only a subset of the items in the table, populating its key attribute only for items that should be indexed.
optionRationales: Correct. DynamoDB index in one GSI only items containing the key attributes of the GSI; a scattered index containing only requests PENDING allows a Query (not Scan) operation that reads only the relevant items, with reading cost proportional to the number of corresponding items, not the whole table.

Incorrect. LSIs should share the same partition key from the base table (OrderId, in this case) and provide only one CHAVE OF alternative ordering within the same partition; as each request has a single OrderId (each one of its own partition), a LSI would not allow to consult 'all requests with Status=PENDING' between different partitions of OrderId — LSIs do not resolve this need for consultation between partitions.

Incorrect. Increasing the RCUs allows the Scan to be completed with less throttling, but does not reduce the fundamental cost/latence characteristic of the Scan (read all items in the table); treats a symptom (throttling), not the root cause (inefficient access standard)).

Incorrect. This introduces a separate and eventually consistent external system that needs to be synced via Streams/Lambda, adding architectural complexity and a new source of consistency lag, when a GSI sparso (a native resource of the DynamoDB designed exactly for this) solves the problem more simply within itself DynamoDB.

questions.text: The database RDS Primary postgreSQL of a company is in us-east-1, serving a global application. Users in Europe face higher reading latency for reports/dashboards queries, as each consultation needs to cross the Atlantic to us-east-1 and back. Writing operations remain centralized in us-east-1 (acceptable), but the team wants to reduce latency of LEITURA specifically for European users who perform reports queries, without changing the way the application is written.
options: Create a Cross-Region Read instance replica RDS PostgreSQL in a European Region (e.g. eu-west)-1), and direct the European reading traffic/reports to the endpoint of this replica
Use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) to continuously replicate data for a new instance RDS in me-west-1, configured as the new primary for both readings and writings of Europe
Enable Multi-AZ deployment for instance RDS in us-east-1
Implement o Amazon ElestiCache in us-east-1 to cache the results of queries from European users
questions.explanation: Correct. A replica of reading between regions replicates asynchronously from the primary, providing a local and low latency reading endpoint for European users to perform reports queries, while all writings continue to go to the primary in us-east-1, No change.
questions.hint: Think of a resource of the RDS which creates a read only copy, asynchronous, in another region, without changing where the writings occur.
optionRationales: Correct. A replica of reading between regions replicates asynchronously from the primary, providing a local and low latency reading endpoint for European users to perform reports queries, while all writings continue to go to the primary in us-east-1, No change.

Incorrect. Multi-AZ creates a standy replica synchronous in an AZ DIFERENTE within the MESMA Region (us-east-1) for the purpose of failure/sustainability; standby is not used for reading traffic (in the standard Multi-AZ RDS) and does not reduce transatlantic latency at all for European reading consultations.

Incorrect. A cache in us-east-1 does not reduce the network latency of European users' requests for CHEGAR us-east-1 first (the latency of going back and forth to the cache is the same as to the database); does not solve the problem of distance between regions.

Incorrect. To make a second instance a 'first for writing' would create a multi-master/dual-write topology, that the RDS standard does not support and would introduce complexity of conflict resolution; the scenario explicitly states that the writings should remain centralized in us-east-1 without changes — this transforms a reading latency problem into a disproportionate writing architecture change.

questions.text: An application uses a volume EBS gp2 of 100 GB for your database. The gp2 provides 300 IOPS Baseline (3 IOPS by GB), which is insufficient for the demand for I/O of the workload, but the real data only occupy about 100 GB capacity — the team does not want to pay for a much larger volume (which the gp2 would require to obtain more IOPS of baseline) just to win IOPS. They want to increase IOPS (ex: for 6.000) and throughput (e.g. for 250 MB/s) regardless of volume storage capacity, the most economical way for this moderate requirement of IOPS (without the need for IOPS extremities of i2).
options: Increase the size of the gp2 volume to 2.000 GB to reach the IOPS necessary (as gp2 provides 3 IOPS per GB)
Add a second volume gp2 of 100 GB and combine them (stripe) with RAID 0 to double the IOPS available
Migrate to i2 Block Express and provide exactly 6.000 IOPS

Migrate volume to gp3 (General Purpose SSD) and configure the IOPS (until 16.000) and throughput (up to 1.000 MB/s) desired regardless of size of 100 GB, paying separately for IOPS/throughput above gp3 baseline (3.000 IOPS / 125 MB/s included in any size)
questions.explanation: Correct. The gp3 disconnects the provisioning of IOPS and throughput of volume size, unlike gp2, where the IOPS scale with (and are limited by) the size provided, allowing the team to get exactly the IOPS/throughput needed for a volume of 100 GB without oversupplying capacity.
questions.hint: Think about what kind of volume EBS allows you to configure IOPS and throughput as independent parameters of the volume size provided.
optionRationales: Correct. The gp3 disconnects the provisioning of IOPS and throughput of volume size, unlike gp2, where the IOPS scale with (and are limited by) the size provided, allowing the team to get exactly the IOPS/throughput needed for a volume of 100 GB without oversupplying capacity.

Incorrect. 6.000 IOPS see stepping IOPS based on gp2 size, but would require payment for 2.000 GB Storage (20x the real need for 100 GB) only to unlock the IOPS — a expensive and wasteful way to get IOPS compared to the independent provisioning of gp3.

Incorrect. Volumes io2 (and io2 Block Express) are designed for the most demanding workloads in IOPS and have a cost per IOPS provided greater than gp3; for a requirement MODERADO of IOPS as 6.000 (right inside the ceiling of 16.000 IOPS of gp3), gp3 is the most economical choice — io2 Block Express is unnecessary here.

Incorrect. RAID 0 adds operational complexity (management of RAID in software, double failure risk since the failure of any volume loses all data) and doubles the paid storage (200 GB) without solving the underlying problem that the gp3 resolves natively and in a simpler way: uncouple IOPS size.

questions.text: A global application has users in EUA and in Asia. The application uses ElastiCache for Redis in us-east-1 for cache reference data read frequently (e.g. product catalogs) that rarely change. Users in Asia face higher latency in cache readings because each cache request crosses the Pacific to us-east-1. The team wants Asian users to read a Redis cache LOCAL, low latency, which remains automatically synchronized with us-east cache-1 (the writings continue to occur in us-east-1), without building custom replication logic.
options: Configure ElastiCache for Redis with Cluster Mode Enabled, with shards distributed between us-east-1 and ap-souteast-1
Configure ElastiCache for Redis Global Datastore with the us-east cluster-1 as a primary and a secondary cluster in an Asia-Pacific region (e.g. ap-souteast)-1)
Use Amazon CloudFront to cache the results of Redis consultations in border locations close to Asian users
Configure a second ElastiCache for Redis cluster independent in ap-souteast-1 and make the application write in AMBOS clusters in each cache update
questions.explanation: Correct. Global Datastore provides fully managed and fast (usually sub-second) replication between regions for Redis, allowing the LEITURAS of the secondary cluster be attended locally, with low latency, in the Asia-Pacific region, while the writings continue to be done in the primary cluster in us-east-1 and are propagated asynchronously.
questions.hint: Think of an ElastiCache for Redis feature designed specifically for quick and managed replication between regions, maintaining a primary for writing and secondary for local readings.
optionRationales: Correct. Global Datastore provides fully managed and fast (usually sub-second) replication between regions for Redis, allowing the LEITURAS of the secondary cluster be attended locally, with low latency, in the Asia-Pacific region, while the writings continue to be done in the primary cluster in us-east-1 and are propagated asynchronously.

Incorrect. ElastiCache's fashion cluster shards (and their replicas) must reside within a Multi-AZ deployment of a ONLY Region; ElastiCache's clusters cannot have shards covering Regions AWS DIFERENTES — replication between regions for ElastiCache Redis requires Global Datastore, not multi-region sharding within a cluster.

Incorrect. Constructing custom double writing logic in the application is operationally complex and prone to errors (to deal with partial faults, to ensure consistency between the two independent caches) — exactly what the managed replication of Global Datastore was designed to avoid.

Incorrect. CloudFront cached responses HTTP/HTTPS of a source server, not data from the gross Redis protocol; this would require building a layer of API HTTP in front of the Redis and would not provide the pattern of access to native reading and low latency of the Redis that the application currently uses directly.

questions.text: An analytics application stores files CSV large (several GB each) in S3, where each file contains many columns, but a typical query needs only 2-3 specific columns and a filter in one of them (e.g. 'lines where region = EU'). Currently, the application lowers the file CSV INTEIRO to obtain the necessary subset, consuming significant bandwidth and processing time for data that are immediately discarded. How the application can reduce the amount of data transferred from the S3 for these consultations?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to speed up file download CSV whole
Use Amazon S3 Select to recover only the required subset of data using a similar expression to SQL (SELECT specific columns WHERE region='EU') directly on the object S3
Convert files CSV for a compressed format (e.g. gzip) before storing them in S3
Use multipart download of S3 (Parallel byte-range GETs) to download the file faster
questions.explanation: Correct. S3 Select performs filtering/projecting of the LADO DO SERVIDOR within S3, returning by the network only the corresponding lines and the requested columns, drastically reducing the amount of data transferred and the necessary processing in the client, compared to downloading the entire object.
questions.hint: Think of a resource of the S3 which allows filtering and projection of columns, similar to SQL, directly on the stored object, before the transfer.
optionRationales: Correct. S3 Select performs filtering/projecting of the LADO DO SERVIDOR within S3, returning by the network only the corresponding lines and the requested columns, drastically reducing the amount of data transferred and the necessary processing in the client, compared to downloading the entire object.

Incorrect. Transfer Acceleration accelerates or CAMINHO OF REDE data transfer, but does not reduce the QUANTIDADE of transferred data — the entire file would still be downloaded, only potentially faster; does not resolve the main inefficiency of transferring unnecessary columns/lines.

Incorrect. Compression reduces the TAMANHO of the file (and therefore the time of file transfer INTEIRO), but the application would still need to download and decompress the file COMPLETO to extract the necessary subset — does not allow the selective recovery of specific columns/lines such as the S3 Select.

Incorrect. Parallel downloads by byte-range can speed up the obtaining of the object INTEIRO using multiple connections, but the application would still receive (and need to process/discard) all unnecessary columns and lines — improves the download speed of the complete file, not the SELETIVIDADE of which is recovered.

questions.text: A serverless application uses functions AWS Lambda which connect directly to a database Amazon RDS MySQL. During traffic peaks, the number of running environments Lambda competitors increases rapidly, each opening its own connection to the database, quickly exhausting the maximum limit of connections of the instance RDS and causing errors of 'too many connections', even if the actual load of queries in the bank is moderate (connections are open, but often become idle or are used briefly).
options: Do each function Lambda close your connection to the database immediately after each query, instead of reuse connections between invocations
Implement o Amazon RDS Proxy between functions Lambda and the instance RDS MySQL
Increase instance max_connections parameter RDS and scale to a larger instance class to support more connections
Configure Provided Competition no Lambda to limit the number of running environments during peaks
questions.explanation: Correct. RDS Proxy groups and multiplex connections, allowing many running environments Lambda share a smaller pool of real connections with the database, avoiding the exhaustion of connections during traffic peaks, while the database sees a stable and manageable number of connections, regardless of how many environments Lambda are competing in execution.
questions.hint: Think of a managed service positioned between an application and the database, designed specifically to group/multiplex many customer connections into a smaller number of real connections with the bank.
optionRationales: Correct. RDS Proxy groups and multiplex connections, allowing many running environments Lambda share a smaller pool of real connections with the database, avoiding the exhaustion of connections during traffic peaks, while the database sees a stable and manageable number of connections, regardless of how many environments Lambda are competing in execution.

Incorrect. Increasing max_connections (using a larger instance class with more memory) raises the TETO, but the competition of the Lambda can scale to very high numbers during peaks, potentially still exceeding a much higher limit, and each additional connection consumes memory/resources of the even idle bank — a more expensive and less scalable approach than pooling via RDS Proxy.

Incorrect. Provided Competition pre-initializes a number DEFINIDO of environments to eliminate cold start, but not LIMITA maximum competition during a peak (the Lambda still can scale beyond the provided value using on-demand environments) — does not directly solve a bank's connection exhaustion problem.

Incorrect. Although this may reduce the number of connections ABERTAS IN ONE DADO MOMENTO for warm invocations, in fact AUMENTARIA the rate of establishment of NOVAS connections (a relatively expensive operation) along the high volume of invocations during a peak, and does not fundamentally solve the problem of many environments Lambda competitors needing each of a connection simultaneously.

questions.text: A big data processing job performed in instances EC2 performs a 'shuffle' phase (similar to Hadoop/Spark shuffle) that records and reads large volumes of TEMPORARY intermediate data on local disk during processing — these temporary data are regulated in each job execution and need not persist beyond the job life cycle, but the shuffle phase is currently limited by I/O using volumes EBS gp3, delaying the completion time of the job.
options: Provide volumes EBS io2 Block Express for the shuffle data directory, maximizing the IOPS
Use instance types EC2 with NVMe-based Forum Store volumes (e.g. family instances 'd' or 'i' with local NVMe SSDs) for the shuffle temporary data directory
Increase settings of IOPS and throughput provided by volume EBS gp3 for maximum values
Use Amazon EFS for the shuffle data directory, mounted in all clusters instances
questions.explanation: Correct. Volumes Forum Store provide IOPS and very high throughput (often significantly higher than the EBS connected via network), ideal for temporary data ephemeral and critical in performance; as shuffle data do not need to persist beyond the job (are regulated in each execution), the ephemeral nature of the instance store (lost data when stopping/finalizing the instance) is an acceptable trade-off for substantial gain in I/O performance.
questions.hint: Think of a type of storage physically local to the instance, with IOPS/very high throughput, but whose data is lost if the instance is stopped or terminated — an acceptable trade-off for manageable data.
optionRationales: Correct. Volumes Forum Store provide IOPS and very high throughput (often significantly higher than the EBS connected via network), ideal for temporary data ephemeral and critical in performance; as shuffle data do not need to persist beyond the job (are regulated in each execution), the ephemeral nature of the instance store (lost data when stopping/finalizing the instance) is an acceptable trade-off for substantial gain in I/O performance.

Incorrect. Although the Io2 Block Express provides IOPS very high, it is a network-connected storage option, persistent and more expensive; for TEMPORARY data that are regulated in each execution and do not need durability, pay for the guarantees of persistence/durability of the io2 Block Express is an unnecessary cost, when the instance store NVMe (frequently included in the instance price) provides comparable or better gross I/O performance for this specific case.

Incorrect. EFS is a network file system with generally higher latency characteristics than local NVMe storage for high workloads IOPS, small files or random access typical of shuffle operations; use a shared network file system for temporary ephemeral data and by instance adds network overhead and unnecessary shared resource containment compared to the local instance store.

Incorrect. IOPS/provided gp3 throughput can help, but maximum gp3 (16.000 IOPS / 1.000 MB/s) is still a network-connected storage limit of EBS; for the performance of I/O absolutely higher for ephemeral data, the local instance store NVMe usually provides greater throughput/minor latency than even a gp3 volume provided to the maximum, without additional storage cost in instance types that include it.

questions.text: A company has one Amazon Kinesis Data Stream with multiple consumer applications (e.g. real-time analytics, fraud detection, archiving in S3), each one needing to process all the stream records independently. Using the standard consumer model (shared throughput), each consumer competes for the same throughput of reading of 2 MB/s per shard, and as more consumers were added, each began to present greater reading latency and occasional throttling, since the 2 Shared MB/s need to be divided among all consumers who read the same shard.
options: Register each consumer application using the Enhanced Fan-Out of Kinesis Data Streams
Change from Kinesis Data Streams for rows Amazon SQS standard, with one row per consumer application
Increase the number of shards in Kinesis Data Stream to provide more throughput total
Make every consumer application read a Kinesis Separated Data Stream with a function Lambda replicating original stream records for each specific consumer stream
questions.explanation: Right. Enhanced Fan-Out provides every registered consumer with their Dedicated Throughput of 2 MB/s POR SHARD (using push via HTTP/2 with SubscribeToShard), eliminating throughput containment among consumers and providing each user with low latency records (~70ms), regardless of how many other consumers are also reading from the stream.
questions.hint: Think of a resource of the Kinesis Data Streams that provides each registered consumer application with its own dedicated delivery channel by shard, instead of a shared throughput among all consumers.
optionRationales: Right. Enhanced Fan-Out provides every registered consumer with their Dedicated Throughput of 2 MB/s POR SHARD (using push via HTTP/2 with SubscribeToShard), eliminating throughput containment among consumers and providing each user with low latency records (~70ms), regardless of how many other consumers are also reading from the stream.

Incorrect. Increasing the number of shards increases the throughput TOTAL of the STREAM (more shards = more total allocations of 2 MB/s), but the readthroughput of 2 MB/s of CADA individual shard AINDA is shared among all consumers who read from it in the standard model — does not give each CONSUMIDOR its own throughput dedicated by shard; only adds more shards to divide among consumers.

Incorrect. Build a custom replication/fan-out mechanism via Lambda adds operational complexity, additional latency (records need first to be processed by Lambda of replication) and cost, when Enhanced Fan-Out provides native dedicated consumer throughput without replicating data on separate streams.

Incorrect. SQS, by design, they usually deliver each message to a consumer of a given row (not to multiple independent consumer applications that need VER all records); get 'multiple independent consumers, each selling all records' with SQS would require multiple rows (e.g. via fan-out of SNS), a different architecture from simply registering enhanced fan-out consumers on a stream Kinesis existing.

questions.text: A table DynamoDB store user activity data, partitioned by UserId. A marketing campaign causes a sudden and massive increase in read/write traffic to a small number of UserIds 'celebrity' (viral content), far exceeding the throughput per partition that would normally be allocated based on the uniform distribution of the table's total provided capacity. Although the table as a whole have sufficient provided capacity, requests for these specific 'hot' partitions are undergoing throttling.
options: Change the table to use a Local Secondary Index (LSI) to distribute UserId 'hot' data among multiple partitions
Enable DynamoDB Streams to detect throttling requests and automatically repeat them with exponential backoff via a function Lambda

Trust in Adaptive Capacity of DynamoDB, which automatically and rapidly increases the throughput capacity allocated to specific high-traffic partitions, relocating unused capacity from the table's total provided capacity to the most demanding partitions
Increase manually WCU/RCU total provided from table in 10x to ensure that each partition individually has sufficient allocated capacity
questions.explanation: Correct. Adaptive Capacity isolates and automatically adjusts the ability of 'hot' partitions without manual intervention, mitigating the throttling caused by unequal access patterns; the team should also consider improving the cardinality design of the partition key in the long term, but Adaptive Capacity solves the immediate problem of throttling.
questions.hint: Think of an automatic resource of DynamoDB which reacts to unequal access patterns between partitions, relocating capacity dynamically without manual intervention.
optionRationales: Correct. Adaptive Capacity isolates and automatically adjusts the ability of 'hot' partitions without manual intervention, mitigating the throttling caused by unequal access patterns; the team should also consider improving the cardinality design of the partition key in the long term, but Adaptive Capacity solves the immediate problem of throttling.

Incorrect. DynamoDB divides the provided capacity in a relatively uniform way between the partitions on a total basis; increase the provided capacity TOTAL in 10x would be extremely expensive and AINDA could not be enough for a single 'celebrity' partition dealing with a disproportionate portion of traffic, since the calculated fraction of each partition would still be a fraction of the total — a costly and imprecise way to solve a hot-spot by partition.

Incorrect. LSIs share the same partition key in the base table; they do not redistribute data/traffic from a single 'hot' partition key between multiple partitions — the problem of hot partition persists independently of defined LSIs.

Incorrect. Repeating requests with throttling (even with backoff) does not increase the underlying throughput capacity available for the hot partition; it would only delay/send the same excessive demand against the same restricted partition capacity, possibly worsening latency without solving the root throughput restriction.

questions.text: A financial trading platform requires a load balancer able to handle millions of requests per second with ultra low and consistent latency (sub-millisecond additional latency), preserve the client's original IP address natively for audit/compliance downstream purposes, and support static IP addresses by AZ (or Elastic IP assignment) to allow allow allow-listing by external counterparts. load balancer should be used?
options: Network Load Balancer (NLB), operating in the Layer 4
Amazon CloudFront, with the servers of the trading platform as origin
Classic Load Balancer (CLB)
Application Load Balancer (ALB), operating in the Layer 7
questions.explanation: Correct. NLB was designed to deal with millions of requests per second with ultra low and consistent latency, natively preserves the client's home IP address (visible for backend targets without proxy protocol parsing, when targets are properly registered) and supports the assignment of a static IP (or Elastic IP) by sub-network/AZ — meeting all declared requirements for this critical financial latency and throughput workload.
questions.hint: Think of what kind of load balancer operates on the transport layer (Cover 4), natively preserving the IP of origin and supporting static IPs by sub-network.
optionRationales: Correct. NLB was designed to deal with millions of requests per second with ultra low and consistent latency, natively preserves the client's home IP address (visible for backend targets without proxy protocol parsing, when targets are properly registered) and supports the assignment of a static IP (or Elastic IP) by sub-network/AZ — meeting all declared requirements for this critical financial latency and throughput workload.

Incorrect. ALB Provides Advanced Layer Resources 7 (path/host based router, native integration with WAF), but usually has higher latency overhead by requisition than the NLB due to layer processing 7, and does not support static IP/Elastic IP allocation by AZ in the same way as the NLB — for declared ultra-low latency requirements, millions of RPS and static IP, NLB is more suitable.

Incorrect. CLB is a kind of load balancer legacy, with lower maximum throughput/scaling characteristics and less modern features compared to NLB/ALB; a AWS recommends NLB or ALB for new workloads, and the CLB does not provide the same static IP support or ultra-low ultra-high-scale latency as the NLB.

Incorrect. CloudFront is a CDN focusing on HTTP/HTTPS, designed for cache and content acceleration; the traffic of a financial trading platform (often custom protocols based on TCP, matching orders in real time) is not suitable for a CDN cached HTTP, and the CloudFront does not provide the same IP preservation characteristics of origin in Layer 4 and static IP by AZ that NLB.

questions.text: A company carries out two separate workloads in the EC2: a Charge A is a memory database (style) SAP HANA or based on Redis) which maintains a very large dataset entirely on RAM and performs relatively simple operations on it, demanding a ALTA VCPU memory report. Load B is a batch video transcoding pipeline, strongly limited by CPU, performing intensive computing on relatively small blocks of data, requiring a ALTA VCPU relationship by memory. Currently, both perform in General Purpose instances of the M family, which the team suspects is not ideal at cost for the resource profile of either of the two.
options: Move A Load to Memory Optimized instances (e.g., R or X family, which provide high memory/vCPU ratio) and B Load to Computer Optimized instances (e.g., C family, which provide high vCPU/memory ratio)
Keep both loads in General Purpose (family M) instances, but increase the size of the instance (scaling vertically) for both
Move both loads to Accelerated Computing instances (e.g. P or G family) with GPUs to download processing
Move both loads to Storage Optimized instances (e.g. family I), which provide high performance local NVMe storage for demanding I/O workloads
questions.explanation: Correct. Align the instance family of each workload with its requirement of dominant recourse (limited by memory vs. limited by CPU) ensures that the resources provided correspond to the actual use, avoiding paying for underutilized vCPUs (Load A in General Purpose) or underutilized memory (Load B in General Purpose)).
questions.hint: Think of which families of instance EC2 offer a memory/vCPU ratio above or below the average of the General Purpose family, and how this aligns with the resource gargalo of each workload.
optionRationales: Correct. Align the instance family of each workload with its requirement of dominant recourse (limited by memory vs. limited by CPU) ensures that the resources provided correspond to the actual use, avoiding paying for underutilized vCPUs (Load A in General Purpose) or underutilized memory (Load B in General Purpose)).

Incorrect. Storage Optimized instances are designed for workloads that need very high local disk I/O and low latency (e.g.: banks) NoSQL, data storage with local storage); none of the loads described are primarily limited by I/O of storage (Load A is limited by memory, Load B by CPU) — this family of instance does not align with the real gargalo of either of the two.

Incorrect. Simply scale vertically instances General Purpose increases both vCPU and memory proportionally (in the fixed relation of the M family); this does not change the underlying misalignment between the resource profile of each workload (intensive in memory vs. intensive in CPU) and the relationship of the family of instance — it would still result in paying for underutilized resources in one dimension for each load.

Incorrect. Accelerated Computing instances are designed for workloads that can take advantage of acceleration by GPU/FPGA (e.g. ML training, certain video encodings supported by GPU); however, the scenario does not indicate that neither of the two loads was designed to use acceleration by GPU (a Load A is a memory database; the transcoding of Load B may or may not support encoding by GPU) — introduce instances with GPU without confirmed software support for acceleration adds cost without guaranteed benefit, and does not directly address memory relationship misalignment/CPU declared.

questions.text: A company serves a web application through CloudFront, with text-based assets (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, answers from API in JSON) representing a significant portion of the total number of bytes transferred to end users. The source server currently does not compress these responses, and the team wants to reduce the size of the data transferred to end users (improve page loading times, especially in slower connections) without modifying the source server to add compression logic.
options: Configure the source server to compress the responses using Gzip before sending them to CloudFront
Use Lambda@Edge to compress the bodies of the responses in the viewer response event before returning them to customers
Enable the automatic compression feature of the CloudFront (Compress Objects Automatically) in relevant behavior caches
Increase TTL Cache from CloudFront for these objects, reducing the number of times that need to be searched and transferred
questions.explanation: Correct. CloudFront can automatically compress text-based eligible content (e.g. text/html, text/css, application/javascript, application/json) using Gzip or Brotli (based on the client's Accept-Encoding header) before serving it from the cache/board, reducing the bytes transferred to compatible customers without requiring any change in the source server.
questions.hint: Think of a native resource of CloudFront which reduces the text-based content size before delivery without requiring any change in origin.
optionRationales: Correct. CloudFront can automatically compress text-based eligible content (e.g. text/html, text/css, application/javascript, application/json) using Gzip or Brotli (based on the client's Accept-Encoding header) before serving it from the cache/board, reducing the bytes transferred to compatible customers without requiring any change in the source server.

Incorrect. Although compression on the origin side is also a valid approach, the scenario specifies that the team wants to avoid modifying the source server; automatic compression of the source server; CloudFront achieves the same benefit for the end user (compressed answers) without requiring changes in origin, being the most appropriate option to the declared restriction.

Incorrect. Increase or TTL reduces the FREQUENCY with which objects are searched/transferred from the origin (less cache masses), but does not reduce the TAMANHO of each individual response given to end users — is a different optimization (reducing the frequency of transfer) of the reduction of the TAMANHO transfer (compression)).

Incorrect. Although technically possible, implement custom compression logic via Lambda@Edge adds cost/overhead execution of Lambda by operational complexity and requisition, when the native automatic compression feature of the CloudFront already provides this functionality (Gzip/Brotli, sensitive to content-type and Accept-Encoding) without any custom code.

questions.text: A company performs analytical consultations in a cluster Amazon Redshift against a large table 'sales_fact' (billions of lines) which is often united (JOIN) to a lower table 'dim_store' by 'store_id', and queries frequently filter/make range scan by 'sale_date'. The query performance is poor — JOINS between sales_fact and dim_store cause significant data movement (redistribution) between computation nodes during execution, and date interval filters run much more data blocks than necessary.
options: Set the DISTSTYLE of 'sales_fact' as KEY in 'store_id' (co-location with 'dim_store', which you can use ALL or also be distributed by the same join key), and define a SORTKEY in 'sale_date' for 'sales_fact'
Increase the number of cluster nodes (add more computation nodes) to parallelize the operations of JOIN and filter between more knots
Set the DISTSTYLE as EVEN for both tables, ensuring a perfectly balanced data distribution between all computational nodes
Create a Global Secondary Index in 'store_id' and 'sale_date' to speed up both the JOIN as the date filter
questions.explanation: Correct. Distributing both tables by the join key ('store_id') ensures that the corresponding lines are co-located in the same computational node, eliminating the redistribution of data between us during the JOIN; sort by 'sale_date' allows the map areas of Redshift ignore blocks outside the date range consulted, drastically reducing I/O for queries filtered by date.
questions.hint: Think of two distinct mechanisms of the Redshift: one that controls where the lines in each table are physically stored between the nodes (for JOINs), and another that controls the physical order of the lines within each node (for interval filters)).
optionRationales: Correct. Distributing both tables by the join key ('store_id') ensures that the corresponding lines are co-located in the same computational node, eliminating the redistribution of data between us during the JOIN; sort by 'sale_date' allows the map areas of Redshift ignore blocks outside the date range consulted, drastically reducing I/O for queries filtered by date.

Incorrect. The distribution EVEN distributes round-robin lines, regardless of any column value, which is good for general storage balancing, but does NOT co-location matching join keys between tables — JOINs between tables distributed as EVEN in 'store_id' would still require significant redistribution of data between us during execution.

Incorrect. Global Secondary Index is a concept of DynamoDB, not Redshift; the mechanisms of optimization of performance of the Redshift for these access patterns are DISTKEY/DISTSTYLE (for joint co-location) and SORTKEY (for block removal via zone maps in interval filters), not secondary indexes.

Incorrect. Add more we increase the overall parallel processing capacity, but if the DISTSTYLE does not co-localize join keys, MAIS We can actually mean MAIS data redistribution traffic between us during the JOIN (more network jumps among more us); this does not solve the fundamental problem of data layout that causes unnecessary block redistribution and scans.

questions.text: A database OLTP of critical mission Amazon RDS for Oracle processes a consistently very high volume of transactions (thousands of IOPS supported, 24/7) with strict performance requirements of consistent and predictable I/O and minimum latency variance — even short falls in IOPS available during peak periods cause transaction timeouts at the application level. The team is evaluating storage options EBS for this instance RDS.
options: Use General Purpose Storage SSD (gp3) and provide maximum of IOPS available (16.000)
Use Storage Provided IOPS SSD (i1 or i2) for the instance RDS, providing IOPS to meet (with margin) the sustained requirement of tens of thousands IOPS
Use Magnetic (standard) storage for cost saving, since the RDS will automatically store the hot cache data in memory to compensate for the slower disk
Enable Multi-AZ of RDS to distribute the I/O load between the primary instance and the standby
questions.explanation: Correct. The Storage Provided IOPS is designed to provide performance of IOPS consistent and predictable, with minimal latency variance, specifically for I/O intensive transactional workloads and latency sensitive, where consistent performance under high sustained load is critical — exactly the requirements of this bench OLTP.
questions.hint: Think about what storage class EBS of the RDS is designed specifically to provide IOPS consistent and predictable, with minimum latency variance, for very demanding transactional loads.
optionRationales: Correct. The Storage Provided IOPS is designed to provide performance of IOPS consistent and predictable, with minimal latency variance, specifically for I/O intensive transactional workloads and latency sensitive, where consistent performance under high sustained load is critical — exactly the requirements of this bench OLTP.

Incorrect. IOPS provided for in gp3 (16.000) can be enough for 'thousands of tens' only at the bottom end, and more importantly, gp3 is designed for a wide range of workloads with 'consistent baseline performance', but usually positioned for transactional loads with requirements MODERADOS Of I/O; for loads OLTP more demanding, sensitive to latency variance, with IOPS very high sustained, the Provisioned IOPS (io1/io2) is the storage class recommended by AWS specifically for consistency under this load.

Incorrect. Magnetic storage provides IOPS more BAIXAS and less consistent between storage options of RDS, completely inadequate for a workload that requires tens of thousands of IOPS sustained with minimum latency variance; RDS uses a cache buffer, but a high-supported transactional load IOPS still generate substantial disk I/O that magnetic storage cannot support.

Incorrect. In the Multi-AZ standard of RDS, the standby instance is NOT used to meet reading or writing traffic (it is a synchronous replica only to failover); it does not distribute or increase the I/O capacity available for the primary instance to deal with the volume of transactions — the Multi-AZ addresses availability/durability, not throughput/I/O consistency.

questions.text: A company has a function AWS Lambda based on Java (using a large dependency framework, such as Spring Boot) that meets synchronous requests via API Gateway. Cold starts of this function take several seconds (due to initialization of the JVM and the framework), causing unacceptable latency peaks for end users during scale-out events or after periods of inactivity. The team wants to drastically reduce the latency of cold start specifically for this Java function, ideally without paying for Provided Competition to keep constantly 'heated environments'.
options: Enable AWS Lambda SnapStart for Java function
Rewrite the function in another runtime (e.g., Node.js), which has faster cold startups
Configure Reserved Competition for the function to ensure available running slots
Increase the function memory allocation to the maximum, to speed up the initialization time of the JVM
questions.explanation: Correct. SnapStart pre-initializes the function (executing all booting, including the start of the JVM and the loading of the framework) UMA VEZ when a new version is published, it takes a snapshot of the memory state/disco of the running environment already initialized and stores it in cache; in subsequent cold start, the Lambda resumes from this snapshot in cache instead of running zero booting, reducing cold start latency from seconds to typically sub-second, without the continuous cost of Provided Competition.
questions.hint: Think of a resource of the Lambda which takes a snapshot of the running environment already fully initialized and reuses it in subsequent cold start, without continuous cost of pre-heated capacity.
optionRationales: Correct. SnapStart pre-initializes the function (executing all booting, including the start of the JVM and the loading of the framework) UMA VEZ when a new version is published, it takes a snapshot of the memory state/disco of the running environment already initialized and stores it in cache; in subsequent cold start, the Lambda resumes from this snapshot in cache instead of running zero booting, reducing cold start latency from seconds to typically sub-second, without the continuous cost of Provided Competition.

Incorrect. Increase memory (and CPU (proportional) may speed up the initialisation of the JVM and the loading of classes, but for a heavy application in framework (e.g. Spring Boot) with cold starts of several seconds, this usually brings only marginal improvement — does not fundamentally eliminate the repeated initialization work of the way the snapshot-and-retread approach of SnapStart does.

Incorrect. Rewriting in another language is a considerable effort (reimplementing business logic, potentially losing access to Java-specific libraries/frameworks on which the team depends) and is not an equivalent solution when the requirement is to reduce cold start 'specifically for this Java function' — SnapStart resolves the Java-specific cold start problem directly, without requiring rewriting.

Incorrect. Reserved Competition guarantees a RENTAL/TETO of competition for the function (avoiding that it is damaged by other functions, and avoiding that it exceeds a limit), but DO NOT pre-initialize nor 'heat' running environments — does not solve the latency of cold start in any way.

questions.text: A database Amazon Aurora MySQL supports both an application OLTP high volume (many small and fast transactional consultations) QUANTO occasional analytical/report consultations that perform whole table aggregations (ex.: SUM/COUNT/AVG in hundreds of millions of lines). These analytical queries currently take a long time because they are processed entirely by the computer layer of the bank instance (single-threaded execution by query, scanning large volumes of data by buffer pool), and during these queries, the CPU of the instance becomes a gargalo, also impacting the responsiveness of the load OLTP.
options: Migrate the analytical load to Amazon Redshift Spectrum, consulting the data of the Aurora directly via federated consultations
Add a Global Secondary Index covering columns used in analytical aggregations
Enable Aurora Parallel Query for these analytical consultations in the cluster Aurora MySQL
Create a read replica and run all the analytical queries against it instead of the primary
questions.explanation: Correct. Parallel Query pushes filtering and aggregation operations to the distributed storage layer and multi-node Aurora, performing parts of the parallel query on many storage nodes (instead of the single instance computing layer), dramatically accelerating large scans/analytical aggregations and reducing the load of CPU in the computation layer that would otherwise impact the performance of the consultations OLTP competitors.
questions.hint: Think of a resource of the Aurora which distributes the scan/aggregation work of a query to the multi-no storage layer, instead of fully processing it in the computer instance.
optionRationales: Correct. Parallel Query pushes filtering and aggregation operations to the distributed storage layer and multi-node Aurora, performing parts of the parallel query on many storage nodes (instead of the single instance computing layer), dramatically accelerating large scans/analytical aggregations and reducing the load of CPU in the computation layer that would otherwise impact the performance of the consultations OLTP competitors.

Incorrect. Download the analytical queries for a read replica isolates its impact on the load OLTP of the primary, but the analytical consultations themselves AINDA would be slow in replica (even single instance execution, limited by the computation layer, for large aggregations) — isolates the impact, but does not accelerate the analytical queries themselves, as parallelism of the parallel Query layer does.

Incorrect. Global Secondary Index is a concept of DynamoDB; no Aurora MySQL, the equivalent would be a secondary index, which PODE help certain query patterns, but whole table aggregations over hundreds of millions of lines (SUM/COUNT/AVG without selective filter) often still require scanning most/all lines regardless of indexing — Parallel Query's parallel scan of the storage layer approaches this large scan scenario more directly than indexing.

Incorrect. Although the Redshift can be a long-term data storage solution, Redshift Spectrum consults data in S3 (not directly in the storage of Aurora), therefore this would require a step of ETL/export to take the data from Aurora to S3 First — a much larger architectural change than enabling a native resource to be Aurora (Parallel Query) designed specifically to speed up large analytical queries against existing data in Aurora, on-site.

questions.text: A company has a single connection AWS Direct Connect of 10 Gbps between your data center and the AWS, used for a high throughput data replication workload. Periodically, during intensive replication windows, demand exceeds 10 Gbps available. The team wants to increase the aggregate bandwidth available in MESMA location of Direct Connect, holding a single session BGP and a unique logical interface for configuration and router purposes.
options: Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN as additional connection to add bandwidth over connection Direct Connect existing
Request AWS the upgrade of the connection door speed Direct Connect existing, without providing additional physical connections
Provide additional connections to AWS Direct Connect in the same location and group them in a Link Aggregation Group (LAG)
Provide a second connection Direct Connect independent in another location and set up ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) between the two connections
questions.explanation: Right. LAG aggregate multiple physical connections of the Direct Connect (of the same capacity, on the same device/location as the Direct Connect) in a single logical interface, adding the aggregate bandwidth and presenting a single session BGP and customer routing configuration — meeting exactly the operational simplicity requirement with greater throughput.
questions.hint: Think of what resource the Direct Connect allows you to combine multiple physical connections in the same location in a single logical interface with a single session BGP.
optionRationales: Right. LAG aggregate multiple physical connections of the Direct Connect (of the same capacity, on the same device/location as the Direct Connect) in a single logical interface, adding the aggregate bandwidth and presenting a single session BGP and customer routing configuration — meeting exactly the operational simplicity requirement with greater throughput.

Incorrect. ECMP between independent connections can add bandwidth and provide geographic redundancy, but requires managing two sessions BGP and separate routing configurations — more complexity than the 'single logical interface' requirement. To combine NA connections MESMA location in a single interface, LAG is the correct remedy.

Incorrect. Direct Connect is linked to the physical interconnection established at the partner location/Direct Connect. It is not possible simply to 'increase' the capacity of an existing physical connection via support request — it is necessary to provide a new connection of greater capacity (with exchange/downtime) or add additional connections via LAG.

Incorrect. Site-to-Site VPN traffics through the public internet and has throughput by tunnel typically limited to about 1,25 Gbps, with latency characteristics distinct from Direct Connect dedicated. It is suitable as backup/failover connectivity, not as a mechanism to linearly add bandwidth to a connection Direct Connect in a single logical interface.

questions.text: An application needs to download a single very large object (a machine learning model file from 50 GB) of the Amazon S3 The team observed that a request for GET unique and sequential reaches a throughput plateau well below the network bandwidth available, because a single connection TCP cannot fully use this capability. They want to parallel download of this ONE object in multiple connections to maximize total throughput.
options: Issue multiple requests GET competitors using the header HTTP 'Range' to download different bytes intervals of the same object in parallel, rebuilding the file locally
Use S3 Multipart Upload to forward the object in smaller parts and then download each part separately
Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to this download
Migrate the instance EC2 that performs the download for a type of instance with Enhanced Networking, increasing the network capacity available
questions.explanation: Correct. Requirements GET parallel with 'Range' (byte-range fetches) allow the application to use multiple connections TCP simultaneously for different parts of the same object, adding the throughput of these connections and significantly accelerating the download of a large object compared to a single GET sequential.
questions.hint: Consider how to split the download of a single large file into multiple requests HTTP competitors operating on different parts of the same object.
optionRationales: Correct. Requirements GET parallel with 'Range' (byte-range fetches) allow the application to use multiple connections TCP simultaneously for different parts of the same object, adding the throughput of these connections and significantly accelerating the download of a large object compared to a single GET sequential.

Incorrect. Transfer Acceleration optimizes the network path via edge locations of the CloudFront, mainly for geographically distant customers. It does not, by itself, parallel the download of a ONE object in multiple connections — a request GET only would remain limited by the throughput features of a single connection.

Incorrect. Multipart Upload is a mechanism of UPLOAD for creating objects; does not apply to DOWNLOAD of an existing object. 50 GB only to allow parallel download of the parts would be extremely costly and inefficient in terms of storage and transfer.

Incorrect. Enhanced Networking increases the capacity ceiling of the instance network interface, but a single connection TCP (a single request GET) typically can't saturate even a moderate network interface due to window/congestion control features of the TCP in long distances — without parallelizing the download itself, more network capacity available is not used.

questions.text: A manufacturing industry executes real-time equipment control software in an on-premises factory that requires latency of milliseconds of single digit for local sensors and actuators — latency even of tens of milliseconds for a region AWS is unacceptable for this control loop. The company wishes to use the MESMAS APIs, services (such as Amazon EC2, Amazon EBS, Amazon ECS) and operational tools (such as AWS CloudFormation, IAM) which already uses in the cloud, with the ability to integrate this on-premises infrastructure into a VPC in the Region AWS nearest.
options: Implement control software in the Region AWS nearest and connect via AWS Direct Connect to obtain the lowest possible latency
Use AWS Wavelength to implement the closest application to the factory
Implant AWS Outposts (rack or server) in the factory installation itself
Use AWS Local Zones, by implementing resources in the Local Zone closest to the factory
questions.explanation: Correct. AWS Outposts it brings infrastructure designed by the AWS, with native services (EC2, EBS, ECS/EKS, etc.) and the same APIs/control tools used in the Regions, directly within the customer's on-premises installation — providing local computing with latency of milliseconds of single digit for latency-sensitive workloads, while integrating into a VPC in the Region AWS anchor for hybrid connectivity and consistent operations.
questions.hint: The key requirement is to have infrastructure AWS native physically within the factory itself, not only geographically close.
optionRationales: Correct. AWS Outposts it brings infrastructure designed by the AWS, with native services (EC2, EBS, ECS/EKS, etc.) and the same APIs/control tools used in the Regions, directly within the customer's on-premises installation — providing local computing with latency of milliseconds of single digit for latency-sensitive workloads, while integrating into a VPC in the Region AWS anchor for hybrid connectivity and consistent operations.

Incorrect. Even with Direct Connect, the latency between the factory floor and the data centers of a region AWS (potentially hundreds of km away) involves propagation delay which typically exceeds much of the milliseconds of single digit. Direct Connect improves latency predictability and bandwidth compared to the internet, but does not make regional latency comparable to a truly LOCAL on-premises.

Incorrect. AWS Wavelength incorporates computing and storage infrastructure AWS within networks 5G of telecommunications operators, specifically for mobile applications/ ultra-low latency edge accessed by devices via 5G — not designed to extend the infrastructure AWS within an on-premises customer installation.

Incorrect. AWS Local Zones are infrastructure deployments AWS in large metropolitan areas, extending a region to closer to population/industrial centers, but still are facilities operated by the AWS in a metropolitan area (not within the customer's own factory). They reduce latency compared to a distant region, but do not provide the placement within the installation that milliseconds control loops of single digit require — the Outposts puts the infrastructure physically inside the customer's installation.

questions.text: An application uses Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in 'Cluster Mode Disabled' mode (a single shard with a primary node). The data set fits comfortably into the memory of a single node, and the volume of writing is low to moderate, but the traffic of LEITURA has grown substantially and is now the limiting factor — network capacity/CPU of the primary node to answer readings is running out, even if the size of the dataset and the writing throughput do not require partitioning.
options: Enable Cluster Mode (Cluster Mode Enabled) with multiple shards to distribute the reading load
Increase the node type to the largest available size (vertical scaling) to support more reading traffic in the single primary node

Add Read Replicas to existing replication group (keeping 'Cluster Mode Disabled') and configure the application to distribute traffic from LEITURA among the replicas, keeping the writings directed to the primary
Implement o Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of ElastiCache for Redis to reduce reading load on Redis
questions.explanation: As the gargalo is specifically capable of LEITURA (not dataset size or write throughput), add read replicas to MESMO shard provides additional reading endpoints to horizontally scale the readthroughput without the additional complexity of Cluster Mode (data partition via hash slots), which would only be required if the dataset size or writethroughput were the restriction.
questions.hint: Identify whether the problem is related to data size/write (which would require partitioning) or only to reading capacity (which can be scaled horizontally without partitioning)).
optionRationales: As the gargalo is specifically capable of LEITURA (not dataset size or write throughput), add read replicas to MESMO shard provides additional reading endpoints to horizontally scale the readthroughput without the additional complexity of Cluster Mode (data partition via hash slots), which would only be required if the dataset size or writethroughput were the restriction.

Incorrect. Enable Cluster Mode and partition into shards is the correct tool when the TAMANHO DO DATASET or the throughput of ESCRITA exceeds the capacity of a single node (requiring data partitioning). Here the dataset fits comfortably into a node and the volume of writing is moderate — partitioning adds unnecessary complexity (management of hash slots) when simply adding read replicas to the existing shard resolves directly the reading gargal described.

Incorrect. Vertical scaling can increase capacity to a certain point, but has a rigid roof (the largest type of knot available) and concentrates TODO the reading traffic and written in a single node; does not provide the scaling HORIZONTAL reading (multiple endpoints) that read replies offer, nor diverts primary readings.

Incorrect. DAX is a specific cache layer for tables of Amazon DynamoDB (using the API of the DynamoDB); is not a cache layer that is positioned in front of ElastiCache for Redis — this combination is not a valid architecture standard in AWS.

questions.text: A company has a Network Load Balancer (NLB) with target groups containing instances EC2 registered in 3 Availability zones, but with unequal number of healthy targets per AZ (AZ-A has 1 instance, AZ-B has 1 instance, AZ-C has 4 insti tutions), due to the way in which Auto Scaling Group launched the instances. With the standard configuration of the NLB (Cross-Zone Load Balancing disabled), each node load balancer in an AZ distributes traffic only between targets DAQUELA AZ, making the unique instances of AZ-A and AZ-B each receive as much traffic as the 4 fora AZ-C receive COMBINADAS — causing severe overload in the AZ-A and AZ-B.
options: Manually adjust Auto Scaling Group to always ensure the exact same number of instances in each AZ
Configure Target Tracking Policies Auto Scaling based on the AZ request count, climbing AZ-A and AZ-B independently
Replace Network Load Balancer by one Application Load Balancer, which always distributes equally among all targets regardless of AZ
Enable Cross-Zone Load Balancing no NLB and in their target groups
questions.explanation: With Cross-Zone Load Balancing enabled, each node of load balancer distributes the traffic received between the targets registered in TODAS enabled AZs (not just in their own AZ), achieving a balanced distribution by TARGET regardless of how targets are distributed among AZs. The trade-off is that data transfer charges between AZs can be applied when traffic is sent to a different AZ target than the one that received the request..
questions.hint: Think about what Network configuration Load Balancer determines whether each balancer node distributes traffic only to local AZ targets or to all registered targets.
optionRationales: With Cross-Zone Load Balancing enabled, each node of load balancer distributes the traffic received between the targets registered in TODAS enabled AZs (not just in their own AZ), achieving a balanced distribution by TARGET regardless of how targets are distributed among AZs. The trade-off is that data transfer charges between AZs can be applied when traffic is sent to a different AZ target than the one that received the request..

Incorrect. Although balancing the NUMBER of instances by AZ helps to mitigate this specific imbalance under the behavior of the FATHER (disabled cross-zone), it is a manual and fragile solution for something that Cross-Zone Load Balancing resolves directly and automatically, even with unequal target counts between AZs — ASGs may naturally present temporary imbalances during staging and replacement events.

Incorrect. Although the ALB have Cross-Zone Load Balancing enabled by default (and cannot be disabled), change the TIPO of load balancer is a much larger architectural change than simply enabling a configuration option in NLB existing — and could mean losing Layer features 4 of the NLB (as static IPs and ultra low latency) that may be needed in other parts of architecture.

Incorrect. This is an overly complex and customised approach to solving a load distribution problem that Cross-Zone Load Balancing solves with a single configuration option. AZ-directed scaling policies based on requisition count are not a standard configuration of ASG and would require substantial custom tools.

questions.text: A table of the Amazon DynamoDB attends to a workload with highly predictable daily traffic pattern: low traffic during the morning, gradual increase during business hours until a well-known peak, and gradual drop after — this pattern is repeated daily with small variations. The team wants the most economic capacity mode for this predictable and gradual pattern, maintaining the automatic capacity adjustment according to the daily standard, without manual intervention.
options: Use capacity mode Provided with capacity FIXA defined in the value of the daily peak, without Auto Scaling
Use the On-Demand capability mode, which automatically scales to any level of traffic without needing configuration
Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to absorb traffic peaks, allowing the base table to use minimum provided capacity throughout the year
Use the Provisioned mode with AWS Implementation Auto Scaling set to table
questions.explanation: Right. For a traffic pattern ALTAMENTE PREVIOUS and gradually variable, the provided mode (which has cost per unit of capacity lower than On-Demand) combined with Auto Scaling (adjusting WCU/RCU provided based on usage targets, following the daily ramp) offers the most economical option, since the price award of On-Demand (designed for unpredictable traffic/with peaks) is not necessary when the pattern is well understood and gradual.
questions.hint: Compare the cost per unit of capacity between modes and consider what automatically accompanies a gradual and predictable traffic pattern without paying the unpredictability award.
optionRationales: Right. For a traffic pattern ALTAMENTE PREVIOUS and gradually variable, the provided mode (which has cost per unit of capacity lower than On-Demand) combined with Auto Scaling (adjusting WCU/RCU provided based on usage targets, following the daily ramp) offers the most economical option, since the price award of On-Demand (designed for unpredictable traffic/with peaks) is not necessary when the pattern is well understood and gradual.

Incorrect.
